papers.title: A Positive Turn: Coupled Quintessence and Cosmological Neutrino Masses
papers.authors: Tian-Nuo Li, William Giarè, Guo-Hong Du, Eleonora Di Valentino, Luis A. Anchordoqui, Shao-Jiang Wang, Xin Zhang, Rong-Gen Cai
papers.abstract: In $\Lambda$CDM, the CMB and DESI BAO upper limits on the total neutrino mass are in tension with the lower bounds from oscillation experiments, and analyses allowing negative effective masses favor negative values. We investigate whether a coupled quintessence (CQ) model in which dark matter interacts with a canonical scalar field $\phi$ through an exponential mass coupling $m_{\rm c}(\phi)\propto e^{-\beta\phi/M_{\rm Pl}}$ can alleviate this tension. Combining CMB, DESI, and supernova data, we find that CQ yields neutrino-mass constraints comparable to those obtained in CPL and consistent with oscillation experiments within $2\sigma$ for normal ordering, without requiring the scalar-field equation of state to cross the phantom divide. We further show that it alleviates the tension more effectively than alternative interacting dark energy models that instead favor more negative effective masses. This comparison shows that whether dark sector interactions can relax neutrino mass bounds ultimately depends on the interplay of their effects on primary CMB anisotropies, geometry, growth, and lensing.

conclusions: **Restoring consistency with neutrino oscillations**: For the joint CMB + DESI DR2 + DES-Dovekie dataset, coupled quintessence (CQ) yields $\sum m_{\nu,\mathrm{eff}} = -0.017^{+0.041}_{-0.063}\ \mathrm{eV}$, with profile likelihood $\Delta\chi^2 < 3.84$ and $9.5\%$ of the posterior above the normal ordering benchmark ($0.06\ \mathrm{eV}$), easing the $>3\sigma$ tension in $\Lambda$CDM down to within $2\sigma$.

**Competitive with CPL without phantom crossing**: CQ achieves neutrino mass limits comparable to the phenomenological CPL ($w_0, w_a$) parametrization (which yields $\sum m_{\nu,\mathrm{eff}} = -0.005^{+0.043}_{-0.059}\ \mathrm{eV}$) through a physical, single canonical scalar field without requiring the equation of state to cross the phantom divide ($w < -1$).

**Coupling parameters and fit improvement**: The joint data prefer energy transfer from cold dark matter to dark energy with coupling strength $\beta = 0.041^{+0.015}_{-0.012}$ and inverse power-law slope $\alpha = 0.39^{+0.17}_{-0.19}$, improving the maximum a posteriori fit relative to $\Lambda$CDM+$\sum m_{\nu,\mathrm{eff}}$ by $\Delta\chi^2_{\mathrm{MAP}} = -5.98$ (primarily from SNe and BAO).

**Interplay of geometry and perturbation dynamics**: Alleviating neutrino mass bounds requires a constructive combination of altered background expansion, CMB acoustic calibration, and clustering/lensing suppression; other interacting dark energy models tested in the study instead push effective neutrino masses to more negative values.

While phenomenological dynamical dark energy (such as CPL $w_0 w_a$) can alleviate this tension, it typically demands crossing the phantom divide ($w < -1$), which is problematic for simple canonical scalar field theories. In this work, the authors implement a coupled quintessence (CQ) model—wherein cold dark matter exchanges energy and momentum with a canonical scalar field through an exponential coupling $m_{\rm c}(\phi)\propto e^{-\beta\phi/M_{\rm Pl}}$—into CAMB and Cobaya to test whether dark-sector interactions can naturally restore consistency with neutrino physics using Planck, ACT DR6, SPT-3G, DESI DR2 BAO, and DES-Dovekie supernova data. They find that energy flow from dark matter to dark energy dilutes the late-time matter density and alters perturbation growth, relaxing neutrino mass constraints to be compatible with normal ordering within $2\sigma$ without any phantom crossing. This demonstrates that dark-sector interactions provide a well-grounded physical mechanism capable of reconciling cosmological datasets with laboratory neutrino mass bounds.

papers.title: Robustness of the Baryonic Acoustic Oscillation Peak Position against Monopole Fluctuations in Galaxy Surveys
papers.authors: Christopher Magnoli, Giovanni Piccoli, Jaiyul Yoo (Zürich), Daniel Eisenstein (Harvard)
papers.abstract: Precise measurements of the baryonic acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak position are one of the key goals in modern galaxy surveys. We investigate the impact of the monopole fluctuations in galaxy surveys on the BAO peak position in the galaxy two-point redshift-space multipole-correlation functions. The background mean density of a galaxy sample is estimated from the survey itself by averaging the observed galaxy number density, and this averaged number density (monopole) is subtracted to obtain the observed galaxy number density fluctuation, which includes an additional contribution from the monopole fluctuations, propagating to galaxy clustering analysis. We compute the contributions of the monopole fluctuations to the redshift-space multipole-correlation functions. While the monopole contributions in galaxy two-point correlation function are anisotropic and non-negligible in amplitude, the contributions are so smooth around the BAO peak position that they are almost completely absorbed in the BAO broadband model, leaving the BAO peak position unaffected at the sub-percent level. Our results demonstrate the robustness of the BAO analysis against the unknown systematic error.

conclusions: **Smoothness over BAO scales**: Although the monopole fluctuation contributes an anisotropic correction of order $5\text{--}10\%$ to the raw galaxy two-point correlation function at separation $s \sim 100\,h^{-1}\text{Mpc}$, its angle-averaged projection onto redshift-space multipoles ($\xi_0, \xi_2$) varies extremely smoothly across the BAO feature.

**Negligible standard ruler shift ($\Delta\alpha \approx 10^{-4}$)**: When applying standard BAO template fitting, the empirical broadband polynomial nuisance parameters $A_l(s)$ absorb the smooth monopole signal almost completely, inducing an isotropic peak shift of only $\Delta\alpha \approx 10^{-4}$, well below the sub-percent statistical precision of current and upcoming surveys like DESI and Euclid.

**Invariance under bias and non-linear damping**: Because the monopole fluctuation traces the underlying galaxy density field, non-linear matter evolution and galaxy bias suppress or enhance both the primary clustering signal and the monopole correction in tandem, keeping the net impact on the BAO peak position negligible.

**Caveat for partial-sky geometries**: While the analytic results assume an idealized full sky ($\Omega = 4\pi$), realistic survey footprints with small or disjoint patches may cause higher angular modes ($l > 0$) to leak into the empirically estimated mean density, which could quantitatively enhance the effect and warrants survey-specific mock testing.
ai.relevance_reason: While directly relevant to galaxy clustering systematics and BAO measurement robustness for surveys like Euclid, the paper addresses standard standard-ruler template fitting rather than beyond-$\Lambda$CDM models, fast simulations/emulators, or relativistic/inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: In observational galaxy clustering, computing overdensities $\delta_g = (n_g - \bar{n}_g)/\bar{n}_g$ requires the cosmic background number density $\bar{n}_g(z)$, which cannot be measured a priori and is instead estimated by averaging observed galaxy counts over the survey footprint at each redshift bin. Because our observable universe is a single realization, this sky average inherently fluctuates around the true ensemble mean due to cosmic variance—a phenomenon called the "monopole fluctuation" ($\delta n(z)$) that adds an anisotropic correction of order $5\text{--}10\%$ to the two-point correlation function at the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) scale. To evaluate whether this observational systematic biases cosmological distance measurements, Magnoli et al. analytically modeled the redshift-space multipoles ($\xi_0, \xi_2$) including the monopole term and tested standard BAO template fits that marginalize over smooth broadband polynomials. They demonstrated that because the monopole contribution is featureless and smooth around the sound horizon scale, standard broadband nuisance terms absorb it almost entirely, shifting the isotropic BAO scale parameter by only $\Delta\alpha \approx 10^{-4}$ and confirming that standard BAO analyses remain remarkably robust.

papers.title: Dark matter alters dwarf galaxy sizes and morphologies
papers.authors: Akaxia Cruz, Robel Geda, Alyson Brooks, Mariangela Lisanti, Annika H. G. Peter, Thomas R. Quinn, Ben Keller
papers.abstract: Dwarf galaxies are the most dark-matter-dominated systems in the Universe, serving as unique laboratories for exploring the fundamental nature of the dark sector. Although the observed diversity in dwarf galaxy sizes and morphologies suggests an interplay between dark matter and baryonic physics, this relationship has remained largely unquantified in existing models. Here, we utilize a set of novel cosmological simulations with baryons to demonstrate how dark matter physics directly drives the structural evolution of these galaxies. By comparing the same systems across cold dark matter and varied self-interacting dark matter models, we find that the evolution of the central density of dark matter significantly impacts a galaxy's half-light radius, but the signal is dependent on morphology. This causal link establishes galaxy size as a direct signature of the underlying dark matter microphysics. Our findings provide a predictive framework for decoding dark matter particle properties from galactic shapes, offering a roadmap for upcoming wide-field surveys, such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, to probe the dark sector through the statistical analysis of galaxy populations.

conclusions: **Co-evolution in irregular dwarfs**: In irregular dwarf galaxies, stellar orbits expand and contract alongside the dark matter potential, maintaining a tight $\sim 1:1$ relation between the stellar half-light radius $r_{1/2}$ and the dark matter core radius $r_c$ (average $r_{1/2}/r_c \approx 0.85 \pm 0.23$ in CDM and $0.86 \pm 0.13$ in velocity-dependent SIDM at $z=0$, and $1.15 \pm 0.24$ in core-collapsing SIDM at $z=0.3$).

**Merger-driven decoupling in disks**: In disk-forming dwarfs, a gas-rich merger with high orbital angular momentum initiates extended disk growth, which decouples stellar size evolution from the dark matter core and drives $r_{1/2}$ well beyond $r_c$.

**Distinct dark matter microphysics signatures**: Velocity-dependent SIDM produces systematically expanded cores ($r_c \sim 1\text{--}4\text{ kpc}$) and larger galaxies than CDM ($r_c \sim 1\text{--}2\text{ kpc}$ set by bursty supernova feedback), whereas strong self-interactions ($\sigma_T = 50\text{ cm}^2/\text{g}$) undergo runaway core collapse that halts and reverses core expansion by $z \sim 0.3$.

**Statistical probe for upcoming surveys**: The morphological diversity creates a cosmology-dependent slope in the $r_c\text{--}r_{1/2}$ plane (linear regression slope of 1.07 in velocity-dependent SIDM vs 1.41 in CDM at $z=0.3$), providing an observational framework to constrain dark matter self-interactions using dwarf galaxy samples from Rubin Observatory's LSST.

ai.summary: Dwarf galaxies are dominated by dark matter, making their inner density profiles a sensitive testing ground for whether dark matter is strictly collisionless (cold dark matter, CDM) or self-interacting (SIDM), where particle scattering can form constant-density cores or trigger runaway core collapse. To investigate how dark matter microphysics influences observable galaxy properties, the authors analyze the "Massive SIDM-SIDM" suite of cosmological hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations (24 isolated halos with $M_{200} \sim 10^{10}\text{--}10^{11}\,{\rm M}_\odot$), comparing CDM against both a velocity-dependent Yukawa model and a strong constant cross-section ($\sigma_T = 50\text{ cm}^2/\text{g}$) model using the ChaNGa code. They find that in irregular dwarf galaxies, stellar orbits expand and contract in tandem with the dark matter potential, establishing a tight co-evolution where the stellar half-light radius $r_{1/2}$ directly mirrors the core radius $r_c$. In contrast, galaxies undergoing high-orbital-angular-momentum gas mergers form rotation-supported disks, decoupling $r_{1/2}$ from $r_c$ and driving stellar sizes significantly larger than the dark matter core. This work demonstrates that the joint distribution of dwarf galaxy sizes and morphologies encodes direct signatures of dark matter particle interactions, offering a predictive test for upcoming wide-field surveys like Rubin's LSST.

papers.title: CosmoSim: Lens-parameter estimation of the Einstein Cross NGC 6505 using machine learning
papers.authors: Ben David Normann, Oda Hjemli, Hans Georg Schaathun
papers.abstract: CosmoSim is an open-source tool for simulating gravitational lenses and reconstructing lens mass distributions, either by ray tracing a parametric lens model or through a Roulette expansion of the lens potential. It is also used to generate the large, labelled synthetic image sets needed to train machine-learning (ML) parameter estimators. We present the first application of CosmoSim to real data. A convolutional neural network trained only on CosmoSim images estimates Singular Isothermal Ellipsoid lens and source parameters directly from observed images. We test the pipeline on 21 images of 19 strong lenses from Euclid and the AGEL survey, after removing the foreground lens light with a custom decontamination tool built on AstroPy. As a case study we reconstruct the Einstein Cross NGC 6505 both from the lens model published by the discovery team and from parameters predicted by our ML model. Both reconstructions recover the observed four-image structure, and the ML-based reconstruction performs at least as well as the literature-based one: it scores better on masked structural similarity, intersection-over-union and Chamfer distance, with an essentially equal Hausdorff distance. Across the ensemble, the predicted Einstein radii are consistent with catalogued values within the quoted uncertainties (mean relative difference 0.08 for Euclid and 0.19 for AGEL lenses), and the enclosed masses agree to within a median of 0.12 dex. The predicted ellipticities differ systematically from the catalogued values, while the comparison of orientations is inconclusive. These results establish CosmoSim as a tool that can be applied directly to observational data.

conclusions: **Successful case study on NGC 6505:** The CNN reconstruction of the Euclid Einstein Cross NGC 6505 reproduced the four-image geometry directly from data, outperforming a literature-based model on morphological metrics with higher masked structural similarity (SSIM of 0.65 vs. 0.54) and intersection-over-union (IoU of 0.55 vs. 0.45), while matching the Hausdorff distance ($\approx 11.7$ vs. 11.5 pixels).

**Accurate Einstein radii and enclosed masses:** Across 21 images of 19 strong lenses from Euclid and AGEL, predicted Einstein radii $\theta_{\mathrm{E}}$ agreed with catalogued values within $1\sigma$ uncertainties (mean relative difference of 8% for Euclid and 19% for AGEL), yielding enclosed masses $M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}})$ consistent within a median of 0.12 dex.

**Systematic bias in lens ellipticity:** The network systematically predicted more flattened lenses ($\epsilon \approx 0.44\text{--}0.54$) than catalogued values ($0.61\text{--}0.88$), caused partly by the lack of external shear in the Singular Isothermal Ellipsoid model (which forces shear to be absorbed as intrinsic ellipticity) and residual artefacts from lens-light decontamination.

**Validation of synthetic-only training:** The results confirm that neural networks trained strictly on synthetic CosmoSim ray-traced simulations can perform zero-shot inference on real space- and ground-based telescope data.

ai.summary: Strong gravitational lensing occurs when the gravitational potential of an intervening galaxy deflects light from a background source into multiple distorted arcs or quadruple configurations known as Einstein crosses, offering a powerful probe of galaxy-scale total mass distributions. Traditional pixel-level lens modelling can be computationally intensive, creating a demand for fast machine learning estimators capable of processing the thousands of strong lenses expected from wide-field surveys like Euclid. In this work, the authors present the first application to real survey data of CosmoSim, an open-source lens simulation code, by training a convolutional neural network solely on synthetic Singular Isothermal Ellipsoid (SIE) images to infer lens and source properties. Applying this pipeline to the Euclid Einstein Cross NGC 6505 and an ensemble of 20 additional images from Euclid and AGEL after subtracting foreground galaxy light, they show that synthetic-only training can reliably recover Einstein radii and overall image morphology on real observational data.

papers.title: Self-interacting Dark Matter signatures from stars extremely magnified by galaxy clusters
papers.authors: Sung Kei Li, Yuxuan He, Yi-Ming Zhong, Jose M. Diego, Jeremy Lim, Amruth Alfred, Thomas Broadhurst, Sangjun Cha, Birendra Dhanasingham, Leo W.H. Fung, Patrick Kelly, Richard Massey, Paloma Morilla, Jose M. Palencia, Derek Perera, Liliya L.R. Williams
papers.abstract: The spatial distribution of cluster-lensed star transients with respect to the macroscopic critical curve (CC) is sensitive to underlying substructures predicted by different classes of dark matter (DM) models. \citet{Broadhurst_2025} have shown that wave-like DM composed of ultra-light bosons better explains both the width and negative skewness (towards the interior of the CC) of the lensed star spatial distribution discovered in the ``Dragon'' lensed galaxy ($z = 0.73$) in the Abell 370 (A370, $z = 0.375$) cluster field, compared with the case of regular cold dark matter (CDM) subhaloes. In this work, we consider the case of self-interacting DM (SIDM) and investigate how the lensed star spatial distribution depends on the velocity-dependent self-interaction cross-section of SIDM particles, and whether constraints can be placed on the cross-section strength at relevant velocities. Establishing a cross-section strength-dependent (sub)halo gravothermal core-collapse probability, we found that the SIDM appears to be the only known class of models thus far in which the sign of skewness is set by its own particle parameters. The observed lensed star distribution in the Dragon galaxy can be well explained, in terms of both skewness and width, when a significant fraction of subhaloes have undergone core collapse and exhibit a steep power-law density slope. Given the cluster redshift, this qualitatively favours an (effective) cross-section strength of $500 -1000\,\textrm{cm}^{2}/\textrm{g}$ for halos with mass $10^{6} - 10^{8}\,M_{\odot}$ (velocity dispersion of $\sim 1-10\,\rm{km}/\rm{s}$), when the role of environmental effects on the core-collapse (de)acceleration is not considered, and limits the three-dimensional inner density slope of the collapsed halo to $\Gamma \gtrsim 2.5$ (Bayes factor of $\sim 10^{2}$).

conclusions: Steep density slopes explain negative skewness: Core-collapsed SIDM subhaloes with steep 3D inner density slopes ($\Gamma \gtrsim 2.5$ for $\rho \propto r^{-\Gamma}$) generate secondary critical curves inside the macroscopic critical curve (negative parity), providing an excellent fit to the Dragon arc observations ($\chi^2_\nu \approx 1.2$) and favored over shallow $\Gamma=2$ profiles by a Bayes factor of $\sim 10^2$.

Favored cross-section: Reproducing the observed lensed star spatial distribution favors an effective self-interaction cross-section of $\sigma/m \approx 500\text{--}1000\,\mathrm{cm}^2/\mathrm{g}$ on dwarf subhalo scales ($M \sim 10^6\text{--}10^8\,M_\odot$, velocity dispersions $\sim 1\text{--}10\,\mathrm{km/s}$), ensuring a substantial core-collapse fraction at the cluster redshift ($z = 0.375$).

Observational prospects for model discrimination: While both SIDM and wave (ultralight axion) dark matter can fit current observations, a total sample of $\sim 200$ cluster-lensed star events could distinguish SIDM from wave dark matter at $3\sigma$, whereas $\sim 160$ events would rule out vanilla collisionless CDM at $5\sigma$.

ai.summary: When background stars are strongly magnified near a galaxy cluster's critical curve—the line of formally infinite geometric magnification—their spatial distribution is extremely sensitive to small-scale dark matter substructures. Standard cold dark matter (CDM) subhaloes perturb the critical curve such that lensed stars should be skewed towards the exterior (positive parity), which conflicts with recent Hubble and JWST detections in the "Dragon" arc behind Abell 370 ($z=0.375$) that show a distinct inward (negative parity) skewness. The authors investigate whether self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), whose subhaloes can undergo gravothermal core collapse to form highly concentrated central cusps, can resolve this puzzle. By generating fine-scale cluster magnification maps combining macroscopic lensing, stellar microlensing, and SIDM subhaloes, they demonstrate that core-collapsed subhaloes produce microscopic critical curves ("milliCCs") in the negative parity, naturally generating the observed negative skewness.

papers.title: A consistent formulation of stochastic inflation II: Reassessing its role in nonlinear cosmological perturbations
papers.authors: Diego Cruces, Tomotaka Kuroda
papers.abstract: We question whether the conventional formulation of stochastic inflation can provide a quantitatively reliable description of cosmological perturbations. More fundamentally, we reassess the role and motivations of the stochastic approach to study cosmological perturbations, distinct from its well-founded motivation for resumming IR secular divergences. To provide a quantitative basis for this reassessment, we extend stochastic inflation beyond the linear regime by incorporating non-Markovian effects arising from infrared-ultraviolet interactions and terms quadratic in ultraviolet fluctuations, which generate non-white noise. We derive three-point correlation functions for a spectator scalar field in de Sitter space and a slow-roll inflaton including metric perturbations, demonstrating exact agreement with in-in quantum-field-theoretic predictions for superhorizon nonlinear evolution. Our results show that both non-Markovian effects and quadratic (higher order) noise terms are essential for quantitative accuracy, implying that the conventional stochastic-inflation framework is, at best, quantitatively justified only at linear order.

conclusions: Conventional stochastic inflation is quantitatively justified only at linear order: assuming linear Gaussian noise in the Langevin equations mathematically restricts the validity of the infrared (IR) classical dynamics to linear perturbation theory.

Matching quantum field theory requires quadratic noise and non-Markovian memory: reproducing the superhorizon bispectrum (three-point correlator) calculated via the in-in formalism requires adding terms quadratic in the ultraviolet (UV) fluctuations as well as non-Markovian backreaction near the horizon cutoff.

Questioning the foundational need for stochastic inflaton models: unlike light spectator fields where stochastic methods resum true secular infrared divergences, inflaton curvature perturbations feature derivative couplings and gauge symmetries that avoid secular IR divergences, removing the primary theoretical motivation for a stochastic treatment over standard in-in QFT.

Implications for primordial black holes (PBHs): widespread stochastic-$\delta N$ predictions for non-Gaussian exponential tails and PBH abundance rely on extrapolations that omit these second-order noise and memory corrections, making their quantitative accuracy unverified.

ai.summary: In early-universe cosmology, stochastic inflation models long-wavelength (infrared, IR) cosmological perturbations as classical fields driven by stochastic "noise kicks" as short-wavelength quantum fluctuations (ultraviolet, UV modes) stretch past the Hubble horizon. While originally developed to resum infrared secular loop divergences, this framework—particularly via the stochastic-$\delta N$ formalism—has recently been widely applied to predict nonlinear perturbations and non-Gaussian tails for primordial black hole formation. Cruces and Kuroda critically re-examine this practice, extending the heuristic Langevin formulation to the nonlinear regime by systematically incorporating non-Markovian memory effects from IR–UV interactions and quadratic (non-white) noise terms. By computing three-point correlation functions for both a de Sitter spectator field and a slow-roll inflaton with metric perturbations, they prove that these higher-order corrections are strictly required to match first-principles in-in quantum field theory on superhorizon scales. Consequently, they demonstrate that conventional stochastic inflation is quantitatively justified only at linear order, meaning that widely cited non-perturbative claims and exponential probability tails remain uncontrolled extrapolations.

papers.title: Non-Gaussian matter fluctuations from primordial magnetic fields and galaxy luminosity function
papers.authors: Teppei Minoda, Yi Mao, Shohei Saga, Hayato Shimabukuro
papers.abstract: Primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) represent a promising candidate for the origin of large-scale magnetic fields observed in astrophysical environments. Through the Lorentz force, PMFs generate matter density perturbations, leaving distinct imprints on the formation of cosmic structures. While previous studies have primarily characterized these imprints via the matter power spectrum --- a two-point statistic --- we demonstrate that the one-point statistics of PMF-induced density fluctuations reveal an intrinsically non-Gaussian probability distribution function (PDF), even when the PMFs themselves are statistically Gaussian. In particular, we find that the high-density tail of the PDF is enhanced by over two orders of magnitude relative to the Gaussian case. Adopting the Press-Schechter formalism, we show that this non-Gaussianity significantly boosts the abundance of rare objects, especially massive halos and those at high redshifts. We further compute the ultraviolet luminosity function of galaxies at $z=6$, $12$, and $16$, and compare our predictions with recent James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations that have reported an excess of high-redshift galaxies at $z\sim 12$ -- $16$ relative to standard $\Lambda$CDM expectations. Intriguingly, in the limiting case where the total density field inherits this PDF, our results suggest that the non-Gaussian density fluctuations sourced by PMFs can explain the bright-end ($M_\mathrm{UV}\lesssim -18$) excess at $z\gtrsim 12$, without requiring additional astrophysical enhancements to star-formation efficiency.

conclusions: Because the magnetic Lorentz force is quadratic in the magnetic field ($\bm{B}\times(\nabla\times\bm{B})$), Gaussian PMFs generate an intrinsically non-Gaussian linear matter density PDF with an exponential tail, boosting the probability density at $|\delta_M|\sim 6\sigma$ by a factor of $\sim 10^3$ compared to a Gaussian distribution.

The shape of the normalized one-point PDF $\nu_M = \delta_M/\sigma$ is nearly universal across field amplitudes ($B_{\mathrm{n}} = 0.1\text{--}2.0\text{ nG}$), featuring a Gaussian core that transitions to an exponential tail at $\nu_{\mathrm{tr}} \approx 1.76\text{--}2.35$ depending mildly on the spectral index $n_B$.

Propagating this non-Gaussian tail into Press--Schechter theory substantially enhances the abundance of rare, massive halos at high redshift (boosting $M \gtrsim 10^{10}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$ at $z=6$ and $M \gtrsim 10^7\,h^{-1}M_\odot$ at $z \ge 12$), where the collapse threshold $\delta_c/\sigma$ probes the exponential tail.

Assuming the total density field inherits this PDF, a PMF model with $B_{\mathrm{n}} = 0.3\text{ nG}$ and $n_B = -2.9$ naturally reproduces the bright-end ($M_{\mathrm{UV}} \lesssim -18$) excess of galaxies observed by JWST at $z \sim 12\text{--}16$ without requiring unphysically high star-formation efficiency.

ai.summary: Primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) generated in the early universe exert Lorentz forces on cosmological plasma, seeding additional matter perturbations that alter structure formation. Because the Lorentz force is quadratic in the magnetic field ($\propto B^2$), the resulting matter density perturbations follow an intrinsically non-Gaussian, heavy-tailed distribution even when the underlying magnetic field itself is purely Gaussian. In this paper, the authors simulate 3D Gaussian PMF configurations, compute the one-point probability distribution function (PDF) of the induced density field, and parameterize its transition from a Gaussian core to an exponential tail enhanced by over two orders of magnitude at high overdensities ($>3\sigma$). Applying this non-Gaussian PDF within the Press--Schechter framework, they demonstrate that the enhanced tail dramatically boosts the abundance of rare, massive halos at high redshifts ($z \sim 12\text{--}16$). This mechanism offers an appealing cosmological explanation for the bright-end galaxy excess reported by JWST at $z \gtrsim 12$ without needing to tune astrophysical parameters or invoke extreme star-formation efficiencies.

papers.title: $r$-Largest Order Statistics for Galaxy Cluster Cosmology I: Reconstruction of the high-mass end of the Halo Mass Function
papers.authors: T. Gayoux, P-S. Corasaniti
papers.abstract: We introduce the $r$-largest order statistics ($r$-LOS) framework for galaxy clusters, a generalization of the standard extreme value statistics (EVS) approach. While conventional EVS focuses on the probability distribution of the most massive cluster within a given volume, the $r$-LOS framework exploits the additional statistical information encoded in the joint distribution of the $r$ most massive clusters, ranked in descending order of mass. We develop the corresponding mathematical formalism, discuss its asymptotic properties, and derive a set of relations relevant to galaxy cluster cosmology. In particular, we demonstrate that the high-mass end of the halo mass function (HMF) can be reconstructed from the generalized extreme value (GEV) parameters inferred using an extension of the block maxima method that incorporates the $r$ most massive clusters in each volume. This provides a means of recovering the high-mass tail of the HMF using only a small subsample of the halo population. We validate these relations using both comoving and light-cone halo catalogues from numerical simulations. Finally, we investigate the sensitivity of the $r$-LOS framework to primordial non-Gaussianity, focusing on its impact on the statistics of massive clusters.

conclusions: The $r$-LOS framework generalizes single-cluster extreme value statistics (EVS) to the joint distribution of the $r$ most massive halos, showing that the cumulative distribution of the $k$-th ranked cluster is given analytically by the regularized upper incomplete gamma function $\mathcal{Q}(k, \mathcal{N}(m))$.

Equating the GEV scaling variable $\tau(m)$ with the cumulative halo number $\mathcal{N}(m)$ allows direct reconstruction of the high-mass tail of the HMF using only a small subsample of the most massive clusters, bypassing standard shot-noise-dominated mass binning.

Physical considerations in hierarchical $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$ restrict the HMF to the Weibull domain of attraction ($-1 < \xi < 0$), establishing an effective maximum cluster mass endpoint $\mathcal{M}^* = 10^{\mu - \sigma/\xi}$ (reaching an asymptotic plateau of $\sim 10^{16.3}\, M_\odot h^{-1}$ for a full-sky Planck 2018 survey).

In simulations, incorporating the joint statistics of the $r$ largest clusters substantially tightens constraints on the shape parameter $\xi$ and provides enhanced sensitivity to local primordial non-Gaussianity ($f_{\rm NL}$) relative to standard single-maximum EVS.

ai.summary: The abundance of the most massive galaxy clusters exponentially traces the high-mass tail of the halo mass function (HMF), providing sensitive constraints on cosmological parameters and primordial density peaks, but standard Extreme Value Statistics (EVS) typically discards information by only considering the single most massive cluster in a volume. To overcome this limitation, the authors introduce the $r$-largest order statistics ($r$-LOS) framework, which exploits the joint probability distribution of the top $r$ rank-ordered cluster masses in a given volume to fit Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) parameters. By establishing an exact mathematical equivalence between the GEV variable and the cumulative halo count in the Poisson limit, they demonstrate that the high-mass tail of the HMF can be reliably reconstructed from a small subsample of extreme clusters without full-population binning. Validated on $N$-body simulations in both comoving space and light cones, the method provides tighter parameter constraints—particularly on the shape parameter $\xi$, which sets a physical upper mass cutoff—and demonstrates heightened sensitivity to local primordial non-Gaussianity.

papers.title: Constraining Dark Matter Gravitational Production with the 21cm Signal at the Cosmic Dawn
papers.authors: André A. Costa, Valdir B. Bezerra
papers.abstract: The origin of dark matter is one of the major problems in modern cosmology. We can infer its existence from the gravitational potential wells around astrophysical objects, but there is no convincing explanation for what its nature and origin are. Moreover, experiments for direct detection, indirect detection, or particle production in accelerators have not shown, until now, any conclusive interaction between dark matter and particles in the standard model. This may imply that dark matter does not interact with ordinary matter and originates from pure gravitational interaction. In this manuscript, we investigate the possibility to constrain the gravitational production of dark matter from the 21cm brightness temperature at the cosmic dawn. Considering only the time when the absorption profile occurs, we can impose upper limits on the dark matter's mass. Future measurements have potential to extend current constraints and help understanding the nature of dark matter.

papers.title: From $3\times2$pt to $4\times3$pt: calibrating galaxy bias and intrinsic alignments with galaxy clustering and weak lensing bispectra
papers.authors: Raphaël Kou, Antony Lewis
papers.abstract: Combining galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing beyond two-point statistics offers a way to extract additional cosmological information while calibrating astrophysical nuisance parameters. We investigate this approach by combining 1-loop power spectra with tree-level bispectra, including all auto- and cross-bispectra of galaxy clustering and weak lensing, a combination that we refer to as $4\times3$pt by analogy with the well-known $3\times2$pt analysis. Modelling two- and three-point statistics consistently, with galaxy bias and intrinsic alignments described by the TATT model, we perform Fisher forecasts of dark energy constraints for a Euclid-like survey, with conservative scale cuts. When combined with CMB data, adding $4\times3$pt bispectra to the $3\times2$pt improves the dark energy figure of merit by about $30\%$, a gain that remains stable when using the three, four or five lowest redshift bins of our ten. To extend the analysis to ten tomographic bins, we compress the bispectra into skew-spectra, which improve the figure of merit by $20\%$ with the CMB and by $37\%$ without. We show that most of this improvement comes from the calibration of second-order galaxy bias parameters by three-point statistics, mainly by the galaxy-auto and the GGL bispectra. We also find that baryonic feedback is correlated with second-order intrinsic alignment parameters once the amplitude of the matter power spectrum is constrained by the CMB, and that bispectra reduce this correlation by calibrating intrinsic alignments, almost entirely through the GGL bispectra, a mechanism that could become more valuable with more flexible baryonic feedback models. These results demonstrate the potential of combined galaxy clustering and weak lensing bispectra to improve cosmological constraints from stage-IV galaxy surveys through the calibration of galaxy bias and intrinsic alignments.

conclusions: **Substantial Dark Energy Gain:** Adding tree-level $4\\times3$pt bispectra ($GGG, GGL, GLL, LLL$) to 1-loop $3\\times2$pt power spectra improves the dark energy figure of merit (FoM) by $\\approx 30\\%$ for a Euclid-like survey combined with CMB data (evaluated across 3 to 5 tomographic bins).

**Galaxy Bias Calibration as the Main Driver:** The improvement is primarily driven by three-point statistics breaking degeneracies between linear ($b_1$) and second-order ($b_2, b_s$) galaxy bias parameters—which enter bispectra at tree level rather than through loop integrals—with galaxy auto-bispectra ($GGG$) alone providing $56\\text{--}65\\%$ of the FoM increase.

**Disentangling Intrinsic Alignments and Baryonic Feedback:** Cross-bispectra involving two galaxy fields and one lensing field ($GGL$) calibrate second-order Tidal Alignment and Tidal Torquing (TATT) parameters, partially breaking degeneracies with baryonic feedback (AGN heating temperature $T_{\\mathrm{AGN}}$) that emerge once the matter power spectrum amplitude is anchored by the CMB.

**Scalable Skew-Spectrum Compression:** To overcome the prohibitive covariance size of full bispectra across 10 tomographic bins, the authors compress the data vector into filtered skew-spectra, retaining most of the constraining power with a $20\\%$ FoM improvement with CMB (and $37\\%$ without CMB).

papers.title: Enhanced Early Structure from Axiodilatons & 21cm Observations
papers.authors: Chan Youn Weon, Carsten van de Bruck, C.P. Burgess, Jeong Han Kim, Adam Smith
papers.abstract: Axiodilatons provide a promising unified model of the Dark Sector whose properties are motivated by the use of accidental approximate symmetries to embed the light fields needed for observations into well-motivated UV physics in a technically natural way. These models turn out to help ameliorate many current puzzles in $\Lambda$CDM phenomenology (e.g. the Hubble tension and the evidence for evolving Dark Energy) `for free' despite not being designed for that purpose. We here explore in more detail another serendipitous feature of these models: their tendency to enhance early structure formation, in a way that seems suggestive given the accumulating evidence for structure arising earlier than expected in $\Lambda$CDM. Since early structure growth is the cleanest to study we explore in detail the expected 21cm signal produced by axiodilaton models, using the same parameter choices that improve agreement with observations elsewhere in cosmology. For fixed astrophysics, we forecast that SKA1-Low could distinguish dilaton couplings as small as a few times $10^{-2}$ from $\Lambda$CDM at $2\sigma$, mainly because of the earlier formation of structure. We provide complete derivations of the mass dependence of the relevant cosmological observables, including how dilaton-dependent baryon and electron masses affect the hyperfine transition, the Ly$\alpha$ coupling, X-ray heating and ionization during cosmic dawn and the epoch of reionization. We provide details of radiative transfer, atomic physics and the equations governing the thermal and ionization state of the intergalactic medium.

conclusions: **Dominant mechanism is enhanced structure growth**: The global 21cm absorption feature and power spectrum are shifted to higher redshifts ($z \sim 15\text{--}25$), driven primarily by enhanced linear growth $\delta_m$ from an attractive dilaton-mediated fifth force rather than time-varying particle masses ($m_e, m_p$) or modified $H(z)$.

**SKA1-Low parameter constraints**: Assuming fixed astrophysics, mock observations indicate that a 5,000-hour SKA1-Low survey can distinguish the dilaton from $\Lambda$CDM at $2\sigma$ outside the bounds $|\mathbf{g}| \lesssim 0.12$ and $|\zeta| \lesssim 0.05$ (tightening to $|\mathbf{g}| \lesssim 0.05$ and $|\zeta| \lesssim 0.02$ for 10,000 hours), where $\mathbf{g}$ and $\zeta$ govern dilaton couplings to baryons and axion dark matter, respectively.

**Observational viability of tension-alleviating benchmarks**: Benchmark parameter sets ($|\mathbf{g}| \sim 0.1, |\zeta| \sim 0.1$) previously shown to mitigate the Hubble tension and mimic evolving dark energy in CMB, BAO, and supernova data are distinguishable from $\Lambda$CDM at $>2\sigma$ with SKA1-Low, even when including a 10% theoretical modeling uncertainty on the power spectrum.

**Key modeling caveats**: Results assume fixed fiducial astrophysics (EOS2021) and standard spherical collapse overdensity ($\delta_c = 1.686$), meaning astrophysical degeneracies, modified collapse thresholds, and solar-system fifth-force constraints remain open challenges for future work.

They demonstrate that the resulting shift of 21cm signals toward earlier cosmic times provides a sensitive testbed for dark-sector fifth forces, with future SKA1-Low radio interferometry able to place tight constraints on dilaton couplings.

papers.title: Can we constrain cosmology with compound gravitational lenses?
papers.authors: Duncan J. Bowden, Tian Li, Aprajita Verma, Thomas E. Collett, Philip Holloway
papers.abstract: Compound lensing in double-source-plane lenses (DSPLs) introduces multiple mass-sheet transformations that bias the inferred distance ratios $\beta$ used to constrain cosmology. We present the recovered $\beta$ from lens models of simulated compound lenses and explore the systematic biases that arise from a mass-sheet transformation in the first source plane. We examined simulated observations based on SDSS J0946+1006, in which we varied the matter distribution of source 1. We found a strong correlation between the stellar-to-halo mass and the recovered $\beta$. We produced a simulated catalogue of DSPLs detectable by the Euclid telescope to see if the same systematic propagates to a more varied population. But at Euclid's resolution, the properties of source 1 were poorly constrained, and any correlated bias was lost in the statistical uncertainty. We inferred $w_0$ and $\Omega_{\rm m}$ for a flat $w$CDM cosmology from our $\beta$ posteriors for our combined sample. We found the cosmology biased when using the full mock Euclid sample, but reduced the bias substantially using a limited, well-modelled ''gold'' sub-sample, bringing it to within $\sim2\sigma$ and $\sim1\sigma$ of the ground-truth cosmology for simulated Euclid and Hubble Space Telescope imaging, respectively. Therefore, we must eliminate systems with unreliable lensing information, and for extreme compound lensing, the model complexity must be sufficient to reproduce the lensing observations. DSPLs remain a promising cosmological probe that could provide independent and complementary constraints to existing probes.

conclusions: **Intermediate deflector bias**: In simulated Jackpot-like systems, approximating the intermediate galaxy's realistic stellar + NFW mass distribution with a simple isothermal profile introduces up to a $\sim 7\%$ systematic bias in the recovered distance ratio $\beta$, which strongly correlates with its stellar-to-halo mass ratio $M_*/M_{\rm h}$.

**Euclid survey limitations**: At Euclid VIS resolution ($0.1''$), the Einstein radius of the intermediate source galaxy is poorly constrained individually, obscuring parameter correlations within noise but leaving large modeling scatter that biases inferred cosmology when using the full mock sample (74 lenses).

**Gold sample mitigates bias**: Filtering the mock Euclid catalog for a "gold" subsample (19 lenses with larger Einstein radii, higher image multiplicity, and clear counter-images) reduces systematic bias, bringing flat $w$CDM parameter recovery to within $\sim 2\sigma$ of the fiducial cosmology.

**High-resolution follow-up gains**: Follow-up imaging at HST resolution ($0.05''$) on the gold sample tightens $1\sigma$ constraints on $w_0$ by $50\%$ and recovers the fiducial cosmology within $\sim 1\sigma$.

**Sensitivity of Einstein zigzags**: Rare compound systems where the intermediate lens further splits images ("zigzags") require higher model complexity (e.g., elliptical rather than spherical profiles) to prevent severe cosmological bias.

ai.summary: Double-source-plane lenses (DSPLs) occur when a foreground galaxy strongly lenses two background galaxies at distinct redshifts, creating a "compound" lens system where the intermediate galaxy acts as both a source and a secondary deflector. The ratio of their deflection angles measures a cosmological angular diameter distance ratio $\beta$ that is independent of the Hubble constant $H_0$ and sensitive to both $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and the dark energy equation of state parameter $w_0$. However, strong lensing suffers from the mass-sheet transformation (MST)—a mathematical degeneracy where rescaling deflector mass profiles and source sizes leaves observed image positions invariant—which compound lenses uniquely introduce in both deflector planes. In this work, the authors simulate both the well-known "Jackpot" lens and a mock Euclid Wide Survey lens population to test how approximating complex intermediate-galaxy mass profiles with simple isothermal models biases $\beta$ and flat $w$CDM constraints. They find that while unconstrained compound lenses severely bias cosmological inference, selecting a well-resolved "gold" subsample with space-based follow-up successfully recovers the true cosmology to within $\sim 1\sigma$.

papers.title: Quasars as a self-sufficient probe of the distance duality relation
papers.authors: Davide Pedrotti, Júlia Laguna-Miralles, Natalie B. Hogg
papers.abstract: The distance duality relation links luminosity and angular diameter distances under standard photon propagation. It is usually tested by combining distances from different probes, which requires matching their redshifts and assuming sky isotropy. Self-sufficient probes, which measure both distances for the same object, avoid the first requirement and make the second testable. We assess whether quasars can serve as such probes, combining luminosity distances from the UV--X-ray relation with angular diameter distances from spectroastrometry and reverberation mapping (SARM). As a proof-of-concept, we apply the test to the quasar Mrk~509 and find $\eta\equiv d_{\rm L}/[(1+z)^2d_{\rm A}] = 0.50^{+0.61}_{-0.27}$, consistent with no violation at $0.8\sigma$. We then forecast the number of quasars needed to detect a constant and a linearly redshift-dependent violation, motivated by the findings of Teixeira et al. (2025) with potential implications for the Hubble tension and dark energy. A constant violation, $\alpha_0=-0.075$, equivalent to a recalibration of the SNIa distance scale, could be detected at $3\sigma$ with 274--840 quasars. Since SARM distances, unlike BAO, do not rely on early-time physics, this would separate an early-time origin of the Hubble tension from a SNIa miscalibration or a distance duality violation. The redshift dependence is harder to detect: 1000 quasars would exclude $\eta=1$ at $3.4$--$6.6\sigma$, but detecting the dependence itself requires $2.6\times10^4$--$8\times10^4$. GRAVITY+ could bring quasar tests of a constant violation within reach.

conclusions: First single-object proof-of-concept: Combining UV--X-ray luminosity distance with a SARM angular diameter distance for the local quasar Mrk 509 ($z = 0.0344$) yields a duality parameter $\eta \equiv d_{\rm L}/[(1+z)^2 d_{\rm A}] = 0.50^{+0.61}_{-0.27}$, which is consistent with the standard Etherington relation ($\eta = 1$) at $0.8\sigma$.

Forecasts for a constant violation ($\alpha_0 = -0.075$): Detecting a constant offset of this magnitude—which corresponds to the SNIa distance recalibration needed to match CMB-calibrated BAO in the context of the Hubble tension—at $3\sigma$ requires between 274 quasars (optimistic scatter, $\sigma_{\ln\eta} = 0.43$) and 840 quasars (current scatter, $\sigma_{\ln\eta} = 0.75$), placing it within reach of upcoming GRAVITY+ surveys.

High barrier for redshift evolution ($\alpha_1$): For an evolving violation ($\eta(z) = 1 + \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 z$), a sample of $N = 1000$ quasars can exclude no-violation ($\eta = 1$) at $3.4\sigma$--$6.6\sigma$ through the average offset, but breaking the parameter degeneracy to detect the redshift slope $\alpha_1 = -0.014$ individually at $3\sigma$ would require an impractical $2.6\times 10^4$ to $8\times 10^4$ quasars.

Disentangling the Hubble tension: Because geometric SARM distances are independent of early-universe physics (unlike BAO calibrated against the sound horizon $r_{\rm d}$), self-sufficient quasar measurements provide a clean, model-independent discriminant between early-time physics (if $\eta \approx 1$) and late-time SNIa miscalibration or photon loss (if $\eta \ne 1$).

papers.title: Improved delensing of CMB $B$-modes with upcoming SO and LSST Year-1 mock dataset: Impact of photometric redshift errors
papers.authors: Kishan Deka, Chandra Shekhar Saraf, Pawel Bielewicz
papers.abstract: In the era of high-precision Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropy measurements, detection of primordial gravitational waves (PGWs) is one of the main goals of current CMB experiments. Detection of a divergence-free ($B$-mode) component in CMB polarisation will provide direct evidence of inflationary PGWs in the early universe. However, weak gravitational lensing of CMB photons due to intervening mass distribution of the Universe distorts the primordial polarisation patterns, introducing an additional lensing-induced $B$-mode signal. Removing these lensing-induced $B$-modes is essential for improving constraints on the amplitude of PGWs. In this work, we present a multi-tracer delensing analysis using simulations of the Rubin Observatory LSST galaxy catalogue and Simons Observatory (SO) CMB maps. We use realistic photometric redshift errors for LSST mock catalogue and high complexity Galactic foregrounds for CMB simulations. By adopting a tomographic multi-tracer approach that combines the CMB and LSST mock data, we achieved a 10-20% higher delensing efficiency compared with using CMB data alone. Our analysis removes approximately 60% of the lensing-induced $B$-mode power. We find that photometric redshift errors in the mock galaxy catalogue introduce biases in the inferred galaxy bias and $\sigma_{8,0}$ parameters. However, these uncertainties do not produce a significant systematic bias in the inferred tensor-to-scalar ratio.

conclusions: **Enhanced delensing efficiency**: Combining Simons Observatory CMB lensing reconstruction with eight tomographic LSST Year-1 galaxy overdensity bins improves delensing efficiency by $10\text{--}20\%$ over internal CMB delensing alone, removing $\sim 60\%$ of the lensing-induced $B$-mode power ($A_{\mathrm{lens}} \approx 0.4$).

**Impact on LSS parameters**: Photometric redshift errors derived via machine-learning estimators (FlexZBoost) systematically bias the recovered galaxy bias $b(z)$ and shift the inferred matter fluctuation amplitude $\sigma_{8,0}$ to higher values when stacking individual redshift posteriors.

**Robustness of primordial tensor constraints**: Despite the parameter biases in the large-scale structure sector, the inferred tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ remains unbiased across all tested fiducial inputs, successfully recovering the true $r$ within $1\sigma$ uncertainties without inducing false inflationary detections.

papers.title: Improved constraints on axion inflation with the new code AxioGen: an efficient generator of curvature perturbations
papers.authors: Matthew Reinhard, Zachary Slepian, Atsushi Taruya
papers.abstract: Axion inflation, in which a pseudoscalar inflaton couples to a $U(1)$ gauge field via a Chern-Simons interaction, has garnered significant interest due to its rich phenomenology. The power spectrum and bispectrum for this model are often parametrized by functions known as $f_2$ and $f_3$, respectively. Previous work computed $f_2$ and $f_3$ using an approximation for the gauge field mode functions. While these approximate solutions are fairly accurate ($\mathcal{O}(10\%)$) for large values of the model parameter $\xi$, which controls gauge field particle production, our recent work has shown them to be quite inaccurate for smaller values of $\xi$. We present new fitting functions for $f_2$ and $f_3$ that are significantly more accurate than those previously used. We use these functions to place new constraints on $\xi$ and also set lower bounds for the energy scale of the axion gauge field coupling for $\phi^{1/3}$ and $\phi^{2/3}$ inflationary potentials. Additionally, we present a new public code to efficiently generate realizations of the primordial curvature perturbation for axion inflation in the weak backreaction regime. This code enables numerical computation of higher order correlators and provides a novel path to initial conditions for large-scale structure formation.

conclusions: Underestimation in standard analytical approximations: The widely used analytical approximation for gauge-field mode functions underestimates the inverse-decay power spectrum and bispectrum at moderate particle-production parameter values ($1.8 \le \xi \le 3$), whereas the authors' numerical grid realizations match full mode-function treatments.

New calibrated fitting functions: From stochastic field realizations, the authors provide accurate power-law fits for the dimensionless power spectrum and equilateral bispectrum amplitudes, obtaining $f_2(\xi) = 1.59 \times 10^{-4} / \xi^{6.42}$ and $f_3(\xi) = 8.78 \times 10^{-7} / \xi^{9.64}$.

Observational bounds on particle production and coupling scale: Applying the Planck $2\sigma$ upper bound on equilateral non-Gaussianity ($f_{\rm NL}^{\rm equil} \le 68$) yields $\xi \le 2.5$, which translates to lower bounds on the axion-gauge interaction energy scale of $\Lambda \ge 3.6 \times 10^{16}\text{ GeV}$ for a $\phi^{2/3}$ potential and $\Lambda \ge 2.8 \times 10^{16}\text{ GeV}$ for a $\phi^{1/3}$ potential.

Public code for non-Gaussian initial conditions (Axiogen): The authors release Axiogen, an efficient public tool that generates 3D grid realizations of primordial curvature perturbations (vacuum plus inverse-decay components) in the weak backreaction regime, enabling initial conditions for N-body simulations and higher-order large-scale structure analyses.

papers.title: Cosmic Ray Heating of the Early IGM: Realistic Galaxy Populations, Reduced Efficiency, and 21-cm Signatures
papers.authors: Michael Pagano, Andrei Mesinger, Carmelo Evoli, Sruthi Ravikularaman
papers.abstract: Cosmic rays (CRs) accelerated by the first supernovae could heat the intergalactic medium (IGM) before reionization. Previous 21-cm simulations, assuming a kinetic-energy power-law spectrum and simplified galaxy populations, found that CR heating can rival X-ray heating from high-mass X-ray binaries, imprint a distinct signature on the 21-cm power spectrum, and flatten the absorption trough of the global 21-cm signal. Here we model CR heating in 21cmFAST with: (i) the momentum power-law spectrum predicted by diffusive shock acceleration; (ii) Coulomb losses off free electrons; and (iii) injection from data-informed populations of atomic-cooling and molecularly cooled galaxies. We find that CR heating is about an order of magnitude weaker than previously estimated because a momentum power law places little energy in the sub-relativistic protons ($\lesssim 40$ MeV) that supply 99% of the heat. For our fiducial spectral slope, at the hard end of those inferred for Galactic supernova remnants, and for matched efficiency, this reduces the heating by a factor of $\approx 12$, and together with a more realistic galaxy model, by a factor of $\approx 28$ at $z = 15$. At the efficiencies that supernovae can supply, CR heating is weaker than standard X-ray heating, and the global signal alone cannot tell the two apart. Distinguishing CR from X-ray heating with the 21-cm power spectrum requires CR efficiencies a few times higher than those expected from local observations. At such efficiencies, CR heating yields up to $\approx 55\%$ more power than X-ray heating at matched global signal (median over scales), compared with only 3-6% at a locally motivated efficiency. A flattened absorption trough, like the one claimed by EDGES, requires efficiencies over two orders of magnitude above the local ones, beyond plausible Population III supernova budgets.

conclusions: **Drastic reduction in CR heating efficiency:** Diffusive shock acceleration (DSA) predicts a momentum power law ($f(p) \propto p^{-\alpha}$) rather than a kinetic-energy power law; because 99% of IGM heating is driven by sub-relativistic protons ($E_{\rm K} \lesssim 40\text{ MeV}$), this physically motivated spectrum reduces heating by a factor of $\approx 12$ compared to previous estimates, and combines with realistic galaxy evolution for an overall suppression of $\approx 28$ at $z = 15$.

**X-rays dominate early IGM thermodynamics:** Within realistic astrophysical supernova budgets ($\eta_{\rm cr} \sim 5\times 10^{47}\text{--}3\times 10^{48}\text{ erg}\,M_\odot^{-1}$ for Pop II stars), cosmic-ray heating is significantly weaker than canonical X-ray heating from high-mass X-ray binaries, shifting the 21-cm global absorption trough to later epochs ($\Delta z \approx 4$) and making the two mechanisms indistinguishable from the global signal alone.

**Small-scale power spectrum signatures are faint:** Disentangling CR from X-ray heating through the 21-cm power spectrum requires injection efficiencies well above local constraints ($\eta_{\rm cr} \sim 10^{49}\text{ erg}\,M_\odot^{-1}$), which produces a scale-dependent power excess of $\sim 20\text{--}55\%$ at matched global signal; at fiducial efficiencies, the difference is only $3\text{--}6\%$, so current upper limits (e.g. from HERA) are unaffected by neglecting cosmic rays.

papers.title: Cosmological Signals from Finite-Lifetime Domain Wall Networks
papers.authors: Fengwei Yang, Kylar Greene, Aurora Ireland, Yuhsin Tsai
papers.abstract: We study cosmological perturbations sourced by metastable domain wall (DW) networks. Using the unconnected segment model, we derive analytic expressions for the scalar and tensor power spectra in the long-wavelength regime, finding a fixed ratio between their amplitudes during the scaling regime. These spectra grow as the network evolves, driven by the increasing correlation length and slower redshifting of the wall energy density relative to radiation, and peak at a scale set by the network's collapse time. Comparing the scalar spectrum with observational constraints, we derive bounds on the DW energy density at collapse, which we apply to $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and axion models. When these bounds are saturated, the resulting CMB $B$-mode signal can be comparable to or larger than the inflationary signal for a tensor-to-scalar ratio $r \sim 0.03$, potentially bringing it within reach of future CMB polarization experiments.

conclusions: The long-wavelength tensor and scalar power spectra sourced by scaling domain walls maintain a fixed ratio ($\mathcal{P}_h^{\rm DW} \simeq 0.386 \mathcal{P}_\zeta^{\rm DW}$), with both spectra growing as $(\eta/\eta_i)^7$ and peaking at the horizon re-entry scale at collapse ($k_p = \eta_c^{-1}$).

Super-horizon tensor modes undergo an additional post-collapse enhancement factor $\mathcal{E}(k\eta_c)$ between $\sim 10.8$ (near the peak) and $\sim 22.7$ (in the infrared limit) due to the matching of constant and decaying tensor modes once the wall source disappears.

Observational limits on curvature perturbations from the CMB, Lyman-$\alpha$, ultra-faint dwarf heating, and microlensing constrain the fractional domain wall energy density at collapse to $f_{\rm DW}^c \lesssim 10^{-1}\text{--}10^{-3}$ for $\eta_c \le 40\text{ Mpc}$, placing tight bounds on the symmetry-breaking scales of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and axion models.

When scalar perturbation bounds are saturated, the resulting CMB $B$-mode polarization can match or exceed inflationary gravitational waves with $r \sim 0.03$ at $\ell \sim 100$, exhibiting a distinctive shape that lacks the low-$\ell$ reionization bump.

ai.summary: Domain walls are sheet-like topological defects formed during spontaneous discrete symmetry breaking in the early universe; because their energy density dilutes more slowly than radiation ($\rho_{\rm DW} \propto a^{-2}$ versus $\rho_R \propto a^{-4}$), stable walls would quickly overclose the universe, but metastable networks that collapse due to a small explicit symmetry breaking can temporarily survive and source cosmological fluctuations. Using the unconnected segment model (USM), the authors derive analytic expressions for the long-wavelength scalar and tensor perturbation spectra generated during the network's scaling regime up to its collapse time $\eta_c$. Because the scalar and tensor modes are sourced by the same anisotropic wall stress-energy tensor, their power spectra maintain a fixed $\mathcal{O}(1)$ ratio and peak at the horizon scale at collapse ($k \sim \eta_c^{-1}$). By confronting the induced scalar perturbations with observational bounds from the CMB, Lyman-$\alpha$, and astrophysical systems, the authors place upper limits on the domain wall energy density at collapse and show that the associated tensor perturbations can generate CMB $B$-mode signals comparable to an inflationary tensor-to-scalar ratio of $r \sim 0.03$.

papers.title: Measuring the growth index in the $w_0w_a$CDM background
papers.authors: Ícaro. B. S. Cortês, Léo G. Medeiros, Ronaldo C. Batista
papers.abstract: We produce a measurement of the growth index, $\gamma$, which is used to parametrize the scale-independent growth of linear matter perturbations on sub-horizon scales, for the $w_0w_a$CDM background model. In 2023, assuming the $\Lambda$CDM background, the value $\gamma =0.633^{+0.025}_{-0.024}$ was obtained, excluding the General Relativity value of $\gamma=0.55$ at $3.7\sigma$ statistical significance. In 2025, an analysis of baryon acoustic oscillation data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopy Instrument (DESI) demonstrated a preference for a dynamical dark energy over the cosmological constant model, $\Lambda$, ranging from $2.8-4.2\sigma$, depending on the external datasets used. Therefore it is important to determine how the $\gamma$ measurement is modified in the context of dynamical dark energy and verify whether the tension with the expected theoretical value persists. Considering data from Planck cosmic microwave background anisotropies, $f\sigma_{8}$, baryon acoustic oscillation from DESI and supernova Ia luminosity distances from Phanteon+, we find $\gamma_{w_0w_a}=0.633\pm0.024$, essentially the same value found for the $\Lambda$CDM background. This result excludes the General Relativity value for the $w_0w_a$CDM background evolution at $3.4\sigma$ level. We also show that the $\gamma$ posteriors across many datasets combinations are consistent with each other and that main driver of the "$\gamma$ tension" is the $f\sigma_{8}$ dataset.

conclusions: Allowing a dynamical dark energy background ($w_0w_a$CDM) does not resolve the growth index tension: combining Planck 2018, $f\sigma_8$, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ yields $\gamma_{w_0w_a} = 0.633 \pm 0.024$ (compared to $\gamma_\Lambda = 0.635 \pm 0.024$), ruling out standard General Relativity ($\gamma \simeq 0.55$) at $3.4\sigma$ ($3.5\sigma$ in $\Lambda$CDM).

The discrepancy is almost entirely driven by the $f\sigma_8$ dataset (from redshift-space distortions and peculiar velocities), which prefers suppressed growth; replacing full Planck CMB data with CMB geometric priors that exclude lensing and ISW still favors $\gamma > 0.55$ at $2.8\sigma$, ruling out CMB lensing systematics as the sole driver.

Bayesian model comparison strongly favors the free-growth model over fixed GR ($\Delta\chi^2 = -10.6$ and Bayes factor $\log_{10}BF_{10} = 1.15$ for the full dataset combination), with growth index $\gamma$ displaying minimal parameter degeneracy with $w_0$, $w_a$, or $\Omega_m$.

Accounting for clustering dark energy ($c_s^2 = 0$) shifts the theoretical expectation to $\gamma \approx 0.564$, only modestly reducing the tension to $2.8\sigma$; physically, a value as high as $\gamma \sim 0.63$ implies a weakened effective gravitational coupling ($G_{\rm eff} < G_{\rm N}$) at late times, challenging standard modified gravity models like $f(R)$ that typically predict enhanced growth.

Recent analyses assuming $\Lambda$CDM have found a '$\gamma$ tension' ($\gamma \approx 0.63$, excluding GR at $>3.5\sigma$), closely mirroring the low-redshift $S_8$ tension, while DESI BAO data simultaneously hints at dynamical dark energy parameterized by an evolving equation of state $w(a) = w_0 + w_a(1-a)$. Here, the authors implement a modified version of CAMB with the Parametrized Post-Friedman framework to test whether adopting a flexible $w_0w_a$CDM background relieves this growth anomaly when fit against Planck 2018 CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ supernovae, and $f\sigma_8$ measurements. They find that dynamical dark energy leaves the inferred growth index virtually unchanged at $\gamma = 0.633 \pm 0.024$ ($3.4\sigma$ tension with GR), demonstrating that the preference for suppressed growth is robustly localized to the $f\sigma_8$ data rather than background geometry or CMB lensing anomalies.

papers.abstract: This paper describes the characteristics of the Euclid visible imager (VIS) data delivered as part of the Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). This data set contains 42092 calibrated frames. Validated nominal exposures cover 2092 deg$^2$ of sky. We outline the minor changes made to the VIS processing function (PF) since previous releases. For the wide survey, the photometric and astrometric accuracy of the reference stellar sample $(18.5 < I_{\rm E} < 19.8)$ is excellent. The internal and external astrometric dispersions are 0.08 and 0.18 mas, respectively, at the quadrant level, and 3.4 and 5.6 mas at the source level. The corresponding internal and external photometric dispersions are 0.76 and 1.4 mmag at the quadrant level, and 11 and 25 mmag at the source level. We characterise remaining astrometric and photometric systematic effects: focal-plane-dependent variations; time-dependent photometric offsets; and colour-dependent centroid shifts. The noise floor in the deepest VIS images appears to be set by the extended diffuse light of faint galaxies. Globally, the DR1 VIS data meet pre-launch mission requirements and the 42092 images it contains provide our first substantial look at the sky as seen by VIS.

conclusions: Euclid DR1 successfully delivers 42,092 calibrated VIS exposures covering 2,092 deg$^2$ of the wide survey sky, demonstrating the pipeline readiness for upcoming larger releases like DR2 ($\sim 5,800$ deg$^2$).

Astrometric precision comfortably satisfies mission requirements ($<3$ mas per exposure for 99.8% of images), achieving internal and external dispersions of 0.08 mas and 0.18 mas at the quadrant level (3.4 mas and 5.6 mas per source).

Photometric calibration of reference stars ($18.5 < I_{\rm E} < 19.8$) reaches 0.76 mmag internal and 1.4 mmag external precision at the quadrant level, with no residual non-linearity or brighter-fatter detector effects detected.

The noise floor in deep exposures is found to be set by the diffuse light of faint background galaxies, while small sub-arcminute distortion residuals and chromatic centroid shifts are identified for further refinement in DR2.

ai.summary: Euclid's core weak lensing mission requires extraordinarily sharp imaging and exquisitely controlled detector systematics in order to measure tiny shear distortions in galaxy shapes. In this Data Release 1 (DR1) paper, the Euclid Collaboration presents the data products and low-level processing pipeline for the Visible Instrument (VIS), which observes in a single wide optical band ($I_{\rm E}$, $550\text{--}900$ nm) across $42\,092$ calibrated frames covering $2092\,\deg^2$ of sky. The authors validate the astrometric and photometric performance across the focal plane, benchmark stability against external surveys, and characterise subtle detector systematics such as color-dependent centroid shifts (chromatic shifts) and focal-plane distortion residuals. The results confirm that VIS meets its pre-launch mission specifications, providing the robust observational foundation required for downstream cosmic shear and galaxy clustering analyses.

papers.abstract: Applications of strong gravitational lensing in astrophysics and cosmology critically depend on building reliable strong lensing models, which require accurate measurements of on-sky positions of multiple images and of the redshifts of the background sources from which they originate. In this context, Euclid is a unique facility, as it simultaneously provides high-resolution multi-band photometric imaging and slitless spectroscopy for an unprecedentedly large sample of gravitational lenses, most of which are newly discovered. In this work, we exploit Euclid slitless spectroscopic data to determine the redshifts of four spatially extended lensed sources, and to reconstruct emission-line images. Specifically, two of the target sources are lensed into giant arcs by the massive galaxy clusters SPT-CLJ0411$-$4819 ($z_\mathrm{d}=0.424$, where "d" denotes the lensing deflector) and Abell 2280 ($z_\mathrm{d}=0.326$). The third system is a quadruply imaged active galactic nucleus (AGN) candidate strongly lensed by a massive galaxy at $z_\mathrm{d}=0.68$, while the fourth is a galaxy-scale Einstein ring produced by a lens galaxy at $z_\mathrm{d}=0.235$. This work represents a proof of concept for the exploitation of Euclid slitless spectroscopic data in the study of strong gravitational lensing, providing one of the first determinations of spectroscopic redshifts for strongly lensed features from NISP spectra. These results demonstrate the feasibility of applying the same methodology to the very large sample of gravitational lenses that Euclid has started to discover and is expected to identify over the course of the mission.

conclusions: Successfully determined the spectroscopic redshifts for four benchmark strong-lensing systems: two cluster-scale giant arcs at $z_s = 1.771 \pm 0.006$ (SPT-CLJ0411$-$4819) and $z_s = 1.670 \pm 0.012$ (Abell 2280), and two galaxy-scale systems at $z_s = 1.366 \pm 0.008$ (the Einstein ring PS1J1821+7130) and $z_s = 2.649 \pm 0.007$ (the quad WHJ181607.9$+$681651).

Identified prominent rest-frame optical lines including $\mathrm{H}\alpha$, $[\mathrm{O}\,\textsc{iii}]\,\lambda 500.8\,\mathrm{nm}$, and $\mathrm{H}\beta$ in the near-infrared, yielding spectroscopic redshifts that agree with multi-band photometric redshift estimates and independent DESI ground-based spectroscopy.

Reconstructed 2D continuum-subtracted emission-line maps whose spatial morphology closely matches the VIS/NISP photometric images, confirming that the detected lines belong to the lensed background sources rather than unassociated line-of-sight contaminants.

Established a viable methodology and pipeline for measuring arc redshifts and identifying multiple images from Euclid NISP slitless spectroscopy alone, paving the way for self-contained strong-lensing mass modeling across the vast sample expected from the full survey.

ai.summary: Strong gravitational lensing—where the intense gravitational field of a foreground galaxy or cluster bends light from a background source into multiple images or giant arcs—is an exquisite tool for mapping cosmic mass distributions, but converting these image configurations into precise physical models requires knowing the exact redshifts of the background sources. Because Euclid observes without physical slits ('slitless spectroscopy' with the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer, NISP), light across the entire field of view is dispersed onto the detector at once, making the extraction and line identification of faint, spatially extended arcs technically challenging. In this Euclid DR1 proof-of-concept study, the authors develop and demonstrate an analysis pipeline to extract 1D spectra, measure spectroscopic redshifts, and reconstruct 2D emission-line maps for four strongly lensed systems (two cluster arcs and two galaxy-scale lenses). By recovering key nebular emission lines such as $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ and $[\mathrm{O}\,\textsc{iii}]$ and proving that their 2D line morphology matches visual imaging, this work confirms that Euclid slitless spectroscopy can independently calibrate the thousands of strong lenses expected over the mission's lifetime without relying entirely on ground-based spectroscopic follow-up.

papers.title: FastBox: A lightweight Python package for rapid cosmological 21cm intensity mapping simulations
papers.authors: Philip Bull, Bruno B. Bizarria, Melis O. Irfan, Geoff Murphy
papers.abstract: FastBox is a Python package for generating fast, physically realistic simulations of cosmological signals in three-dimensional co-moving boxes, with the primary focus of its application being 21cm intensity mapping (IM) experiments. It provides a framework for producing cosmology-dependent Gaussian and log-normal density fields, as well as modelling the effects of redshift-space distortions and linear biasing, among others. Models of instrumental systematics are incorporated, including radiometer noise and beam convolutions. Diffuse and point source foreground models are included, along with a number of foreground filtering strategies such as PCA, ICA, and transfer function correction via mock signal injection. Lastly, estimators are provided for power spectra, the two-point correlation function, and the equilateral bispectrum. The same underlying density field can also be Poisson-sampled into a discrete galaxy catalogue, so that 21cm and galaxy tracers are simulated from common initial conditions and their cross-power spectrum can be measured. Simulation grids may be cubic or anisotropic, with independent side lengths and cell counts along each Cartesian axis. FastBox is designed as a lightweight but realistic test-bench for the development and validation of end-to-end cosmological analysis pipelines.

conclusions: **Integrated end-to-end framework:** FastBox unifies fast cosmological field generation (interfacing with `pyccl` for non-linear matter spectra), log-normal density transforms, and redshift-space distortions on arbitrary cubic or anisotropic grids without heavy external dependencies.

**Instrumental and foreground realism:** Incorporates parameterised Galactic synchrotron and extragalactic point-source foregrounds, dish array radiometer noise, and telescope beam convolutions (Gaussian, KATBeam, Zernike).

**Signal restoration via transfer functions:** Implements PCA, ICA, and NMF foreground separation alongside mock signal injection to evaluate the transfer function $T(k)$, correcting for large-scale 21cm cosmological power loss induced by component separation.

**Multi-tracer cross-correlations & higher-order statistics:** Features Poisson-sampling for correlated galaxy catalogues to model HI-galaxy cross-spectra with gridding corrections, plus native estimators for the two-point correlation function and equilateral bispectrum $B(k, k, k)$.

ai.summary: In 21cm neutral hydrogen (HI) intensity mapping, telescopes map large-scale cosmic structure by measuring the diffuse aggregate emission of HI across cosmic time without resolving individual galaxies; however, astrophysical foregrounds from our Galaxy and extragalactic sources are several orders of magnitude brighter than this faint cosmological signal. To address the need for fast, realistic validation of analysis pipelines, the authors present `FastBox`, a lightweight, open-source Python package that generates three-dimensional cosmological mock data in co-moving boxes. The package couples log-normal density fields and redshift-space distortions with realistic Galactic synchrotron and point-source foregrounds, telescope beam models, and radiometer noise. It further includes foreground cleaning filters (PCA, ICA, NMF) with mock-injection transfer function corrections, multi-tracer galaxy catalogue generation for HI–galaxy cross-correlations, and summary statistic estimators including power spectra and the equilateral bispectrum. This provides an accessible, modular test-bench for validating foreground cleaning and pipeline systematics before deploying them on computationally expensive simulations or real survey data.
