papers.abstract: We present the pipeline design of the photometric redshift processing function for Data Release 1 (DR1) of the $Euclid$ mission, and the validation and performance of our cosmology-related products that are released as part of DR1-Foundation. The $Euclid$ mission aims to constrain the equation-of-state parameter of dark energy, $w$, to percent-level accuracy through the measurement of large-scale structure via weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering. As part of DR1-Foundation we release determinations of photometric redshifts (photo-$z$), corrected photometry, and object classes that are used to form the basis of the cosmological samples. The release furthermore includes estimates of the spectral energy distributions of stars and galaxies for the careful modelling of the point-spread function for weak-lensing measurement. We estimate the performance of the photo-$z$ point estimates and probability distribution functions using overlapping spectroscopic redshifts, which are weighted to match different flux-limited target samples. We find that the current performance is somewhat below mission design requirements ($40\%$ in scatter and a factor of 2 in outlier fraction) at the nominal survey depth ($I_{\rm E}<24.5$), but closely matching requirements at slightly brighter magnitudes ($I_{\rm E}<24$), consistent with pre-launch analyses and the slightly shallower external data (up to $0.3\,\mathrm{mag}$) with respect to end-of-mission expectations. Data from Rubin-LSST will help alleviate this issue by the time of the final cosmology analyses. The other cosmology-related outputs are tested to the extent that is possible with currently available comparison data. This paper is partnered by an article describing the measurement of the physical properties of galaxies for the purpose of non-cosmological science.

conclusions: **Photo-$z$ pipeline and core DR1 products:** The pipeline successfully implements the `NNPZ` nearest-neighbour method calibrated on deep COSMOS photometry to generate individual redshift PDFs, star/galaxy/AGN classifications, and SED templates for chromatic PSF modelling across 93.6% of DR1 tiles (~95% of the usable survey area).

**Performance vs. mission requirements:** At the nominal survey depth limit ($I_{\rm E} < 24.5$), the photo-$z$ scatter is $\sim 40\%$ above and the catastrophic outlier fraction is a factor of $\sim 2$ higher than strict mission requirements, though performance meets requirements at brighter flux levels ($I_{\rm E} < 24.0$).

**Impact of auxiliary ground-based data:** The faint-end performance shortfall is primarily caused by external optical ground-based imaging being up to $0.3\,\mathrm{mag}$ shallower than end-of-mission targets; this will be resolved in future releases by deeper ground imaging, notably from the Rubin Observatory (LSST).

**Classification and SED validation:** Star/galaxy classification matches DESI spectroscopic labels with high stellar purity and high galaxy completeness; stellar SED templates faithfully reproduce continuous Gaia spectra in the South, while galaxy SED effective wavelengths still require expanded spectroscopic training sets to meet final mission precision.

These products define the observational foundation of the upcoming DR1 cosmological analyses, with future depth enhancements—especially from the Rubin-LSST survey—expected to bring faint-end photo-$z$ precision into full mission compliance.

papers.title: Transient early reionization allows for a high optical depth while remaining consistent with kSZ measurements
papers.authors: Prakhar Bansal, Nicholas Kern, Dragan Huterer
papers.abstract: Recent works have shown that a CMB optical depth of $\tau\approx0.09$, above the Planck low-$\ell$ polarization value of 0.054, would weaken the preference of DESI data for dynamical dark energy and for a low neutrino mass. Apart from the low-$\ell$ CMB, another probe that prefers a $\tau\sim0.055$ is the kinetic Sunyaev--Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect when combined with the end of hydrogen reionization as measured by the Ly$\alpha$ forest. In this work we use a new self-consistent model of supermassive Population~III stars, which partially ionize the intergalactic medium at high redshifts ($z\approx20$--$25$), to predict the kSZ signal. We show that such an early, transient reionization phase can raise $\tau$ to $\approx0.09$ while remaining consistent with current kSZ and Ly-$\alpha$ forest constraints. We forecast that the Simons Observatory, combined with Ly-$\alpha$ forest and UV luminosity function data, can constrain the optical depth accumulated above $z=12$ to $\pm0.008$ in our fiducial supermassive Pop~III scenario.

conclusions: **Early flash reionization can yield $\tau \approx 0.1$ without altering the end of reionization:** A transient ionization phase from supermassive Pop~III.1 stars at $z \approx 20$--$25$ (peaking at $23\%$ ionized fraction) adds $\Delta\tau = 0.037$ to reach $\tau = 0.096$, with $95\%$ of this excess accumulated at $z > 12$, leaving the late-time reionization history and Lyman-$\alpha$ constraints ($z_{90} \approx 6.0$) completely intact.

**Small bubble sizes hide the signal from current $\ell = 3000$ kSZ limits:** Because the early ionized regions are compact ($R_{\rm HII} \approx 1.5\,{\rm cMpc}$), their patchy kSZ power peaks at very small angular scales ($\ell \approx 1.7 \times 10^4$). At the standard benchmark $\ell = 3000$, the flash adds only $0.48\,\mu{\rm K}^2$ (yielding $D_{3000}^{\rm pkSZ} = 2.13\,\mu{\rm K}^2$), which remains consistent with current SPT-3G upper limits that strongly penalize extended galaxy-driven reionization models.

**Simons Observatory multi-band kSZ can directly isolate early optical depth:** Assuming negligible early reionization biases kSZ-inferred $\tau$ toward low values. By measuring the pkSZ spectrum across multiple multipole bins ($\ell = 3000$--$6000$) with the Simons Observatory and anchoring late-time reionization with Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data, future surveys can break this degeneracy and measure the early optical depth to $\sigma(\tau_{z>12}) \approx 0.008$.

However, high values of $\tau$ are traditionally thought to be ruled out by the patchy kinetic Sunyaev–Zel'dovich (pkSZ) effect—Doppler shifts from CMB photons scattering off moving ionized gas bubbles—combined with Lyman-$\alpha$ forest constraints on when reionization ends. In this work, the authors simulate an early, transient "flash" of reionization at $z \approx 20$--$25$ powered by hypothetical supermassive Population~III.1 stars using the semi-numerical code `21cmFAST`. They demonstrate that because these early ionized relics are very small, their pkSZ power peaks at very high multipoles ($\ell \sim 1.7 \times 10^4$) and easily evades current upper limits at $\ell = 3000$, allowing a high optical depth ($\tau \approx 0.096$) while predicting distinct high-$\ell$ signatures testable with the Simons Observatory.

papers.title: A flash before dawn: 21 cm signatures of transient reionization from supermassive Pop III stars
papers.authors: Nicholas Kern, Prakhar Bansal, Dragan Huterer
papers.abstract: Recent data from cosmological galaxy surveys combined with cosmic microwave background (CMB) data give a preference for a departure from $\Lambda$CDM, favoring a model with an evolving dark energy equation of state or a small neutrino mass. However, recent works have shown that the electron scattering optical depth to the CMB ($\tau$) can reduce this preference if $\tau\sim0.09$, larger than that preferred by CMB low-$\ell$ E-mode polarization data. With standard monotonic hydrogen reionization histories, such a high value of $\tau$ is in strong tension with spectroscopic galaxy data constraining the end of reionization. Thus, high-$\tau$ models are restricted to non-standard reionization scenarios, where astrophysical sources inject an appreciable amount of ionizing photons at early times. One recently studied model for this is a supermassive population III star scenario, where radiative feedback from a self-annihilating dark matter particle enables a pathway to form $M\sim10^5 M_\odot$ stars that, upon collapse, photoionize a surrounding volume large enough to source appreciable contributions to $\tau$ as a population. Here we present the first self-consistent treatment of the feedback from these supermassive population III stars within a large semi-numerical cosmological simulation, accounting for their ionizing, Lyman-Werner, and X-ray feedback on the intergalactic medium. We use it to predict the distinct signatures on the large-scale 21 cm signal at Cosmic Dawn, and forecast its detectability. We find that the 21 cm power spectrum probed by future radio survey arrays like the Square Kilometre Array could detect signatures of these supermassive population III at high significance and set model-dependent constraints on $\tau$ that approach $\sigma_\tau\sim0.012$, enough to distinguish our fiducial $\tau\sim0.097$ scenario from current Planck values at $>3\sigma$.

conclusions: **Distinct 21 cm signature at Cosmic Dawn**: Supermassive Pop III stars shift the global 21 cm Lyman-$\\alpha$ absorption trough to $z > 20$ and substantially boost the high-redshift 21 cm power spectrum, driven primarily by strong kinetic temperature ($T_K$) contrasts between hot relic HII bubbles ($T \\sim 10^4\\text{ K}$) and the surrounding cold, adiabatically expanding IGM.

**High-significance detection with SKA-Low**: Next-generation radio interferometry with SKA-Low will be capable of detecting this early power spectrum enhancement at high statistical significance, distinguishing it from standard Pop II galaxy-driven reionization models.

**Independent constraints on $\\tau$**: Mock observations yield a projected precision on the optical depth of $\\sigma_\\tau \\sim 0.012$, which is sufficient to differentiate a high-optical-depth scenario (fiducial $\\tau \\approx 0.097$) from the Planck value ($\\tau \\approx 0.054$) at $>3\\sigma$ without relying on low-$\\ell$ CMB polarization data.

**Self-regulating transient phase**: The combination of isolation exclusion zones, Lyman-Werner suppression of $H_2$ cooling, and late-time IGM X-ray pre-heating naturally halts supermassive Pop III formation by $z \\sim 15$, keeping the early ionized flash decoupled from late-time ($z \\sim 5.5$) quasar absorption constraints.

To achieve this without violating late-time quasar Lyman-$\\alpha$ forest limits, hypothetical supermassive Population III stars—which could grow to $\\sim 10^5\\,M_\\odot$ in pristine halo cores sustained by dark matter annihilation heating before collapsing—can trigger a transient burst of early reionization at $z > 15$. In this work, the authors implement the first self-consistent treatment of radiative feedback from these supermassive Pop III stars within the semi-numerical simulation code `21cmFAST`, tracking ionizing, Lyman-Werner, and X-ray emission alongside relic bubble cooling and recombinations. They model the resulting 21 cm brightness temperature fluctuations across Cosmic Dawn and forecast their detectability with the upcoming Square Kilometre Array (SKA-Low). This provides a concrete framework to test whether high-redshift Pop III astrophysics can account for an elevated $\\tau$ independently of large-angle CMB polarization systematics.

papers.title: Shear, vorticity, and $f(R)$ theories
papers.authors: Antonino Del Popolo
papers.abstract: We study how an extended spherical collapse model (ESCM), including shear, vorticity and chameleon screening, modifies the collapse threshold $\delta_c(z)$ and $\delta_c(M)$, the turnaround density $\delta_t$, the turnaround radius $R_t$ and the halo mass function in the Hu-Sawicki $f(R)$ model, and whether these quantities can distinguish $f(R)$ from General Relativity (GR). Unlike the standard spherical collapse model (SSCM), in the ESCM $\delta_c$ depends on mass, redshift and $|f_{R0}|$; we use it to compute the halo mass function with the excursion set approach. Between GR and the large-field (LF) limit of $f(R)$, $\delta_c$ differs by a few percent within the ESCM and by about 20% between GR in the ESCM and the LF limit in the SSCM; $\delta_t$ differs by about 27-29% and $R_t$ by about 6.5%. With screening, the difference between GR and screened $\delta_c$ is 2.5% for $|f_{R0}|=10^{-4}$ (F4) and vanishes for $|f_{R0}|=10^{-6}$ (F6); for $\delta_t$ it is larger than 20% (F4), about 10% (F5) and 0 (F6); for $R_t$ about 6.5% (F4), 3% (F5) and 0 (F6). Since observations exclude F4 and F6 is practically identical to GR, only F5 could discriminate, but the ~20% uncertainty on measured turnaround radii rules out $R_t$ and related quantities as tests of $f(R)$. The halo abundance predicted by $f(R)$, especially at high redshift, can instead distinguish $f(R)$ from GR.

conclusions: **Impact of shear and vorticity vs modified gravity**: Non-radial shear and vorticity from surrounding tidal fields act as effective rotational support opposing collapse, increasing the linear collapse threshold $\delta_c$ by $\sim 20\%$ relative to the standard spherical collapse model; this stabilizing effect dominates over the gravitational boost from $f(R)$, which only modifies $\delta_c$ by $\sim 1.7\text{--}2.5\%$.

**Turnaround density and radius variations**: In the extended spherical collapse model, the turnaround overdensity $\delta_t$ deviates from GR by $>20\%$ for F4 ($|f_{R0}|=10^{-4}$), $\sim 10\%$ for F5 ($|f_{R0}|=10^{-5}$), and vanishes for F6 ($|f_{R0}|=10^{-6}$), while the turnaround radius $R_t$ shifts by $\sim 6.5\%$ (F4), $\sim 3\%$ (F5), and $\sim 0\%$ (F6).

**Turnaround radius ruled out as an observational test**: Because current cluster observations already constrain $|f_{R0}| \lesssim 10^{-4.5}$ (ruling out F4) and F6 is virtually indistinguishable from GR, only F5 is theoretically viable to test; however, typical observational uncertainties on measured cluster turnaround radii are $\sim 20\%$, rendering $R_t$ incapable of discriminating $f(R)$ from GR.

**High-redshift halo mass function remains viable**: In contrast to turnaround radii, the excursion-set halo mass function computed with the mass- and redshift-dependent collapse barrier exhibits enhanced halo abundance in $f(R)$ that grows with redshift, maintaining cluster counts as a promising probe for future surveys.

In modified gravity theories such as Hu–Sawicki $f(R)$, an additional scalar degree of freedom enhances gravity via a fifth force, which is dynamically suppressed in high-density regions through the chameleon screening mechanism. In this paper, the author develops an Extended Spherical Collapse Model (ESCM) that incorporates realistic environmental tidal shear, vorticity, and chameleon screening for the F4, F5, and F6 variants of Hu–Sawicki gravity to calculate corrections to $\delta_c(M, z)$, the turnaround overdensity $\delta_t$, the turnaround radius $R_t$, and the resulting excursion-set halo mass function. The author demonstrates that while shear and vorticity provide significant dynamical support that delays collapse, existing $\sim 20\%$ observational uncertainties on cluster turnaround radii prevent $R_t$ from distinguishing viable $f(R)$ models (such as F5) from General Relativity, leaving high-redshift halo abundance as the primary discriminative probe.

papers.title: Origin of the angular momentum of filaments in the local Universe
papers.authors: V.G. Gurzadyan, N.N. Fimin, V.M. Chechetkin
papers.abstract: Velocity gradients compatible with rotation have been reported across certain nearby cosmic filaments. We show that rotational momentum might be generated in filaments in the local Universe in the presence of a cosmological constant (local dark energy) based on the theorem stating the general function for the equivalence of the gravitational field of a sphere and that of a point mass. We investigated how the cosmological constant modifies the finite-time acquisition and retention of angular momentum in an open filamentary core. Although its isotropic force exerts no direct axial torque, rotational motion can be seeded by tidal interactions with surrounding matter and incoming streams. Early tidal torques establish an imbalance in axial angular momentum, while the subsequent orbit crossing amplifies the resulting rotation, and ultimately, the cosmological constant is able to modify tidal-mode growth and finite-time angular momentum delivery.

conclusions: **Zero direct axial torque from $\Lambda$**: Because the cosmological constant exerts a purely isotropic, radial acceleration ($\ddot{\boldsymbol{r}}_\Lambda = \omega_\Lambda^2 \boldsymbol{r}$ with $\omega_\Lambda^2 = c^2\Lambda/3$), it cannot directly torque the filament ($\partial_\phi \Phi_\Lambda = 0$); its effect is entirely indirect via altering stream trajectories and arrival times.

**Tidal mode modification**: In the linearized Jacobi equation for trajectory separation, $\Lambda$ lowers the effective restoring tidal curvature ($\ddot{\xi}_i + (\mu_i - \omega_\Lambda^2)\xi_i = 0$), turning marginally stable or restoring matter tides ($0 < \mu_i < \omega_\Lambda^2$) into exponentially growing modes with growth rate $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\omega_\Lambda^2 - \mu_i}$.

**Condition for true spin-up**: Increasing angular momentum alone does not guarantee an increased spin rate; rotational acceleration requires the fractional angular momentum delivery to outpace the growth of the moment of inertia, $\dot{L}_z/L_z > \dot{I}/I$, which depends critically on the radial redistribution of infalling mass.

**Differential delay boosts net rotation**: In an idealized 1 Mpc cylindrical potential with counter-infalling streams, $\Lambda$ delays stream crossing times by $\sim 0.07\text{--}0.16\text{ Gyr}$, reducing cancellation between opposing flows and yielding a $6.6\%$ higher angular momentum ($L_z \approx 1.70 \times 10^8\,M_\odot\text{ Mpc}^2\text{ Gyr}^{-1}$) and a $7.3\%$ higher effective spin ($\Omega \approx 33.6\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$ vs $31.3\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$) after 5 Gyr.

ai.summary: Recent spectroscopic observations have uncovered surprising transverse velocity gradients across several 10–15 Mpc cosmic filaments at low redshift, suggesting that these massive structures of the cosmic web may actually rotate. In this paper, the authors investigate whether late-time dark energy (modeled as a local repulsive Hooke-type force proportional to the cosmological constant, $\Lambda$) can influence how an open cylindrical filament core acquires its spin. Because an isotropic expansion force exerts no direct axial torque on matter, the authors model how $\Lambda$ modifies the linearized Jacobi tidal equations of infalling cold matter streams and shifts the timing of boundary mass flux across the filament. They show that by altering trajectory divergence and delaying counter-rotating stream arrivals, $\Lambda$ can reduce destructive cancellations between opposing flows and modestly boost the net spin-up of local filaments.

papers.title: Galaxy Clustering Topology in Observations and Cosmological Simulations
papers.authors: Fuyu Dong, Changbom Park
papers.abstract: We present a genus topology analysis of the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data (SDSS), comparing the observed topology with mock galaxy samples from the Horizon Run 4 (HR4) $N$-body simulation and four cosmological hydrodynamical simulations. We construct nine volume-limited samples and measure their genus curves at Gaussian smoothing scales of $4$--$12~h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$. Overall, the modern galaxy models reproduce the observed genus statistics substantially better than the HGC, HOD, and SAM models examined by Choi et al. (2010). Among the models considered here, the HR4 Most-Bound-Halo Particle galaxy-assignment model shows somewhat better overall agreement with the SDSS topology than IllustrisTNG300 and FLAMINGO. The observed scale dependences of the genus shift parameter $\Delta\nu_f$ and void abundance parameter $A_V$ are somewhat steeper than those predicted by the simulations, but their joint discrepancy from HR4 is not statistically significant. The smaller-volume TNG100 and EAGLE realizations show significant excesses in $A_C$, at $4.5\sigma$ and $7.0\sigma$, respectively, relative to the observational uncertainties. When the expected cosmic variance of the simulations is taken into account, they do not necessarily indicate failures of the galaxy-formation prescriptions, but they caution that individual small-volume realizations may not be representative of the observed galaxy topology. Overall, modern galaxy formation models reproduce the observed topology substantially better than earlier models, while residual differences remain that can be tested more precisely with denser future surveys.

conclusions: **Improved galaxy–halo modeling:** Modern galaxy assignment methods—in particular HR4 using Most-Bound-Halo Particles (MBP)—and large hydrodynamical simulations (TNG300, FLAMINGO) reproduce the observed SDSS genus topology significantly better than older halo-galaxy correspondence (HGC), halo occupation distribution (HOD), or semi-analytic models (SAMs).

**Cosmology-sensitive genus amplitude:** The observed genus amplitude $g R_G^3$ is slightly elevated ($1\text{--}2\sigma$) relative to the HR4 fiducial cosmology ($\Omega_m = 0.26$), but aligns with HR4 when rescaled to a higher matter density ($\Omega_m = 0.305$), reflecting the genus amplitude's sensitivity to the matter power spectrum shape.

**Scale-dependence and cosmic variance:** SDSS exhibits steeper scale dependence in the genus shift parameter $\Delta\nu_f$ and void abundance $A_V$ than predicted by HR4, but accounting for correlated mock volumes yields a joint discrepancy probability of $7.3\%$, indicating statistical consistency with cosmic variance.

**Caution with small simulation boxes:** TNG100 and EAGLE display large nominal excesses in isolated cluster abundance $A_C$ ($4.5\sigma$ and $7.0\sigma$ over SDSS uncertainties), which drop to $1.7\sigma$ and $2.3\sigma$ once simulation cosmic variance is incorporated, underscoring that $\sim 100\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$ boxes are too small to represent cosmic topology.

The genus statistic uses the Gauss–Bonnet theorem on smoothed density contours to measure the connectivity and topology of large-scale structure, distinguishing between isolated clusters, voids, and sponge-like filamentary networks. In this work, the authors measure the redshift-space genus curves across smoothing scales of $4\text{--}12\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$ using nine volume-limited galaxy samples from SDSS DR7, comparing them against mock catalogs from the Horizon Run 4 (HR4) $N$-body simulation and four modern cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (IllustrisTNG300, FLAMINGO, TNG100, and EAGLE). They find that modern galaxy-halo assignments—especially HR4's Most-Bound-Halo-Particle method—and hydro simulations reproduce observed topological structures substantially better than older semi-analytic and simple halo occupation models, though small-volume simulations suffer from extreme cosmic variance that severely biases topological measurements.

papers.title: Minimal vacuum histories beyond $Λ$CDM: model comparison within VCDM
papers.authors: Antonio De Felice, Eleonora Di Valentino, Luis Escamilla Torres, Jack Zidich
papers.abstract: Recent cosmological observations motivate alternatives to $\Lambda$CDM with evolving dark energy. We compare three such models, each introducing one additional cosmological parameter: F42, with equation of state $w(a)=w_0/\sqrt{a}$, and two smooth sign-changing effective dark-energy profiles, Ag and Qui. All models are implemented within VCDM, which determines the background and linear perturbations without introducing an additional propagating gravitational degree of freedom. We use CMB observations from SPT, Planck, and ACT, combined with DESI DR2 distance measurements, with and without the DESY5 Dovekie supernova sample. All three alternatives improve the best-fit likelihood relative to $\Lambda$CDM. When supernovae are included, the Akaike information criterion favors F42, while Ag and Qui remain nearly indistinguishable from $\Lambda$CDM on this criterion. The Bayesian evidence, however, does not establish a robust preference among the three alternatives. Our results show that improved fits to current observations can arise from physically different dark-energy histories, motivating complementary measurements of expansion and structure growth to distinguish them.

conclusions: All three one-parameter VCDM extensions improve the maximum-likelihood fit over $\Lambda$CDM when fitted to CMB, DESI DR2, and DESY5 Dovekie data ($\mathcal{D}_1$), with F42 favored by AIC ($\Delta\widehat{\mathrm{AIC}} = -4.02$), whereas Ag and Qui show marginal AIC improvements ($\Delta\widehat{\mathrm{AIC}} \approx -0.25$).

Bayesian model selection yields inconclusive Bayes factors once prior volume effects and numerical/box-boundary corrections are included, showing no robust statistical evidence favoring any alternative over $\Lambda$CDM.

The models predict divergent background parameters: F42 favors lower expansion and higher matter density ($H_0 = 67.40^{+0.53}_{-0.50}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, $\Omega_m = 0.3144 \pm 0.0048$, with phantom crossing at $z_\times \approx 0.42$), whereas Ag and Qui favor higher expansion and lower matter density ($H_0 \approx 68.70\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, $\Omega_m \approx 0.3030$, with sign transitions centered at $z_\dagger \approx 2.7$).

All three alternatives shift the structure growth parameter upwards to $S_8 \approx 0.834\text{--}0.837$ (compared to $0.822 \pm 0.006$ in $\Lambda$CDM), underscoring that geometric data alone cannot uniquely resolve the nature of dark energy without complementary structure growth constraints from surveys like Euclid.

To test whether minimal extensions can explain these trends without adding new propagating gravitational degrees of freedom, the authors implement three single-parameter dark energy histories within VCDM (a type-II minimally modified gravity theory where background and linear perturbations are consistently derived from an auxiliary potential). They examine F42 (a smooth equation-of-state parameterization $w(a) = w_0/\sqrt{a}$) alongside two smooth sign-changing dark energy density profiles ('Ag' and 'Qui') using joint CMB (Planck, ACT, SPT), DESI DR2 BAO (including Ly$\alpha$ Alcock–Paczyński info), and DESY5 Dovekie supernova data. papers.title: Euclid First Data Release 1 (DR1) - Data release overview
papers.authors: Euclid Collaboration : Herve Aussel
papers.abstract: This paper describes the contents of the Euclid First Data Release (DR1), together with the set of papers that document the data-processing and the data products. DR1 consists of two parts: first `DR1-Foundation', releasing images, spectra, and catalogues in November 2026. Second, the shear measurements and the `Level~3' products required for cosmological analyses will be added in June 2027 to complete the full DR1. This data set contains around a billion catalogued objects, mainly from the Euclid Wide Survey (1975\,deg$^2$) and the Euclid Deep Fields (77\,deg$^2$)

conclusions: **Staggered DR1 release strategy**: DR1 is split into *DR1-Foundation* (November 2026; delivering calibrated images, spectra, and source catalogues) and *Full DR1* (June 2027; adding shape measurements, Level 3 clustering/weak lensing correlation functions, and cosmological analyses) after finding that the initial VIS point-spread function (PSF) model underestimated PSF size, which would have compromised shear calibration.

**Survey coverage and footprint**: Encompasses $\sim 12$ months of validated survey operations covering $1975\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ in the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and $77\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ in the Euclid Deep Fields (EDS), omitting an initial $\sim 3$-month 'ice age' of VIS throughput loss that was successfully cured by thermal decontamination.

**Unprecedented source counts**: Releases $\sim 1.7\,\mathrm{PB}$ of data cataloguing over one billion total objects, including 818 million wide-survey galaxies with photometric redshifts and classification, alongside 60 million quasar candidates.

**Deep slitless spectroscopy**: Extracts over 170 million 1D spectra from NISP dispersed images down to $H_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} < 23.5$ (a full magnitude deeper than the early Q1 release), with spectroscopic redshift comparisons against DESI halving the scatter seen in Q1.

**High operational reliability**: Pre-planned telemetry and science retrieval exceeded 99%, with completed nominal VIS exposures reaching 87% of schedule (meeting mission specs) and post-decontamination VIS throughput remaining stable to within $1\text{--}1.5\%$ over 2.5 years.

ai.summary: Euclid is ESA's flagship space mission designed to probe dark energy, dark matter, and gravity through two primary cosmological probes: cosmic shear (weak gravitational lensing) from high-resolution imaging and large-scale galaxy clustering from slitless spectroscopy. This overview paper details the contents and data-processing architecture of Euclid's First Data Release (DR1), representing approximately one year of survey operations. The consortium adopts a two-stage release schedule: 'DR1-Foundation' is released now with calibrated images, extracted spectra, and multi-band catalogues, whereas the Level 3 cosmological products—including shape measurements, cosmic shear catalogues, and correlation functions—are deferred to June 2027 to resolve a point-spread function (PSF) modeling issue that underestimated the VIS PSF size. Across roughly $2000\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ of the Wide and Deep surveys, DR1-Foundation catalogues over one billion sources (including nearly 820 million wide-survey galaxies with photometric redshifts) and extracts over 170 million near-infrared spectra down to $H_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E} < 23.5$. This milestone release provides the observational foundation and data-quality benchmarks that will underpin upcoming cosmological analyses and large-scale structure tests.

papers.abstract: Accurate photometric-redshift estimation and calibration of the weak-lensing point-spread function (PSF) for Euclid require complementary ground-based optical imaging with high photometric precision and spatial homogeneity. The Organisation Unit for External Data (OU-EXT) integrates heterogeneous ground-based surveys into the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), delivering uniformly calibrated, co-added images, and associated PSF models. To minimise systematics in spectral energy distribution (SED) reconstruction and photometric-redshift estimation, these data must achieve relative photometric stability at the $\sim$10 mmag level on Euclid-tile scales. We present the ground-based imaging component of Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), comprising $\sim2500$ deg$^2$ across the wide, deep, and auxiliary fields. We summarise the OU-EXT production workflow and validation framework, and quantify the achieved data quality of the co-added products in terms of depth, photometric zero-point stability, and spatial colour homogeneity. In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the point-source $10\sigma$ depths in the $griz$ bands reach 24.8/24.3/24.0/23.0 AB mag, with the deep fields extending 1--2 magnitudes deeper. Most EWS DR1 tiles meet the 10 mmag relative photometric requirement, with 1.1% and 1.5% showing offsets exceeding 50 mmag in the northern and southern hemispheres, respectively. Spatial colour variations remain typically below 5--10 mmag across the southern EWS footprint, while larger residual structures of 10--25 mmag appear in some northern regions. These results demonstrate that the EXT production chain provides a largely homogeneous framework for integrating ground-based datasets into Euclid, while identifying calibration and co-addition limitations that have to be addressed in DR2 to meet the mission's most stringent cosmological requirements. (Abridged)

conclusions: Delivered uniformly calibrated $ugriz$ co-added image stacks, PSF models, and weight maps across $\sim 2500\text{ deg}^2$ for Euclid DR1, combining heterogeneous ground surveys (CFHT/MegaCam, Subaru/HSC, Pan-STARRS1, and DECam).
Achieved $10\sigma$ point-source depths in the Euclid Wide Survey of $24.8, 24.3, 24.0,$ and $23.0$ AB mag in $g, r, i, z$, with $78\text{--}98\%$ of tiles meeting nominal mission depth requirements.

Demonstrated relative photometric stability at the required $\sim 10\text{ mmag}$ ($1\%$) level across $>95\%$ of EWS-South tiles using Gaia XP synthetic photometry, while northern tiles show larger residual spatial variations ($10\text{--}25\text{ mmag}$) slated for pipeline refinement in DR2.

ai.summary: To measure accurate photometric redshifts (photo-$z$) and calibrate point-spread function (PSF) colour dependencies for weak lensing, Euclid requires broad optical colour information ($u, g, r, i, z$) that its spaceborne instruments cannot capture alone. The Organisation Unit for External Data (OU-EXT) homogenises and recalibrates heterogeneous ground-based imaging from CFHT, Subaru HSC, Pan-STARRS1, and DECam onto the Euclid survey tiling. This Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) paper presents the pipeline and validation of $\sim 2500\text{ deg}^2$ of co-added ground-based imaging tied to a common Gaia XP spectrophotometric standard. Establishing this optical calibration across wide and deep survey footprints is essential to keep systematic errors in tomographic redshift distributions below the strict tolerances required for precision cosmology.

papers.abstract: This paper describes the Euclid DR1 photometric masks, which trace spatial variations in the survey properties (e.g. satellite position angles, integration time, sky tiling, and survey footprint); in the instrumental performance of Euclid and the external data (EXT) it uses (e.g. survey coverage, depth, PSF width, quality flags, systematic effects and astrometric uncertainties); and in possible contamination from sky emission (e.g. galactic extinction and zodiacal light emission). Among this, the effective coverage mask is particularly important as it defines the effective survey area and can be used to exclude spurious objects when selecting Euclid photometric samples for scientific analyses. The Euclid photometric masks are built for each observed sky region (tile) and are provided as full-sky HEALPix maps (nested ordering and explicit indexing) at Nside = 16 384, equating to a resolution of 12"88, for both the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and Euclid Deep Survey (EDS). We estimate the total area of the DR1 EWS (EDS) to be 2008.8 (74.7) deg$^2$ and find that 82 (81)\% of this area is preserved by the effective coverage mask. We observe that Euclid's instrumental properties are consistent with expectations, showing only minor relative variations across the sky. For DR1 EWS the standard deviation of the depth (computed for a 2" aperture and at 5 $\sigma$) is below 0.2 AB mag, with median values of 25.69, 24.14, 24.3, and 24.29 for the Euclid IE, YE, JE, and HE bands. Finally, we expect these photometric masks to be key to many science applications and in particular for cosmological analyses.

conclusions: **High-resolution survey mapping**: The photometric masks are compiled into high-resolution HEALPix maps at $N_{\mathrm{side}} = 16\,384$ ($\approx 12.9''$ pixel resolution), characterizing exposure time, instrumental noise, PSF variations, Galactic extinction, and stellar contamination.

**Survey footprint and effective area**: Euclid DR1 covers $2008.8\ \mathrm{deg}^2$ in the Wide Survey (EWS) and $74.7\ \mathrm{deg}^2$ in the Deep Survey (EDS); after masking bright stars, diffraction spikes, and image defects, the clean effective coverage preserves $82\%$ ($1645\ \mathrm{deg}^2$) of EWS and $81\%$ of EDS.

**Instrumental stability and depth**: Spatial variations in depth across the wide survey are under $0.2\ \mathrm{mag}$, with median $5\sigma$ depths (2" aperture) reaching $25.69$ in the visual band ($I_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}$) and $24.14\text{--}24.30$ in the near-infrared bands ($Y_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, J_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, H_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}$).

**Deep fields performance**: Multiple overlapping visits in the Deep Survey smooth out instrumental patterns, yielding deeper median thresholds of $26.91$ in $I_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}$ and $\approx 25.3\text{--}25.5$ across near-infrared bands.

ai.summary: When measuring large-scale structure with galaxy surveys, variations in observing conditions, instrument sensitivity, and bright foreground stars can mimic real cosmological density fluctuations if not properly mapped out. This paper presents the official photometric masks for Euclid's Data Release 1 (DR1), providing pixel-level data products that track spatial variations in survey depth, point spread function (PSF) size, satellite pointing, and Galactic extinction across both the Wide and Deep surveys. The team produced full-sky HEALPix maps at $N_{\mathrm{side}} = 16\,384$ ($\approx 12.9''$ resolution) combining Euclid visual ($I_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}$) and near-infrared ($Y_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, J_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, H_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}$) bands with complementary ground-based optical data. Most importantly, they construct an "effective coverage mask" that cuts contaminated areas around bright stars and detector defects while preserving over $80\%$ of the survey footprint. These masks form the foundation for deriving unbiased selection and window functions needed in downstream galaxy clustering and weak lensing cosmological analyses.

papers.title: Kinessence, phantom crossing and sign-switching dark energy
papers.authors: Philippe Brax, Tom Canaguier, Andrei Lazanu
papers.abstract: We introduce Kinessence models where combining K-mouflage and quintessence leads to phantom-crossing of the dark energy equation of state and sign-switching of the dark energy density. This is realised by joining a dark scalar sector comprising K-essence kinetic terms and a quintessence potential together with a Yukawa coupling to matter. We investigate the dynamics of these models in the Jordan frame at the background and perturbative levels. We concentrate on the effective equation of state and the matter fraction for the background. The CMB spectra, the linear power spectrum and the growth of structure via $f\sigma_8$ are also analysed at the perturbative level. The quintessence potential drives the acceleration of the Universe at low redshift with an equation of state greater than -1. The Yukawa coupling to matter leads to a phantom crossing behaviour depending on its strength. The potential fifth force mediated by the scalar field is screened by the K-mouflage mechanism triggered by the K-essence kinetic terms and passes Solar System tests. This allows for relatively large Yukawa couplings to matter $\beta\sim 0.1$, large enough to lead to the crossing of the phantom divide at $z\sim 0.5$. Despite a significant scalar interaction on large scales, we find that the growth of structure is reduced compared to LCDM. The matter fraction deviates from the standard model by a few percent and the Hubble rate is larger at low redshift than at recombination whilst the CMB spectra show small deviations from LCDM. The dark energy fraction becomes negative at redshifts greater than 2. All these features should alleviate the various tensions such as the larger value of $H_0$ at small redshift, a possible reduction of growth as measured by $S_8$ and the bound on the sum of the neutrino masses. Deviations from LCDM of the CMB lensing spectrum may provide a detectable window for these models.

conclusions: **Phantom crossing via matter coupling:** Combining an exponential quintessence potential with a Yukawa coupling to matter ($\beta \sim 0.04\text{--}0.09$) naturally drives an effective equation of state that crosses the phantom divide ($w_{\rm DE} = -1$) at $z \approx 0.5$ and switches the dark energy density to negative values at $z > 2$, mimicking recent DESI trends without ghost instabilities.

**K-mouflage screening of fifth forces:** While a coupling $\beta \sim 0.1$ ordinarily violates Solar System gravity bounds, non-linear kinetic terms trigger K-mouflage screening; an $\arctan(\chi)$ kinetic function successfully satisfies both the Cassini tracking and lunar periastron constraints.

**Suppression of structure growth:** Despite introducing an attractive scalar fifth force, the coupled scalar increases cosmological Hubble friction, resulting in a net decrease in growth ($f\sigma_8$, with $\sigma_8 \approx 0.79\text{--}0.81$) and a lower matter fraction $\Omega_m$, simultaneously easing the $S_8$ and $H_0$ tensions.

**CMB consistency and lensing signatures:** Linear perturbation spectra computed with $\mathcal{H}$-EFTCAMB show only sub-percent to percent-level deviations in CMB temperature and polarization relative to $\Lambda$CDM, pointing to CMB lensing reconstruction (e.g. Simons Observatory, CMB-S4) as a crucial discriminant.

ai.summary: Recent observational hints from DESI BAO and supernovae suggest that dark energy might be dynamical, crossing the phantom divide ($w < -1$) and exhibiting a negative energy density at high redshift ($z > 2$), which standard quintessence models cannot achieve without pathological instabilities. To physically realize this behavior, the authors propose "Kinessence," a framework uniting non-canonical $K$-essence kinetic terms, an exponential runaway quintessence potential, and a conformal Yukawa coupling ($\beta \sim 0.1$) to matter in the Jordan frame. In this setup, the potential drives late-time cosmic acceleration with $w > -1$, the matter coupling forces the effective equation of state across the phantom line at $z \approx 0.5$, and non-linear kinetic gradients provide K-mouflage screening that suppresses the resulting fifth force in dense environments to pass Solar System tests. Using linear perturbation theory implemented in $\mathcal{H}$-EFTCAMB, they demonstrate that the model reduces linear structure growth (alleviating the $S_8$ tension) and accommodates a higher low-redshift expansion rate while keeping CMB temperature and polarization spectra compatible with Planck.

papers.title: Efficient Standard Siren Cosmological Inference with Posterior Reuse
papers.authors: Alexander Papadopoulos, Michael J. Williams, Christian E. A. Chapman-Bird, Rachel Gray, Christopher Messenger
papers.abstract: Standard siren cosmology depends on several modelling assumptions, including the underlying source population, galaxy catalogue, and detection selection function. Quantifying the effect of each choice typically requires a full, independent analysis. As gravitational-wave catalogs grow incrementally, much computational effort is spent re-analysing largely overlapping datasets. We apply the recently developed ASPIRE (Accelerated Sequential Posterior Inference via Reuse) sampler to the joint estimation of cosmological and population parameters with dark sirens. ASPIRE updates existing posterior samples into the posterior under a new hypothesis without restarting from the prior. It combines normalising flows with a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) scheme to produce accurate posteriors and unbiased evidence estimates. Applying ASPIRE to a number of dark siren analysis cases with GWTC-5.0, we recover posteriors consistent with nested sampling, while recording a performance improvement of between 6-28 times over the set of analyses when using an existing posterior. This enables efficient exploration of modelling choices and rapid updates as catalogs grow, without duplicating existing computational effort.

conclusions: Full posterior and evidence fidelity: ASPIRE posteriors matched benchmark nested sampling (dynesty) across all test cases within the empirical sampling noise floor (maximum marginal Jensen–Shannon divergence $D_{\mathrm{JS}}^{\mathrm{max}} < 4.2\text{ mnat}$), while returning fully consistent Bayesian evidences ($\Delta \ln Z$ consistent with zero, e.g., $+0.05 \pm 0.19$ for the spectral-to-dark transition).

Significant computational speed-ups: Reusing existing posteriors yielded acceleration factors between $6.6\times$ and $28.9\times$ on an Nvidia H100 GPU (e.g., dropping dark siren inference from $134.4\text{ hr}$ down to $4.6\text{ hr}$), requiring roughly an order of magnitude fewer likelihood evaluations.

Overcoming correlation shifts and proposal broadening: While SMC naturally excels at narrowing distributions, broadening a tight proposal or handling rotated parameter degeneracies (notably between $H_0$ and the low-mass binary black hole peak parameters $\lambda_g, \mu_{g,\mathrm{low}}$) can degrade sampling; the authors successfully resolved this by drawing those specific degenerate parameters from the prior while retaining proposal information for the remainder.

Superior robustness over naive importance sampling: Simple posterior- or flow-based importance sampling failed to yield adequate effective sample sizes whenever models or event catalogs changed substantially, whereas ASPIRE's tempered mutation steps smoothly bridged large distribution shifts without retaining residual bias from the flow.

ai.summary: In gravitational-wave (GW) cosmology, "standard sirens" (compact binary coalescences) provide direct measurements of luminosity distances, but without an electromagnetic counterpart, inferring the Hubble constant $H_0$ requires statistically associating mergers with galaxy catalogs ("dark sirens") or relying on features in the source mass distribution ("spectral sirens"). Constraining cosmology this way demands computationally demanding hierarchical Bayesian inference to jointly fit cosmological and astrophysical population parameters. Currently, testing different mass models, swapping galaxy catalogs, or adding newly detected events requires restarting nested sampling from scratch, discarding all previous computing investment. The authors apply ASPIRE (Accelerated Sequential Posterior Inference via Reuse)—a framework that trains a normalizing flow on an existing posterior and uses Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) with tempered annealing and MCMC mutations—to update standard siren analyses using the GWTC-5.0 catalog without restarting from the prior. They demonstrate that ASPIRE recovers unbiased posteriors and accurate Bayesian evidences while speeding up cosmological inference by factors of $6\times$ to $28\times$ compared to standard nested sampling.

papers.abstract: The Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) contains catalogues of sources covering 1900 deg2, including deep coverage of legacy fields that enable an extensive comparison between Euclid imaging and multiwavelength observations from other instruments. The Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field, observed by Euclid and included in DR1, has been observed with the James Webb Space Telescope, resulting in the COSMOS2025 catalogue. We compare the Euclid DR1 photometry with the multiwavelength COSMOS2025 data to assess the accuracy of the photometric measurements produced by the different methods implemented in the OU-MER pipeline. We use both the Euclid Wide and Deep Surveys, focussing exclusively on extragalactic sources. We use the fluxes of COSMOS2025 to predict the expected fluxes in the Euclid bands via spectral energy distribution fitting, while the redshifts are either spectroscopic, for a sample of brighter sources, or photometric, to include fainter sources. Both the fluxes in the common Hyper Suprime-Cam bands and the SEDs from COSMOS2025 are used to validate the analysis and to characterise any biases or limitations of the method. The predicted fluxes and the OU-MER measurements are in good agreement, especially for bright and isolated sources. Median offsets depend on band, photometric method, survey depth, and redshift sample, most well within 10%, the largest offset seen in the NIR bands for the deep photo-z model-fitting measurements. However, complementary measurements on Gaia stars show an opposite trend, highlighting that photometric validation approaches may suffer from intrinsic uncertainties that prevent a thorough assessment of systematic effects. Among the three methods, template-fitting photometry generally shows the smallest offset from the SED-based predictions in the NISP bands and toward fainter magnitudes, while aperture photometry and model-fitting are comparable in IE.

conclusions: Euclid DR1 photometric measurements generally agree with SED-based predictions to within $\sim 10\%$ across optical ($I_{\rm E}$) and near-infrared ($Y_{\rm E}, J_{\rm E}, H_{\rm E}$) bands, with measured fluxes typically a few percent brighter than predictions.

Template-fitting photometry (T-PHOT) delivers the highest accuracy and stability in the near-infrared bands and at faint magnitudes, whereas aperture photometry (A-PHOT) and profile model-fitting (SE++) yield comparable performance in the optical $I_{\rm E}$ band.

Offsets are slightly larger in the Deep survey than in the Wide survey, partly due to faint-end Eddington-like selection bias and intrinsic reference-catalogue/SED modeling uncertainties (which are themselves on the order of a few percent).

ai.summary: For wide-field cosmological surveys like Euclid, extracting accurate multi-band galaxy fluxes (photometry) is crucial for determining photometric redshifts and galaxy properties required for clustering and weak lensing. In this Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) paper, the collaboration validates the extragalactic photometry produced by the OU-MER pipeline by comparing Euclid observations of the COSMOS field (at both Wide and Deep survey depths) against the multi-wavelength COSMOS2025 catalogue. The authors use spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting anchored by COSMOS photometry and secure redshifts to predict expected Euclid fluxes, and test three photometric extraction pipelines: aperture photometry (A-PHOT), template fitting (T-PHOT), and profile model fitting (SE++). This validation confirms the overall reliability of Euclid DR1 galaxy fluxes while identifying pipeline- and band-dependent systematics that impact faint source measurements.

papers.title: Localization of gravitational-wave source behind galaxy clusters by gravitational-wave lensing
papers.authors: Brian H. Y. Cheng, Laura Uronen, Souvik Jana, Samuel Lange, Thomas E. Collett, Otto A. Hannuksela
papers.abstract: Gravitational-wave observations have opened new opportunities to study massive object events like merging binary black holes. When combined with electromagnetic counterparts, accurate localization of gravitational-wave sources could allow us to identify their host galaxies and carry out follow-up studies, such as study the environment of merging black holes and determine the Hubble constant. One of the possible methods for precise localization is strong gravitational-wave lensing. Previous studies have considered strong gravitational-wave lensing with galaxy lenses. However, galaxy clusters have yet to be investigated due to the complexity of their mass structures. Here we take the list of known cluster lenses from the Hubble Frontier Fields, simulate lensing properties of gravitational waves from their reconstructions as they would be observed by the ground-based gravitational-wave detectors. When same model family is used in simulation and localization, we find that the correct lens is identified for around 90\% of the simulated events. We also show that the source positions within the cluster can be pinpointed at sub-arcsecond precision with an estimate on source redshift. When we marginalize over all possible lens models for the clusters, the lens identification and localizations remain valid as long as the correct lens model is contained in the available cluster lens models. However, most localization attempts fail at initialization if the correct cluster model is excluded. These tests establish a proof of concept of localization under idealized conditions, while more work is needed to understand the cluster lens modeling discrepancies and reconstruction bias to validate the approach further.

conclusions: **High cluster identification success under matched models:** In idealized simulations of 5-image lensed events across six Hubble Frontier Fields clusters, the framework correctly identifies the lensing cluster in 53 of 60 cases ($88.3\%$ with posterior odds $\log_{10}\widetilde{O}_{\rm det} \ge 3$), with odds exceeding $10^5$ for the top 90% of events even with source redshift left free.

**Sub-arcsecond source localization:** Combining relative time delays ($\Delta\tau_k$) and effective luminosity distances ($D_{L,\rm eff}$) yields median 90% credible intervals of $\overline{\delta\beta_x} = \overline{\delta\beta_y} = 0.33''$ in the source plane and $\overline{\delta z_s} = 0.27$ in source redshift, sufficient to isolate candidate host galaxies.

**Vulnerability to cluster modelling systematics:** While marginalizing over multiple lens models succeeds if the generating model is included, excluding the true model during recovery (tested on 4-image configurations) causes most initialization searches to fail, underscoring that realistic application requires overcoming systematic discrepancies among cluster mass reconstructions.

In this paper, the authors simulate five-image cluster-lensed GW events across six Hubble Frontier Fields clusters using numerical mass reconstructions in `lenstronomy`, extracting relative arrival-time delays ($\Delta\tau_k$) and magnification-altered effective luminosity distances ($D_{L,\rm eff}$). Using a differential evolution and MCMC framework, they demonstrate that matching these observables against cluster lens models correctly identifies the responsible cluster $\approx 88\%$ of the time and localizes the source to sub-arcsecond precision ($\approx 0.33''$) while constraining its redshift ($\Delta z_s \approx 0.27$). This offers an exciting proof of concept for pinpointing dark mergers with third-generation GW detectors, though the method currently struggles if the true cluster mass distribution is not accurately represented in the model library.

papers.title: Modelling redshift-space distortions with tracer-centred split densities
papers.authors: Aritra K. Gon, Yan-Chuan Cai, Mark Neyrinck, Andrew Repp, Ravi K. Sheth, István Szapudi
papers.abstract: Analysing galaxy clustering in split environmental densities has been demonstrated to offer an advantage over standard two-point clustering for extracting cosmological information. A major challenge to realising this potential with the density-split (DS) technique is that the observations are in redshift space. This complicates its modelling, primarily because the density-split centres may not be conserved between real and redshift space. We develop a modelling framework that splits on the tracer-centred density PDF, rather than the volume-weighted density PDF commonly used in previous studies. We derive the linear bias associated with the threshold density in redshift space, enabling us to connect large-scale DS clustering to the density PDF. We find that the threshold density field consists of doughnut-like structures, which we term `Island(s)'. We propose an empirical model, analogous to the halo model framework, that comprises linear, non-linear, and stochastic terms and accurately reproduces the anisotropic redshift-space clustering of tracers in each DS bin. Using this model, we confirm that DS clustering can provide tighter constraints on cosmological parameters than the standard two-point statistic. Furthermore, we show that the gain in cosmological information from DS analyses relative to standard two-point statistics arises primarily from knowledge of the density PDF, which incorporates small-scale perturbation modes below the smoothing scale.

conclusions: **Tracer-centred splitting overcomes RSD mapping challenges**: Evaluating smoothed environmental densities at tracer locations rather than across volume-weighted grid cells ensures tracer conservation between real and redshift space, effectively recasting density-split clustering as a marked point process.

**Analytical derivation of density-split bias**: By mapping the real-space counts-in-cells density PDF to a redshift-space tracer-centred lognormal distribution, the authors derive an analytical environmental linear bias $b_{\rm DS}$, which governs the large-scale clustering amplitude of each density bin.

**An empirical 'Island' halo-model framework**: Slicing the tracer density field isolates doughnut-like structures termed 'Islands', whose anisotropic redshift-space power spectra (monopole and quadrupole) are accurately captured by a linear two-Island term plus empirical non-linear and stochastic one-Island terms.

**Physical origin of information gain**: Fisher forecasts demonstrate that density-split clustering yields tighter parameter constraints than standard two-point statistics primarily because $b_{\rm DS}$ encodes small-scale perturbation modes below the smoothing scale ($R = 5\ h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$) into the large-scale power spectrum amplitude.

**Degeneracy breaking**: Although marginalising over five empirical nuisance parameters per density bin degrades raw constraints, combining density-split spectra with standard global power spectra substantially tightens cosmological parameter bounds by breaking parameter degeneracies.

However, modelling DS clustering in observed redshift space is notoriously challenging because peculiar velocities (redshift-space distortions, or RSD) shift density cells non-locally, breaking cell conservation between real and redshift space. To bypass this issue, the authors introduce a tracer-centred framework that evaluates smoothed densities directly at galaxy positions rather than across volume-weighted grid cells, ensuring that the tracked objects remain identical in both real and redshift space. They analytically map the volume-weighted density probability distribution function (PDF) to the redshift-space tracer-centred PDF to derive the environmental linear bias ($b_{\rm DS}$), embedding it into an empirical halo-model-like formulation that models bounded density structures ("Islands") in $z=2$ mock catalogues. Using Fisher forecasts, they show that DS clustering extracts tighter cosmological constraints than the global power spectrum because the environmental bias intrinsically folds in small-scale density modes from below the smoothing scale.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): The Euclid surveys at DR1
papers.authors: Euclid Collaboration : I. Tereno, J. Dinis, X. Dupac, R. Scaramella, B. Altieri, H. Aussel, I. Baldry, P. Battaglia, G. Buenadicha, C. Burigana, B. Carry, P. Casenove, J.-C. Cuillandre, C. Dominguez-Tagle, A. Franco, B. R. Granett, M. Granvik, A. Gregorio, B. Y. Irureta-Goyena, R. Kohley, K. Kuijken, P. Liebing, E. L. Martin, J. Martin-Fleitas, J. Mendes, L. Miller, A. A. Nucita, R. Nakajima, K. Paterson, V. Pettorino, M. Pontinen, G. D. Racca, E. Romelli, M. Schirmer, M. Schmidt, T. Schrabback, D. Scott, C. Sirignano, R. Tata, T. Trombetti, R. Vavrek, A. Zacchei, M. Zerjal
papers.abstract: Euclid is a surveying mission that is progressively imaging and spectroscopically mapping a wide area of extragalactic sky in visible and near infrared bands. The Euclid mission is, however, not restricted to the Euclid Wide Survey, but it includes data from various other survey components. This paper presents the Data Release 1 (DR1) status of the multiple Euclid surveys and fields, including the Euclid Deep Survey, Euclid Auxiliary Fields, calibration fields, the Euclid Medium-Deep Survey, the Euclid Ecliptic Survey, and the Independent Legacy Scientists' field, in addition to the Euclid Wide Survey. Some of these fields were observed during the initial Performance-Verification phase, others during the Phase-Diversity calibration campaign, and the majority during the subsequent science operations phase. This paper describes the different procedures of survey implementation applied in the various phases of the mission, from the set of requirements, constraints, and limitations, to the final operational products used to operate the spacecraft and execute the science surveys. The resulting main component of the Euclid surveys, the Euclid Wide Survey, covers at DR1 an area of 2100$\,{\rm deg}^2$, in two separate regions, of which 1900$\,{\rm deg}^2$ corresponds to data validated in higher-level processing.

The release documents the scheduling and execution across all early mission phases, encompassing the Performance Verification (PV) phase, the Phase-Diversity Calibration (PDC) campaign, and routine science operations.

In addition to the Wide Survey, the release incorporates distinct survey components including the Euclid Deep Survey (EDF North, South, and Fornax), Medium-Deep and Ecliptic surveys, calibration fields, and auxiliary target fields, establishing the spatial footprint essential for selection function modeling.

This work establishes the primary DR1 survey layout—spanning $2100\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ observed and $1900\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ validated in the Wide Survey—which defines the spatial footprints and selection functions necessary for subsequent large-scale structure and weak lensing cosmology.

papers.title: On-the-Fly Gaussian Process Reconstruction of the Galaxy Redshift Distribution for 3$\times$2pt Cosmology
papers.authors: Jip de Buck, Guadalupe Cañas-Herrera, Henk Hoekstra, Angus H. Wright
papers.abstract: The joint analysis of weak gravitational lensing, photometric galaxy clustering, and their cross-correlation, the so-called 3$\times$2pt analysis, is one of the primary probes Stage-IV surveys will use to constrain the dark-energy equation of state. Its accuracy depends critically on the calibration of the underlying photometric redshift distributions, $n(z)$, whose residual uncertainties can bias cosmological inference. However, conventional parametric nuisance models may not adequately capture the full range of plausible $n(z)$ uncertainties. We therefore present a cosmological inference framework that instead reconstructs $n(z)$ on the fly using Gaussian Processes (GPs), replacing per-bin shift-and-width parameterisations by a non-parametric, data-driven model. We validate the method on synthetic Euclid-like 3$\times$2pt data vectors representative of Euclid Data Release 1, sampling GP hyperparameters jointly with cosmological and nuisance parameters to reliably propagate $n(z)$ uncertainties into the posterior distributions. We find that the dependence of the inferred parameters on the adopted $n(z)$ model is markedly stronger in $w_0w_a$CDM than in $\Lambda$CDM. Opening the dark-energy sector both amplifies the biases induced by a given $n(z)$ treatment and changes which $n(z)$ reconstruction the data prefer, so that a model validated in $\Lambda$CDM does not automatically remain adequate once $w_0$ and $w_a$ are free. Our results thus indicate that Stage-IV surveys should define $n(z)$ uncertainty marginalisation requirements separately in cosmologies beyond $\Lambda$CDM to ensure unbiased dark-energy constraints.

**Severe cosmology dependence**: While different $n(z)$ parametrisations yield consistent constraints in $\Lambda$CDM, opening the dark-energy parameter space ($w_0, w_a$) drastically amplifies biases and alters the preferred $n(z)$ shape due to degeneracies between dark-energy projection kernels and redshift deformations.

**Validation warning for Stage-IV surveys**: Systematics marginalisation schemes (e.g., shifts-and-widths, PCA, or mode projections) validated strictly under $\Lambda$CDM can fail and induce false dynamical dark energy signals; hence, nuisance models must be validated directly within $w_0w_a$CDM prior to unblinding Euclid/LSST data.

**Contour tightness is deceptive**: More flexible GP configurations often produced artificially tight parameter contours (high figure-of-merit) despite significant parameter biases, and were strongly penalised by Bayesian evidence for opening unconstrained prior volume.

The authors introduce a flexible, non-parametric framework that reconstructs $n(z)$ on the fly during MCMC sampling using Gaussian processes conditioned on a handful of sampled nodal points, enforcing positivity by modelling $\sqrt{n(z)}$. This provides a crucial cautionary lesson for Euclid cosmological inference, highlighting that photometric redshift systematic models must be thoroughly stress-tested in beyond-$\Lambda$CDM spaces rather than validated purely under standard $\Lambda$CDM.

papers.title: The 21 cm-Lyman-$α$ forest cross-power spectrum with a minimal effective field theory
papers.authors: G. Autieri, V. Iršič, M. Viel
papers.abstract: Intensity maps of the 21 cm line and the Lyman-$\alpha$ (Ly$\alpha$) forest trace the same cosmic volume at $2\lesssim z\lesssim 4$. Their cross-power spectrum is insensitive to foregrounds that do not correlate between the two probes and, together with the Ly$\alpha$ auto-spectrum, separates the mean 21 cm brightness temperature from the neutral hydrogen (HI) bias. Effective field theory models of each tracer exist, but at one loop they carry tens of nuisance parameters. We test whether a minimal effective field theory (mEFT), consisting of the tree-level Kaiser model with leading-order counterterms and stochastic terms, previously validated for the Ly$\alpha$ auto-spectrum, describes the 21 cm auto-, Ly$\alpha$ auto- and cross-power spectra jointly. We use the Sherwood 80 $h^{-1}$Mpc hydrodynamical simulation with HI painted onto halos at $z=2.4$-$4.2$, and reduce sample variance with Zel'dovich control variates. Each spectrum is validated separately and then in a joint fit with shared parameters. With scale cuts $k_{\rm max}=0.5$, $1.2$ and $2.0\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ for the 21 cm auto-, cross- and Ly$\alpha$ auto-spectra, the mEFT fits all three spectra at all five redshifts. In the joint fit the mEFT determines the HI bias to 2.0-2.5% and the Ly$\alpha$ density bias to 2.1-2.3%. The scale cuts follow the HI velocity dispersion and the Ly$\alpha$ pressure-smoothing scale. When the brightness temperature is left free, the fits that include the cross-spectrum prefer values 20-30% above the true one, at 1-2$\sigma$, while the two auto-spectra together do not constrain it. A prior on the HI bias recovers the true value of the brightness temperature.

conclusions: The minimal EFT (mEFT)—consisting of the tree-level Kaiser RSD model plus leading counterterms and stochastic noise—reliably models all three spectra across $z=2.4\text{--}4.2$ with scale cuts of $k_{\rm max} = 0.5\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ (21 cm auto), $1.2\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ (cross), and $2.0\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ (Ly$\alpha$ auto).

These scale cutoffs are physically governed by the line-of-sight HI velocity dispersion inside halos (fingers-of-God) and intergalactic gas pressure smoothing, both of which evolve weakly with redshift, rather than the dark matter non-linear scale.

In joint fits, sample variance cancellation allows mEFT to determine the HI bias $b_{\rm HI}$ to $2.0\text{--}2.5\%$ and the Ly$\alpha$ density bias $b_{\rm F}$ to $2.1\text{--}2.3\%$, with all nuisance parameters well-constrained by data without prior dependence.

Leaving the mean 21 cm brightness temperature $\bar{T}_{\rm b}$ free leads to a $20\text{--}30\%$ ($1\text{--}2\sigma$) bias towards higher values in cross-spectrum fits; however, imposing an external prior of a few percent on $b_{\rm HI}$ successfully recovers the true $\bar{T}_{\rm b}$.

The authors test a 'minimal EFT' (mEFT)—combining the tree-level Kaiser redshift-space distortion model with leading counterterms and stochastic noise terms—on simulated auto- and cross-spectra from the Sherwood hydrodynamical simulation using Zel'dovich control variates to suppress sample variance. They demonstrate that mEFT accurately models all three spectra up to physical scale cuts dictated by halo fingers-of-God and gas pressure smoothing, delivering percent-level bias constraints without relying on informative nuisance priors.

papers.title: Parallel alignment of radio AGN jets and large cosmic web structures in the direction of the Shapley supercluster
papers.authors: I. Baronchelli, T. Venturi, V. Casasola, P. Merluzzi, C. Burigana, G. Busarello, M. Bonato, O. Smirnov, T. Ronconi, M. Massardi, E. Liuzzo
papers.abstract: Aims. We investigated the potential large-scale alignment of radio active galactic nuclei (AGN) jets in the proximity of the Shapley Supercluster (SSC) area and its correlation with the identified cosmic web structures. Methods. We analyzed 28 radio AGNs divided into two populations with comparable sky coverage north and south of a diffuse X-ray filamentary structure connecting clusters in the SSC core. We measured the average jet position angles (PAs) and combined them with spectroscopic redshifts to assess the persistence of the alignment along the line of sight. Results. We detected a significant large-scale alignment of the radio AGN jets with the foreground X-ray filament (oriented at PA $\sim$ 115$^\circ$ $\pm$ 10$^\circ$). Both the northern (PA $\sim$ 117$^\circ$) and southern (PA $\sim$ 129$^\circ$) groups align with this axis, yielding an overall statistical significance of 4.5 $\sigma$ (upper and lower bounds: 6.1$\sigma$, 3.8 $\sigma$). Although the projected alignment is highly significant, sparse spectroscopic coverage (seven sources spanning 0.048 $\lesssim$ z $\lesssim$ 0.55) suggests that this spatial coherence may extend beyond the SSC (z $\sim$ 0.048), hinting at a line-of-sight correlation across significantly larger cosmic scales. Conclusions. The observed alignment cannot be explained by localized dynamical processes alone. These findings may indicate a persistent influence of the large-scale structure of the cosmic web, or preferred directions of matter collapse, on supermassive black hole spin axes, highlighting a connection between AGN jet morphology and the underlying dark matter distribution. Such alignments represent an important systematic that must be accounted for in precision cosmology with surveys such as Euclid.

conclusions: MeerKAT L-band observations reveal that radio AGN jets across northern ($PA \sim 117^\circ$) and southern ($PA \sim 129^\circ$) corridors align with the central Shapley X-ray filament ($PA \sim 115^\circ \pm 10^\circ$) at an overall statistical significance of $4.5\sigma$ ($3.8\sigma\text{--}6.1\sigma$).

Spectroscopic redshifts for a subset of seven sources span $0.048 \lesssim z \lesssim 0.55$, suggesting that the projected 2D coherence is not confined to the virialized Shapley Supercluster core ($z \approx 0.048$) but may reflect large-scale tidal field alignments or projected filamentary structures along the line of sight.

The results support tidal torque models where large-scale filamentary collapse imprints a preferred spin orientation on host galaxies and supermassive black holes, serving as a reminder that astrophysical alignments can act as subtle systematic contaminations in cosmic shear surveys like Euclid.

Finding a coherent alignment along this axis across both northern and southern corridors, the study highlights how environmental tidal fields can couple SMBH accretion disks to cosmic filaments across multi-megaparsec scales, providing empirical context for the intrinsic alignment systematics that affect cosmic shear surveys.

papers.title: Shedding light on modified recombination scenarios with Rayleigh scattering of the CMB
papers.authors: Debabrata Adak, Elena Vanetti, R. T. Génova-Santos, Jens Chluba, Carlos Hernández-Monteagudo, J. A. Rubiño-Mart\'ın
papers.abstract: Rayleigh scattering (RS) of cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons by neutral hydrogen and helium, during and shortly after the last scattering surface, adds a frequency-dependent contribution to the CMB anisotropies that scales approximately as $\nu^4$ at leading order. The RS signal is most relevant at $200\,{\rm GHz}\lesssim\nu\lesssim800\,{\rm GHz}$ and could be detected using future CMB experiments. Because RS acts in a frequency-dependent manner which is sensitive to the ionisation history of the cosmological recombination process, it provides an additional probe of the recombination history. This makes it a natural test of modified recombination scenarios, such as variable electron mass $m_{\rm e}$ or fine-structure constant $\alpha$, which have been proposed to ease the Hubble tension. The correlation between the RS and primary CMB signal, both in temperature and polarisation, further enhances its usefulness for constraining cosmological parameters. Using a multi-frequency Fisher analysis with realistic noise and foregrounds, we forecast parameter constraints and biases for PICO and LiteBIRD + Planck. For PICO, adding RS improves the $\Lambda$CDM constraints on cosmological parameters by $\lesssim7\%$, but improves the constraints on some parameters ($H_0$, $m_{\rm e}$, $\alpha$, $\Omega_{\rm b}h^2$, $\Omega_{\rm c}h^2$) by $\simeq31\%$ for some modified scenarios in the recombination history. However, the improvement for LiteBIRD + Planck is limited to less than $2\%$ for most of the parameters. Neglecting RS biases the cosmological parameters by up to $\simeq1\sigma$ for PICO and below $1\sigma$ for LiteBIRD + Planck. Therefore RS must be modelled in the analyses of future CMB data.

conclusions: Rayleigh scattering imprints a steep $\nu^4$ frequency-dependent signature and shifts acoustic peaks to larger angular scales, an effect that is most pronounced at high frequencies ($200\text{--}800\,{\rm GHz}$) and in the CMB $EE$ polarisation power spectrum.

For a future high-resolution space mission like PICO, including RS breaks the near-exact scaling degeneracy between $m_{\rm e}$, $\Omega_{\rm b}h^2$, $\Omega_{\rm c}h^2$, and $H_0$, improving parameter constraints by $\simeq 31\%$ in modified recombination models (compared to a $\lesssim 7\%$ improvement in standard $\Lambda$CDM).

For LiteBIRD + Planck, the parameter improvements from RS are modest ($\lesssim 2\%$) for most parameters due to lower angular resolution, but still reach $55\text{--}58\%$ along the unconstrained $m_{\rm e}$ degeneracy direction.

Neglecting Rayleigh scattering in future PICO analyses induces parameter biases up to $\sim 1\sigma$; furthermore, failing to consistently modify both Thomson and Rayleigh cross-sections when varying $m_{\rm e}$ causes severe mis-modelling biases that can completely mask a true $2\%$ variation in $m_{\rm e}$.

ai.summary: While standard analyses assume CMB photons only undergo frequency-independent Thomson scattering off free electrons during recombination, the neutral hydrogen and helium atoms produced at the last-scattering surface also induce Rayleigh scattering (RS), whose cross-section scales sharply with frequency as $\propto \nu^4$. Because RS is frequency-dependent and peaks slightly later in the recombination epoch, it provides a unique probe of the ionization history and can test early-universe modifications proposed to relieve the Hubble tension, such as varying fundamental constants ($m_{\rm e}$ or $\alpha$). In this work, the authors implement modified atomic physics into Recfast++ and CAMB to model the RS opacity across frequency channels, performing a multi-frequency Fisher matrix forecast with realistic noise and foregrounds for PICO and LiteBIRD + Planck. They demonstrate that observing the RS signal at high frequencies ($200\text{--}800\,{\rm GHz}$) can break stubborn cosmological degeneracies in modified recombination models, and that failing to account for RS in future CMB experiments could bias inferred parameters by up to $\sim 1\sigma$.

papers.title: Characterising a population of fast-declining SNe Ia in galaxy cluster cores
papers.authors: A. Eranhalodi, J. Nordin, M. Kowalski, U. Burgaz, F. Fischer, M. Ginolin, Y.-L. Kim, T. E. Müller-Bravo, J. Sollerman, A. Townsend, A. Drake, M. Graham, D. Hale, J. C. Jaimes, R. R. Laher, J. Purdum
papers.abstract: Galaxy cluster cores, characterised by old stellar population and suppressed star-formation are ideal for studying the environmental dependence of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia). It is unclear whether the diversity of SNe Ia, parametrised by light curve stretch, stems from distinct explosion mechanisms or varying initial conditions, both closely tied to progenitor age. We analyse the light curve stretch and colour distribution of photometrically identified SNe Ia within the galaxy clusters cores, utilising the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) archival data. Using the AMPEL platform, we filter 89,025 ZTF transients spatially coincident with our galaxy cluster catalogues to identify 4,969 likely SN Ia candidates. We split this sample into three populations: core cluster SNe Ia $r \le 0.5R_{500}$, outer-core cluster SNe Ia $0.5R_{500}< r\le 2R_{500}$, and a reference population of non-cluster SN Ia. We present the largest sample of photometrically identified cluster SNe Ia to date, notably isolating a population of 242 SNe Ia within innermost cluster cores $r \le 0.5R_{500}$. This fast-declining SN Ia population is statistically different from the outer-core cluster and field SN Ia population at $\sim4\sigma$ level. A marginal statistical preference for a bimodal distribution over a unimodal one $\Delta AIC$ of 1.53 and 2.3 for each catalogue, indicate cluster cores almost entirely host fast-declining SNe Ia. Conversely, the colour distribution show no significant environmental variation. By filtering out the prompt SN Ia population, cluster cores provide an environment to directly probe the delayed SN Ia progenitor channel. Our observations support a two-population model where progenitor age drives the light curve stretch diversity. The low-stretch values observed in core cluster SNe Ia suggest sub-Chandrasekhar mass double degenerate systems as their likely progenitors.

Cluster core SNe Ia show a significant preference ($\sim 4\sigma$) for fast-declining light curves ($\bar{x}_1^{\rm low} = -1.95 \pm 0.09$ for $z \le 0.1$) compared to outer-core ($0.5 R_{500} < r \le 2 R_{500}$) and field SNe, while optical colour distributions show no significant environmental variation.

The strong environmental clustering of low-stretch events supports a two-population delay-time distribution where the prompt channel is suppressed in quiescent cores, pointing to sub-Chandrasekhar double-degenerate (white dwarf merger) progenitors.
