Galaxy cluster cores ($r \le 0.5 R_{500}$) offer an ideal laboratory to isolate older progenitor populations, as star formation is heavily suppressed and the stellar populations are uniformly old. Using the AMPEL broker framework on archival Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) observations matched to SDSS and DESI cluster catalogues, the authors compiled the largest sample to date of photometrically selected cluster SNe Ia ($z \le 0.2$). They find that cluster cores almost exclusively host fast-declining (low-stretch) SNe Ia, confirming that progenitor age drives the stretch diversity and providing observational evidence that delayed sub-Chandrasekhar double-degenerate systems dominate in passive environments.

papers.title: Simulation-Based Priors and BAO Shifts from the Lyman-$α$ Forest at the Field Level
papers.authors: Divij Sharma, Roger de Belsunce, Mikhail M. Ivanov
papers.abstract: We present an analytic forward model for the Lyman-alpha (Ly-alpha) forest flux field based on cubic-order large-scale structure perturbation theory (effective field theory) calculations. We validate our cubic model on two sets of hydrodynamic simulations spanning $2 \leq z \leq 4$: the small-volume CAMELS suite, which spans a wide range of cosmological and astrophysical parameters, and the large-volume, high-resolution Sherwood simulations. We find qualitatively similar results for both at the power-spectrum level. The perturbative model reproduces the three-dimensional flux power spectrum of the simulations to $\sim 5\%$ down to $k \simeq 1$-$1.5\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, depending on the redshift. This improves compared to previous quadratic perturbative forward models by up to 40%. Exploiting cosmic-variance cancellation in the field-level approach, we carry out precision measurements of the Lyman-alpha forest bias parameters from the CAMELS simulation suite. We use these measurements to analytically predict the shifts in the Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO) scaling parameters induced by nonlinearities in the three-dimensional Lyman-alpha forest clustering as a function of cosmological parameters. We find sub-percent shifts in both the radial and transverse directions with a noticeable dependence on cosmology and redshift. Finally, from the field-level fits we construct simulation-based priors that can be used for cosmological analyses of the Lyman-alpha forest with the currently observing Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). In addition, our cubic model captures the connected four-point function (trispectrum) of the forest, which opens up novel opportunities for accurate covariance matrix estimation for DESI and its successor, DESI-II.

conclusions: **Cubic EFT reaches $\sim 5\%$ accuracy down to $k \simeq 1\text{--}1.5\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$**: Going to cubic order improves the 3D flux power spectrum modeling by up to $40\%$ over quadratic forward models and accurately reproduces the spatial morphology of the flux decrement at the pixel/field level across $z=2\text{--}4$.

**Sub-percent non-linear BAO shifts**: Non-linearities shift the Ly-$\alpha$ BAO peak positions at the sub-percent level, with median shifts across CAMELS evolving from $(\Delta\alpha_\perp, \Delta\alpha_\parallel) = (-0.0095\%, +0.137\%)$ at $z=2$ to $(-0.033\%, -0.030\%)$ at $z=4$ (and $(\Delta\alpha_\perp, \Delta\alpha_\parallel) = (-0.054\%, +0.108\%)$ at $z=2$ for near-Planck cosmology); this confirms that non-linear shifts are small but non-negligible for the DESI systematic error budget.

**Field-level simulation-based priors (SBPs)**: Cosmic-variance cancellation enables robust, high-precision measurement of all 22 EFT bias coefficients across the 1024 CAMELS-SB35 hydrodynamical simulations, delivering correlated priors on nuisance parameters for DESI 1D and 3D full-shape analyses.

**Analytical covariance via trispectrum**: Including cubic operators automatically captures the tree-level connected four-point function (trispectrum), offering a promising route to generate accurate non-Gaussian covariance matrices for DESI and DESI-II without thousands of expensive full hydro runs.

ai.summary: The Lyman-$\alpha$ (Ly-$\alpha$) forest—the dense series of neutral hydrogen absorption lines seen along distant quasar sightlines—probes the high-redshift cosmic web ($z \sim 2\text{--}4$) well into the quasi-linear regime, but interpreting its 3D clustering requires keeping complex baryonic and non-linear effects under theoretical control. In this paper, the authors develop a field-level forward model for the transmitted Ly-$\alpha$ flux up to cubic order in the Effective Field Theory of Large-Scale Structure (EFTofLSS), mapping 22 Lagrangian operators to redshift space while analytically resumming bulk flows. By fitting this model directly to hydrodynamical simulations (the 1024-run CAMELS-SB35 suite and the high-resolution Sherwood simulation) mode-by-mode, they cancel cosmic variance and extract precise scale-independent EFT bias parameters across diverse cosmologies and astrophysics. They use these calibrated parameters to compute non-linear shifts in the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) peak scales and construct simulation-based priors (SBPs) on EFT nuisance parameters, providing crucial systematic error budgets and modeling tools for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI).

papers.title: MAHA-z: A Mahalanobis distance kNN estimator for photometric redshifts
papers.authors: Paula S. Ferreira, Ribamar R. R. Reis, Renyue Cen
papers.abstract: We present \texttt{MAHA-z}, a photometric-redshift (photo-$z$) estimator that combines $k$-nearest neighbour ($k$NN) regression with a Mahalanobis distance metric learned from the covariance of a spectroscopic reference sample. For each target galaxy, \texttt{MAHA-z} performs a neighbour search in a colour-magnitude feature space with optional morphological parameters, and returns both a point estimate and a redshift posterior $p(z\mid\mathbf{f})$ obtained by kernel density estimation over the neighbour redshifts. The Mahalanobis metric accounts for correlated features and heterogeneous units, eliminating ad hoc normalisation, and its subspace restriction allows \texttt{MAHA-z} to handle missing bands on a per-galaxy basis without imputation. We validate the method on four datasets spanning simulations and survey photometry: the Euclid Flagship~2 mock, the Legacy-KiDZ calibration sample, VIPERS, and the DES Year~3 BAO sample. On Euclid Flagship~2 (LSST+NISP) we achieve $\sigma_{\rm NMAD}=0.0148$ with a $0.27\%$ outlier fraction, and on DES Y3 we obtain $\sigma_{\rm NMAD}\approx0.023$ with $<1\%$ outliers and posterior calibration comparable to the \texttt{ANNz2} catalogue. \texttt{MAHA-z} processes millions of galaxies in minutes and provides competitive PDFs at substantially lower computational cost than trained machine-learning models, making it a practical option for iterative photo-$z$ production and validation in Stage-IV surveys.

conclusions: **Euclid Flagship 2 performance:** On the Euclid Flagship 2 simulation mock (combining LSST optical and Euclid NISP near-infrared photometry), MAHA-z reaches a normalized median absolute deviation scatter of $\sigma_{\rm NMAD} = 0.0148$, an outlier fraction of $f_{\rm out} = 0.27\%$, and empirical 68% coverage of 93.3%. Including morphological features halves the photo-$z$ scatter for near-infrared-only data ($0.101 \to 0.046$) by helping break colour-redshift degeneracies.

**Parity with deep learning on real survey data:** Benchmarked on the DES Year 3 BAO sample, MAHA-z achieves $\sigma_{\rm NMAD} \approx 0.023$ with $f_{\rm out} < 1\%$ and delivers redshift posterior PDFs whose Kolmogorov-Smirnov calibration ($D_{\rm KS} = 0.102$) and 68% coverage ($77.8\%$) are statistically indistinguishable from the neural-network code ANNz2 ($D_{\rm KS} = 0.101$ and $79.6\%$).

**Extreme computational speed and native handling of missing bands:** By restricting the covariance matrix to observed bands per object, MAHA-z handles missing survey photometry natively without artificial imputation, processing $7 \times 10^6$ galaxies in ~10 minutes on a single CPU without the multi-hour training required by complex neural architectures.

ai.summary: For Stage-IV cosmological surveys such as Euclid and LSST, obtaining spectroscopic redshifts for billions of galaxies is unfeasible, making fast and robust photometric redshift (photo-$z$) estimation—inferring line-of-sight distances and full redshift probability density functions (PDFs) from multi-band colours and fluxes—vital for cosmological inference. In this work, the authors present MAHA-z, a non-parametric estimator that combines $k$-nearest neighbour ($k$NN) regression with a Mahalanobis distance metric derived from the feature covariance matrix of a spectroscopic calibration sample, alongside adaptive kernel density estimation to reconstruct redshift posterior distributions. By using the Mahalanobis metric rather than an unweighted Euclidean distance, the algorithm naturally accounts for correlated colour distributions and heterogeneous units while seamlessly accommodating missing photometric bands via sub-matrix projections without data imputation. Validated across the Euclid Flagship 2 mock, KiDS, VIPERS, and DES Year 3 data, MAHA-z delivers point estimates and posterior calibrations competitive with complex neural-network models while processing millions of galaxies in minutes with virtually no training overhead.

papers.title: The NANOGrav 15-year data set: A Limit on Continuous Spin Gravitons
papers.authors: Chinmay Ambasht, Olivia Bitcon, Tanner Trickle, the NANOGrav Collaboration
papers.abstract: Continuous spin particles (CSPs) are massless particles characterized by a dimensionful spin scale, $\rho$, which, when non-zero, changes their helicity under Lorentz boosts. Since CSPs reduce to ordinary particles when $\rho \rightarrow 0$, the photon or graviton could be CSPs and only appear to behave as ordinary particles due to a small value of $\rho$. Therefore, it is important to determine what value of $\rho$ is experimentally allowed. Recent work has shown that the physical effects of CSPs scale as powers of $\rho/\omega$ when $\rho \ll \omega$, where $\omega$ is a frequency scale, making low-frequency probes particularly beneficial for highlighting these phenomena. In this paper we use pulsar timing arrays to set constraints on the spin scale of the continuous spin graviton. Pulsar timing arrays are uniquely suited for this application as they have exceptional sensitivity to low, nanohertz frequency gravitational waves, as demonstrated by their recent evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave background. Using standard Bayesian data analysis techniques, we find that the NANOGrav 15-year data set constrains the graviton spin scale to $\rho_\text{g} < 1.23 \times 10^{-23} \, \text{eV} $ at the 95% credible level.

conclusions: Derived the timing residuals and modified overlap reduction function (ORF) for a continuous spin graviton (CSG), showing that a non-zero spin scale $\rho_\text{g}$ damps spatial correlations and introduces a low-frequency turnover below $f \sim \rho_\text{g}/(2\pi)$.
Set a 95% credible level upper limit of $\rho_\text{g} < 1.23 \times 10^{-23}\text{ eV}$ on the continuous spin scale of the graviton using the NANOGrav 15-year pulsar timing array data set.

Confirmed that because CSG modifications enter at $\mathcal{O}(\rho_\text{g}^2/\omega^2)$, nanohertz gravitational-wave experiments (with baseline observation times $T \sim 15\text{ yr}$, corresponding to $\omega \sim 2\pi/T \sim 10^{-23}\text{ eV}$) provide the most sensitive experimental arena for testing continuous spin representations of gravity.
ai.relevance_reason: While this paper tests fundamental modifications to general relativity, it focuses on nanohertz gravitational-wave backgrounds and pulsar timing arrays rather than large-scale structure, Euclid observables, or cosmological simulations.
ai.summary: In standard field theory, massless gravitons possess strictly two Lorentz-invariant helicity states ($\pm 2$), but Poincaré group representation theory also permits "continuous spin particles"—massless states characterized by a dimensionful scale $\rho$ that mixes helicities under Lorentz boosts and smoothly approaches ordinary particles as $\rho \to 0$. Because continuous spin graviton (CSG) corrections scale as $(\rho_\text{g}/\omega)^2$ at frequency $\omega$, low-frequency gravitational wave detectors such as pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are uniquely sensitive to these departures from general relativity. The authors derive the CSG-modified timing residuals and overlap reduction function—the generalization of the standard Hellings–Downs angular correlation pattern—and incorporate it into a full Bayesian MCMC analysis of the NANOGrav 15-year data set. They find no significant deviation from standard general relativity and set the first observational bound on the graviton's continuous spin scale, demonstrating how nanohertz stochastic backgrounds probe exotic spacetime representations.

papers.title: ViViViT: a Video-to-Video Vision Transformer for Cosmological Lightcone Reconstruction
papers.authors: Federico Semenzato, Alvise Raccanelli, Michele Liguori
papers.abstract: Moving along the line of sight of a cosmological lightcone also moves through cosmic time, as in a video of cosmic structure traced by an evolving observable. We recast the reconstruction of the underlying matter field from observed lightcones as a video-to-video translation task by introducing ViViViT, a vision transformer that factorizes attention across transverse frames and radial evolution. On reconstructed matter fields from 21cm neutral hydrogen simulations over $z\in[7.66,16.00]$, ViViViT preserves spectral power and phase alignment within a few percent of the ground truth up to the Nyquist scale, and three-point correlations for all triangle configurations with sides up to $k\simeq0.77\,h/\mathrm{Mpc}$, outperforming a convolutional 3D-U-Net baseline across all measured statistics. By encoding the evolving geometry of the cosmological observable itself, ViViViT marks a step toward field-level architectures that natively respect cosmic time, opening the path to time-aware reconstruction of cosmic tracers and targeted searches for redshift-dependent signatures in 21cm data.

conclusions: Preserved two-point power and phase alignment: ViViViT recovers the matter power spectrum within a few percent up to the grid Nyquist scale and maintains tight phase coherence (r(k) > 0.99 up to k ≃ 0.9 h/Mpc at intermediate redshifts), whereas the 3D U-Net baseline experiences early power suppression and loses coherence beyond k ≃ 0.6 h/Mpc.

Accurate three-point non-Gaussian structure: The model recovers the matter bispectrum to within ~5% for closed triangle configurations with sides up to k ≃ 0.77 h/Mpc, retaining non-linear mode coupling even at lower redshifts (z ≲ 10) where ionized bubbles locally extinguish the 21cm signal.

Recovery of line-of-sight correlations: For triangle configurations aligned along the line of sight (μ_long ≥ 0.8), ViViViT maintains accurate bispectrum amplitudes, whereas the convolutional U-Net suffers severe deficits (squeezed bispectrum ratio dropping to ~0.5 at small scales) due to its bounded receptive field.

Tractable lightcone scaling: Factorizing attention into spatial planes and line-of-sight columns slashes the quadratic computational complexity from O(N_t² N_s²) to O[N_t N_s (N_t + N_s)], making full-volume transformer lightcone translation feasible on modest GPU resources.
ai.relevance_reason: While the factorized transformer architecture is an interesting tool for field-level lightcone reconstruction, the paper focuses on high-redshift 21cm reionization astrophysics rather than Euclid large-scale structure, modified gravity, or beyond-ΛCDM simulation emulators.
ai.summary: Observations of the 21cm hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen map the high-redshift intergalactic medium across Cosmic Dawn and the Epoch of Reionization (z ~ 7.7–16.0), where the first luminous sources heat and ionize the gas. However, inverting the observed 21cm brightness temperature lightcone into the underlying dark matter density field is complicated by highly non-linear, non-monotonic astrophysical processes—such as spin-temperature coupling and expanding ionized bubbles—that evolve rapidly along the line of sight (which simultaneously acts as a look-back time axis). To address this, the authors introduce ViViViT (a Video-to-Video Vision Transformer), recasting lightcone reconstruction as a video translation problem by factorizing self-attention into independent transverse-spatial and radial-temporal components. Trained on semi-numerical lightcone simulations from 21cmFAST, the model translates entire 3D brightness temperature lightcones directly into matter density fields in a single forward pass, significantly outperforming a standard 3D U-Net baseline in recovering sharp cosmic web filaments and avoiding spurious smoothing. This architecture illustrates how factoring spatiotemporal attention can natively handle the evolving geometry of cosmological lightcones for field-level reconstruction tasks.

papers.title: Quantum Computing Enhanced Search for Wavelike Dark Matter
papers.authors: Yunjia Bao, Yu Cheng, Liang Jiang, Lian-Tao Wang
papers.abstract: Identifying a weak, stochastic signal hidden within a broad frequency band is a central challenge in the search for wavelike dark matter. We explore quantum computing enhanced sensing based on the Grover search algorithm to address this problem and find that a long integration time stabilizes the accumulated sensing phase, reducing quantum signal processing (QSP) errors induced by dark matter fluctuations. We further propose alternating the signs of the QSP angles between oracle calls to suppress the coherent accumulation of the intrinsic QSP approximation errors during the search. Combining these strategies in a transmon-based benchmark, we obtain a projected sensitivity to axion dark matter beyond existing astrophysical limits. This opens access to substantial unexplored parameter space across the $10$-$100\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$ mass range and offers an accelerated discovery channel for wavelike dark matter. With $10^6$ entangled sensing qubits, the projected sensitivity reaches the QCD axion band. Although illustrated with transmons, the protocol can be adapted to other experimental platforms for wavelike dark matter detection.

conclusions: **Quantum speedup for frequency scans**: Applying Grover's search algorithm to broadband wavelike dark matter detection achieves a quadratic speedup over classical step-and-integrate scans, requiring only $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$ oracle queries (e.g., searching $N = 22{,}500$ frequency bins with $G = 117$ iterations).

**Stochastic and oracle error mitigation**: Integrating each sensing unit over times much longer than the halo coherence time ($T = 5 \times 10^5 \tau_{\rm DM} = 140\,\mathrm{s}$) suppresses dark matter amplitude fluctuations to $\sigma_\theta / \bar{\theta} \sim \sqrt{\tau_{\rm eff}/T}$, while alternating the signs of quantum signal processing (QSP) angles between iterations reduces accumulated polynomial approximation errors from $\mathcal{O}(N \epsilon_{\rm QSP})$ to $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon_{\rm QSP})$.

**Transmon sensitivity reach**: For a single transmon sensor in a $5\,\mathrm{T}$ magnetic field, the protocol achieves a 95% single-search sensitivity to the axion-photon coupling of $|g_{a\gamma\gamma}| \simeq (3.18\text{--}9.71) \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ across $m_a \in [10, 100]\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$ in $\sim 364\,\mathrm{hours}$ of search time, surpassing existing astrophysical limits.

**Prospects for QCD axions**: Scaling the setup to $n_s = 10^6$ entangled sensing qubits scales the accumulated phase by $n_s$ and improves coupling sensitivity by $1/\sqrt{n_s} = 10^{-3}$, allowing the search to probe the standard KSVZ and DFSZ QCD axion parameter space.

ai.summary: Ultralight or "wavelike" dark matter (such as the QCD axion) behaves as a classical oscillating field with an unknown frequency set by its mass, making laboratory haloscope searches notoriously slow because wide frequency bands must typically be scanned point by point. To accelerate this search, the authors propose a quantum-enhanced protocol using Grover's search algorithm, which provides a quadratic speedup ($\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$ queries instead of $\mathcal{O}(N)$) over a discrete bank of candidate frequency bins. To overcome the decoherence and noise caused by the stochastic amplitude and phase fluctuations of the galactic dark matter halo, they accumulate an off-resonant AC Stark phase over long integration times ($T \gg \tau_{\rm DM}$) and alternate the signs of the quantum signal processing (QSP) control angles to prevent coherent accumulation of oracle approximation errors. Modeling a benchmark platform of superconducting transmon qubits over the $10\text{--}100\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$ mass window, they show that this strategy surpasses current astrophysical limits and could reach the benchmark QCD axion band if scaled to $10^6$ entangled sensing qubits.

papers.title: FRIDA: Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies. I. Programme overview, resolved gas density profiles, and HI mass-size relation
papers.authors: Pavel E. Mancera Piña, Tom Oosterloo, Filippo Fraternali, Elizabeth A. K. Adams, Andrea Afruni, Cecilia Bacchini, Enrico M. Di Teodoro, Lexi Gault, Anastasia A. Ponomareva, Justin I. Read, Barbara Šiljeg
papers.abstract: Gas-rich ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) provide powerful tests of galaxy formation models at low surface densities. However, the structure of their neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) remains poorly constrained, hampering our understanding of this population. We present FRIDA (Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies), a MeerKAT and VLA programme providing high-resolution HI data of 12 gas-rich UDGs. In this paper, we introduce our sample and delve into the associated observations and data reduction. We derive HI fluxes, masses ($M_{\rm HI}$), and resolved surface density profiles ($\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)$). We find extended ($\sim 7-30\ \rm{kpc}$ in radius) and regular HI emission in our UDGs, and we report the discovery of a satellite around one of them. Most UDGs in FRIDA have $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)$ profiles with flat inner parts reaching $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)\approx 4\ M_\odot\ \rm{pc^{-2}}$ near their centres, which then decline exponentially in their outer parts. By modelling the HI morphology of the UDGs, we find a median inclination of $43^\circ$, in agreement with theoretical expectations for disc galaxies under UDG selection effects. Moreover, we place our UDGs in the $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm HI}$ and $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm 50,HI}$ mass-size relations, where $R_{\rm HI}$ is radius at which $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)=1\ M_\odot \rm{pc^{-2}}$, and $R_{\rm 50,HI}$ is the radius enclosing $50\%$ of $M_{\rm HI}$. While our UDGs lie within the scatter of the relations, they systematically fall on their upper side, being slightly (by $\sim 15-25\%$) more extended and of lower mean $\Sigma_{\rm HI}$ (by $\sim 25-35\%$) than average galaxies at similar $M_{\rm HI}$. Moreover, we find that $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R/R_{\rm HI})$ and $M_{\rm HI}(<R)/M_{\rm HI}$ for UDGs follow an intermediate trend between late-type discs and early-type galaxies, with a large overlap with Sa galaxies.

conclusions: **Expanded high-resolution sample**: The FRIDA survey expands the number of gas-rich ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) with resolved radio interferometry from 2 to 12, mapping regular, symmetric neutral hydrogen discs with masses $M_{\rm HI} = (0.2\text{--}3.6) \times 10^9\ M_\odot$ spanning radial extents of $7\text{--}30\ \rm{kpc}$.

**Characteristic density plateaus**: Radial $\rm H\,I$ surface density profiles show flat inner cores reaching $\Sigma_{\rm HI} \approx 4 \pm 1\ M_\odot\ \rm{pc}^{-2}$ before decaying exponentially at large radii, mimicking the normalized gas distribution of Sa spirals rather than standard late-type dwarf discs.

**Offset in $\rm H\,I$ mass-size relation**: The galaxies lie along the upper edge of the standard $M_{\rm HI}\text{--}R_{\rm HI}$ and $M_{\rm HI}\text{--}R_{\rm 50,HI}$ relations, exhibiting $\sim 15\text{--}25\%$ larger sizes and $\sim 25\text{--}35\%$ lower mean surface densities than average galaxies of matching $\rm H\,I$ mass.

**Inclination distribution and satellite discovery**: 3D tilted-ring modelling yields a median inclination of $i \approx 43^\circ$, confirming that gas-rich UDGs are not merely normal dwarfs biased by face-on selection effects, and reveals the first detected gas-rich dwarf satellite orbiting a UDG (AGC 198540).

ai.summary: Ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) are low-surface-brightness dwarf systems whose stellar components are extended across galactic scales ($R_{\rm e} \ge 1.5\ \rm{kpc}$), yet in isolated environments they often hold substantial reservoirs of cold neutral hydrogen ($\rm H\,I$). Previous dynamical studies suggested these gas-rich systems rotate anomalously slowly for their baryonic mass and may possess low dark matter halo concentrations, but progress has been stalled by a lack of spatially resolved radio data. Here, the authors introduce the FRIDA survey, using 250 hours of MeerKAT and VLA 21 cm interferometry to obtain high-resolution $\rm H\,I$ kinematics and column-density maps for 12 isolated gas-rich UDGs. They model the 2D gas morphology and radial surface density profiles ($\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)$), finding extended, regular discs reaching radii of $7\text{--}30\ \rm{kpc}$ with a characteristic central density plateau near $4\ M_\odot\ \rm{pc}^{-2}$. These observations establish baseline structural and mass-size scaling relations for UDGs, setting up forthcoming tests of dwarf galaxy formation channels and dark matter halo models in low surface density regimes.

papers.title: Variations in the Extinction Curve at High Galactic Latitudes as seen by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument
papers.authors: Sarv Parteek Singh, Edward F. Schlafly, Rongpu Zhou, Sergey E. Koposov, Joan R. Najita, J. Aguilar, S. Ahlen, C. Allende Prieto, D. Bianchi, D. Brooks, A. Carnero Rosell, F. J. Castander, E. Chaussidon, T. Claybaugh, A. P. Cooper, A. Cuceu, K. S. Dawson, A. de la Macorra, Biprateep Dey, P. Doel, S. Ferraro, J. E. Forero-Romero, E. Gaztañaga, Satya Gontcho A Gontcho, G. Gutierrez, J. Guy, C. Hahn, H. K. Herrera-Alcantar, R. Joyce, T. Karim, R. Kehoe, D. Kirkby, A. Kremin, A. Lambert, C. Lamman, M. Landriau, L. Le Guillou, M. E. Levi, M. Manera, P. Martini, A. Meisner, R. Miquel, J. Moustakas, A. D. Myers, S. Nadathur, J. A. Newman, E. Paillas, W. J. Percival, C. Poppett, F. Prada, I. Pérez-Ràfols, C. Ravoux, G. Rossi, R. Ruggeri, L. Samushia, E. Sanchez, C. Saulder, D. Schlegel, M. Schubnell, H. Seo, J. Silber, M. Siudek, G. Tarlé, B. A. Weaver, H. Zou
papers.abstract: The dust extinction curve, characterized by the total-to-selective extinction ratio, $R(V)$, varies with grain size and composition. Accurate $R(V)$ values are crucial for dereddening astronomical colors and understanding the interstellar medium. We measure extinction toward stars with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) spectroscopy using a machine-learning-based relative of the "pair method," matching reddened and unreddened stars. We use XGBoost to predict stars' intrinsic colors from their spectroscopic parameters ($T_\mathrm{eff}$, $\log g$, $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]$) and subtract them from observed colors to measure reddening in combinations of the $g$, $r$, $z$, $W1$, and $W2$ bands. This approach directly measures reddening, unlike the common thermal-emission-based method of Schlegel et al. (1998; SFD). The reddening is accurate to roughly 0.02 mag in $g-r$ and $r-z$. We develop a forward model to map $g-r$ and $g-W1$ reddenings to $R(V)$ and find significant variation in $R(V)$, with $\sigma_\mathrm{NMAD}(R(V)) = 0.23$, in dusty regions ($E(g-r) > 0.1$) at high Galactic latitudes observed by DESI. In this footprint, $R(V)$ is bimodal, with modes at 2.9 and 3.4, likely due to large-spatial-scale correlations in the shape of the extinction curve combined with the relatively small number of distinct sightlines with substantial reddening. We find no strong relationship between $R(V)$ and other tracers of the interstellar medium, such as thermal emission, dust temperature, spectral emissivity index $\beta$, and $H\alpha$. However, the error in the SFD-predicted extinction correlates well with $R(V)$, implying that a single optical reddening combined with the far-infrared dust brightness can predict variations in the extinction curve.

conclusions: **Empirical reddening via machine learning**: An XGBoost model trained on 1.5 million low-reddening stars successfully predicts intrinsic stellar colors from DESI spectroscopic parameters ($T_{\mathrm{eff}}, \log g, [\mathrm{Fe/H}]$), yielding direct dust reddenings across 3.3 million stars with small residual uncertainties of roughly $17\ \mathrm{mmag}$ in $g-r$ and $77\ \mathrm{mmag}$ in $g-W1$.

**Significant variation and bimodality in $R(V)$**: In dusty high-latitude sightlines ($E(g-r) > 0.1$), the extinction curve parameter exhibits substantial scatter ($\sigma_{\mathrm{NMAD}}(R(V)) = 0.23$) and a bimodal distribution with peaks at 2.9 and 3.4, departing significantly from the canonical diffuse ISM benchmark of $R(V) = 3.1$.

**Cloud-scale origins**: The non-Gaussian bimodal distribution arises because dust grain properties are spatially correlated across a modest number of discrete interstellar clouds intercepted at high Galactic latitudes, demonstrating that assuming a single Gaussian prior for $R(V)$ in survey pipelines is inadequate.

**Predicting extinction curves from optical and infrared data**: While $R(V)$ shows no strong correlation with dust temperature, dust emissivity index $\beta$, or $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ emission, its variation correlates well with the residuals in SFD-predicted extinction, showing that combining a single optical reddening measurement with far-IR thermal emission can effectively diagnose extinction curve variations.

ai.summary: Extragalactic observations must be corrected for foreground Milky Way dust, which dims and reddens background light according to an extinction curve parameterized by the total-to-selective extinction ratio, $R(V) = A(V)/E(B-V)$ (where larger values correspond to larger average dust grain sizes). Traditional dust corrections, such as the widely used SFD map, infer extinction indirectly from far-infrared thermal dust emission, introducing systematic errors into galaxy selection and cosmological distance measurements if dust properties vary across sightlines. In this work, the authors introduce a machine-learning implementation of the classical stellar 'pair method,' training an XGBoost model on low-extinction stars to predict intrinsic stellar colors directly from DESI DR2 spectroscopic parameters ($T_{\mathrm{eff}}$, $\log g$, and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]$). Applying this model to 3.3 million DESI stars and forward-modeling the observed color excesses, they map extinction across high Galactic latitudes and uncover substantial, bimodal variations in $R(V)$ (peaking at 2.9 and 3.4) across dusty sightlines. These findings demonstrate that assuming a canonical diffuse-ISM value of $R(V) = 3.1$ can bias cosmological analyses, while showing that combining a single optical reddening with far-infrared emission can successfully calibrate extinction curve variations.

papers.title: VIDE 2.0: Robust, Scalable Void Finding for Extremely Large Galaxy Surveys
papers.authors: Paul M. Sutter, Benjamin D. Wandelt
papers.abstract: Current and future spectroscopic and photometric galaxy surveys will deliver unprecedented numbers of galaxies, with expected counts in the tens of millions. To answer the computational challenges posed by these surveys, in this paper we present VIDE 2.0, a significantly improved and enhanced void finding algorithm and analysis pipeline based on VIDE. Leveraging the parameter-free identification of voids via a Voronoi tessellation and watershed scheme, we implement a robust mechanism for handling survey boundaries and incompleteness without relying on vast numbers of boundary particles. This new method identifies edge galaxies and flags voids contaminated by their presence. The mechanism is fully deterministic, producing bit-for-bit reproducible catalogs from identical inputs. An automatic rule for setting the mask resolution renders the entire pipeline parameter-free. Combined with other performance enhancements to the underlying VIDE engine, we find significant ($>100\times$) speedups and a dramatic reduction in memory usage compared to previous versions: a 12-million-galaxy DESI Y1-class mock catalog now completes in roughly 15 minutes on a single laptop, where VIDE 1.0 could not run a catalog of even $10^6$ galaxies on the same hardware. We are also able to identify voids existing closer to survey boundaries via deterministic per-void contamination flags, maximizing their statistical potential. We exercise the upgraded pipeline on two large mock suites (MultiDark-Patchy DR12 and AbacusSummit DESI Y1 ELG), demonstrating converged cosmic-variance covariances for the void number function, the void-galaxy cross-correlation, and the void ellipticity distribution -- key ingredients for Stage IV void cosmology. VIDE 2.0 is now well suited to handle large numbers of galaxies in mock and real observations, and ready to tackle the challenges of future campaigns.

conclusions: Replaced random boundary-particle flooding with a deterministic ray-casting method along HEALPix mask boundaries, making void catalogs bit-for-bit reproducible and tagging individual sources of boundary contamination.

Eliminated arbitrary mask resolution tuning via an analytical criterion that sets NSIDE_auto = min(NSIDE_mask, NSIDE_data) by matching the volume-weighted pixel scale to the survey's mean tracer separation.

Achieved a >100x speedup and drastic memory reduction over VIDE 1.0 using voro++, enabling a 12-million-galaxy DESI Y1 mock catalog to run in ~15 minutes on a single laptop where VIDE 1.0 crashed on 10^6 galaxies.

papers.title: Rapidly Spinning Primordial Black Holes from Confinement
papers.authors: Michael Zantedeschi
papers.abstract: Confinement can turn widely separated particles into rapidly spinning primordial black holes. A flux tube pulls a heavy quark--antiquark pair together, converting its stored energy into relativistic motion. The same mechanism is possible in the magnetic dual, where a Higgs phase confines magnetic flux into a string joining a monopole--antimonopole pair. As the particles approach, cosmological tides and string bends can deflect their motion and make them miss. These disturbances can originate during inflation or be generated later. Black-hole formation then requires rare close passages from a smooth, broad encounter distribution. The resulting natal spin density therefore rises linearly to extremality, with mean dimensionless spin two thirds. Numerical string evolutions recover this law. Pairs that miss can remain bound, radiate and later collapse into lighter, near-extremal holes, sourcing a stochastic gravitational-wave background. Although the abundance remains model dependent, confinement leaves a unique spin signature that gravitational-wave observations can test.

conclusions: **Universal linear spin law:** Rare close encounters mediated by confining flux tubes yield a leading natal dimensionless spin distribution of $p(a_*) = 2a_*$ (with mean $\langle a_* \rangle = 2/3$ and standard deviation $\sigma_{a_*} \approx 0.24$), set purely by the 2D geometric impact parameter distribution.

**Distinction from standard PBHs and mergers:** While PBHs from standard primordial overdensities in the radiation era are born with negligible spin ($a_* \approx 0$) and hierarchical mergers exhibit peaked spin distributions, confinement-driven PBHs uniquely rise linearly toward extremality ($a_* = 1$) across both radiation and matter domination.

**Delayed collapse and near-extremal population:** Pairs that miss on their first passage can remain gravitationally bound and shed orbital angular momentum via gravitational radiation, eventually undergoing delayed collapse into lighter, near-extremal black holes ($a_* \to 1$).

**Stochastic gravitational-wave background:** GW emission from oscillating bound pairs before delayed collapse produces an integrated stochastic GW background of $\Omega_{\rm GW} \sim 10^{-13}$, falling in the deci-Hz band (DECIGO/BBO) for asteroid-mass PBHs ($\sim 10^{18}\,\mathrm{g}$) or the nano-Hz band (pulsar timing arrays) for solar-mass holes.

**Viable dark matter candidate:** For string tensions $\alpha_{\rm gr} \equiv G\mu \sim 10^{-8}$ and tidal perturbations $\Phi \sim 10^{-5}$, this mechanism allows asteroid-mass PBHs to account for up to 100% of the cosmological dark matter fraction ($f_{\rm PBH} \sim 1$).

papers.title: Enhancing Graviton--Photon Conversion through Galactic Magnetic Turbulence
papers.authors: Hongliang Tian, Lei Wu, Yang Zhang, Bin Zhu
papers.abstract: Plasma dispersion suppresses coherent graviton-photon conversion over astrophysical distances. We show that Galactic magnetic turbulence enables phase matching by compensating the plasma-induced mismatch, allowing matched magnetic modes to contribute coherently. In the long path limit, the ensemble-averaged conversion probability grows linearly with propagation distance in the phase matched regime and is governed by the projected magnetic power spectrum. Applied to photon background observations, this mechanism yields characteristic strain limits that are stronger than previous Galactic conversion bounds in the inertial range phase matching window, with improvements of up to two orders of magnitude.

Clear spectral scaling: In the turbulent inertial range (k_{\rm L} \ll \Delta \ll k_{\rm H}), the ensemble-averaged conversion probability grows linearly with path length and scales as \langle P_{g\gamma}\rangle \propto L f^\beta (f^{5/3} for standard Kolmogorov turbulence), flanked by a flat low-mismatch plateau and a steep \Delta^{-2} high-mismatch tail.

Tighter strain limits: Combining the enhanced conversion probability with diffuse photon background observations and extragalactic background light (EBL) synthesis models tightens upper limits on the characteristic gravitational-wave strain h_c in the 10^{12}–10^{18} Hz window by up to two orders of magnitude compared to previous Galactic conversion bounds.

Robustness against field variance: Numerical tests over 10,000 Gaussian magnetic field realizations show that 90% of individual realizations fall within [0.18, 2.37] \times \langle P_{g\gamma}\rangle, confirming that the analytical ensemble average is a reliable benchmark despite Galactic variance.

papers.title: Discrete Supernovae and the Limits of Continuous Models in Low-Mass Dark Matter Halos
papers.authors: C. Power (ICRAR-UWA), S. Balu (U Seville)
papers.abstract: Many galaxy formation models represent supernova feedback by a continuous energy injection rate averaged over the stellar initial mass function (IMF). This approximation can fail in low-mass dark matter halos, where single, discrete supernovae can unbind more gas than the reservoir holds. We investigate this using a one-zone model that characterises continuous and discrete supernova feedback at redshifts $z\geq5$. Both feedback modes inject the same expected energy per unit stellar mass formed. In the discrete model, individual supernovae are resolved and energy is injected instantaneously; in the continuous model, supernovae are IMF-averaged and energy injection is spread over a finite time interval. Once stars form, a supernova can unbind 1.5-2.7 times the gas present. Continuous feedback begins removing gas after $\sim 4$ Myr, whereas the first discrete supernova occurs after $\sim 10$ Myr, which produces a stellar mass excess before feedback takes effect. The excess persists because the reservoir responds nonlinearly: an event removes at most the gas present, and star formation halts once it is empty. It depends strongly on halo mass: from 135 per cent at $10^7\, \rm{M}_\odot$, to 15 per cent at $10^8\, \rm{M}_\odot$, to negligible at $10^9\, \rm{M}_\odot$ by $z=5$. Fixing the number and timing of supernovae does not remove the stellar excess, which indicates that it is not caused by stochastic IMF sampling. Instead, it vanishes when the same energy is divided among more, smaller events. Matching the energy released per unit stellar mass therefore does not guarantee equivalent feedback in halos that retain gas until the first supernova.

**Strong halo mass dependence:** The stellar mass discrepancy at $z \ge 5$ is most severe in the shallowest potential wells, producing a $135\%$ stellar mass excess in $10^7\,\rm{M}_\odot$ halos and $15\%$ in $10^8\,\rm{M}_\odot$ halos, while becoming negligible in larger halos ($\sim 10^9\,\rm{M}_\odot$) whose deeper potentials prevent single supernovae from unbinding the entire gas reservoir.

**Energy-matching fails to guarantee equivalent feedback:** The discrepancy is not an artifact of stochastic initial mass function (IMF) sampling—it persists even with fixed supernova timing—and only disappears when the discrete energy is partitioned into many smaller events, showing that matching total energy per unit stellar mass in subgrid models is insufficient for low-mass halos.

papers.title: Triple-Massive-Exchange Bispectrum of Quasi-Single-Field Inflation
papers.authors: Xingang Chen, Zhong-Zhi Xianyu
papers.abstract: The triple-exchange bispectrum of the scalar quasi-single-field inflation model has resisted analytic evaluation across its full parameter space since its advent, despite rapid progress in cosmological collider physics. In this Letter, we solve it for general mass and mixing strength as a convergent double series, by applying the Mellin-Barnes representation directly to the mixed propagator between the massless and massive modes. The result is exact, non-perturbative, and physically transparent; the method is broadly applicable.

conclusions: Exact double-series solution: By expressing the mixed massless-massive propagator in Mellin space, the authors reduce the triple-exchange time integral to a convergent double series over the pole residues at scaling dimensions $\Delta^0 = 2$ (analytic background) and $\Delta^\pm = 3/2 \pm \mathrm{i}\widetilde{\nu}$ (non-analytic cosmological collider signals, with $\widetilde{\nu} = \sqrt{m^2 - 9/4}$).

Convergence and spurious singularities: The series converges throughout the interior of the physical momentum triangle ($0 < r_1 \le r_2 \le 1$, $r_1 + r_2 > 1$) when evaluated in a specific summation order (summing over $n_1$ and its branch modes before $n_2$), which successfully eliminates spurious folded divergences at $r_2 = 1 - r_1$.

Squeezed and equilateral asymptotics: Tailored expansions in the squeezed limit ($r_1 \ll 1$) analytically reproduce the characteristic cosmological collider clock oscillations $\propto r_1^{1/2} \cos(\widetilde{\nu} \log(r_1/4) - \pi/4)$, while the equilateral limit correctly recovers the expected EFT decoupling behaviour $\propto 1/m^6$ for heavy spectators.

Non-perturbative mixing: The partial Mellin-Barnes framework generalizes to arbitrarily strong inflaton-spectator coupling $\rho$, where the effective clock frequency is shifted to $\widetilde{\nu}_\rho = \sqrt{m^2 + \rho^2 - 9/4}$, yielding exact shape templates across all mixing regimes.

papers.title: The Dark Side of the Periodic Table: Theory and Signatures of Nuclear Atomic Dark Matter
papers.authors: Pouya Asadi, Zackaria Chacko, David Curtin, Micah Mellors, Ethan T. Neil
papers.abstract: We study the theory and signatures of a Mirror Twin Higgs (MTH) scenario in which stable twin neutrons constitute most of the dark matter (DM), while a subdominant component of twin elements survives as nuclear atomic dark matter (naDM). This framework offers a solution to the $matter~coincidence~problem$ ($\Omega_{\rm DM}\simeq5\Omega_b$), as the twin $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry can correlate the visible and DM mass scales and their number densities. We analyze twin nucleon freeze-out and the onset of twin Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) to estimate the total naDM abundance, and determine which elements in the dark periodic table could be populated. An appreciable but subdominant naDM component generally requires a fractional nucleon mass splitting near the percent level, with twin-BBN creating heavy elements up to twin carbon. Strong twin neutron-proton scattering allows nearly all of the dark matter, not only the atomic sub-component, to participate in $dark~acoustic~oscillations$ (DAO) at early times, giving rise to a characteristic two-stage DAO signature that may be detected with future cosmological probes. Interactions between the twin and visible sectors, including the irreducible Higgs portal, make this scenario a well-motivated target for future directional direct-detection searches, and the naDM sub-component is expected to exhibit highly exotic astrophysics. We outline a supersymmetric twin Froggatt-Nielsen realization in which spontaneous $\mathbb{Z}_2$ breaking in the flavon sector can generate the required fermion spectrum and Higgs potential.

conclusions: **Solution to the Coincidence Problem via Twin Neutrons**: Setting the twin neutron mass to $m_{n,B} \approx 5\text{ GeV}$ alongside a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-correlated baryon asymmetry naturally reproduces the observed density ratio $\Omega_{\rm DM} \simeq 5\Omega_b$, with neutral twin neutrons constituting $\ge 80\%$ of the total dark matter.

**Dark BBN and Dark Nuclei up to Carbon**: A fractional twin nucleon mass splitting $|\Delta m_{np,B}|/m_{N,B} \sim 0.1\%\text{--}10\%$ allows twin Big Bang nucleosynthesis to overcome the deuterium bottleneck and synthesize elements up to twin carbon ($\mathcal{Z}_{\max} \le 6$), resulting in a surviving $0.01\%\text{--}20\%$ nuclear atomic dark matter (naDM) sub-component after accounting for post-recombination twin electron capture.

**Characteristic Two-Stage DAO Signature**: Because strong twin neutron–proton scattering tightly couples the dominant neutral twin neutrons to ionized twin nuclei at early times, the entire dark matter sector participates in dark acoustic oscillations (DAO), producing a distinctive two-scale power spectrum suppression near current dwarf galaxy / UV luminosity function limits.

**Multifaceted Observational Signatures**: The framework satisfies Bullet Cluster self-interaction bounds ($\sigma/m \sim 0.1\text{--}1\text{ cm}^2/\text{g}$) and features an irreducible Higgs-portal direct detection signal near the solar neutrino floor, providing a concrete target for future directional recoil detectors.

papers.title: Dual-species atom interferometry for axion dark matter
papers.authors: Maike Reckermann, John Carlton, Michael Werner, Agnese Mariotti, Guillermo A. Perez-Lobato, Nathaniel Sherrill, Naceur Gaaloul, Dennis Schlippert, Elina Fuchs
papers.abstract: Atom interferometers are sensitive to oscillations of the masses and transition frequencies of atoms, which can be induced by axion dark matter. The main limitation is the sensitivity to gravity gradient noise (GGN). Including a comprehensive noise analysis, we demonstrate that the Very Long Baseline Atom Interferometer (VLBAI) in Hannover with a baseline of 10m can probe the axion decay constant at levels almost competitive with leading laboratory constraints. The proposed 100m-baseline Atom Interferometer CERN Experiment (AICE) can extend this sensitivity by up to two orders of magnitude, surpassing laboratory constraints for axion masses of $10^{-19}\;\text{eV}/c^2 \lesssim m_a \lesssim 3\times10^{-15}\;\text{eV}/c^2$.

papers.title: Cubic Curvature Deformations to the Kerr Black Hole Shadow
papers.authors: Alireza Allahyari, Shinji Mukohyama, Yi Pang
papers.abstract: We investigate the effects of cubic curvature corrections on the shadows of rotating black holes within the effective field theory of gravity. Starting from a perturbatively corrected Kerr metric incorporating two independent cubic curvature couplings, we construct black hole shadows through numerical integration of null geodesics, without assuming separability of the geodesic equations. Using a Hamiltonian ray-tracing approach, we systematically examine the dependence of the shadow geometry on the higher-curvature couplings, black hole spin, and observer inclination. We find that cubic curvature interactions can produce discernible deviations from the Kerr shadow, modifying its apparent size and shape. In particular, the two cubic interactions exhibit distinct effects on the shadow boundary, with the magnitude of the deviations depending sensitively on the coupling strengths and black hole spin. We validate our numerical results through independent convergence tests of the geodesic integration and shadow-boundary determination, and recover the analytical Kerr shadow in the vanishing-coupling limit. Our results provide a complementary probe of higher-curvature gravity in the strong-field regime and illustrate the potential of black hole shadow observations to constrain departures from general relativity.

conclusions: Distinct geometric deformations: The two independent cubic curvature couplings ($\beta_5$ and $\beta_6$) produce distinct morphological distortions and apparent area shifts in the shadow boundary compared to the standard Kerr silhouette.

Spin and sign sensitivity: The magnitude of the shadow deformation is amplified at higher dimensionless spins (tested at $\chi = a/M = 0.6$ and $0.9$), whereas negative couplings (e.g., $\beta_6 = -0.001$) produce deviations that are nearly indistinguishable from Kerr.

Non-separable Hamiltonian ray tracing: Because the cubic curvature metric breaks Petrov type-D algebraic symmetry and destroys the Carter constant, the geodesic equations cannot be separated analytically; the authors establish a robust numerical framework coupling an 8th-order Dormand–Prince integrator ($\mathrm{rtol}=10^{-9}$) with a 13-step bisection algorithm.

Rigorous numerical convergence: Independent refinement tests varying integration tolerances and bisection depths confirm that numerical errors ($\mathrm{max}|H| < 10^{-3}$ and momentum deviations $< 10^{-5}$) are orders of magnitude smaller than the physical metric deformations.

Such higher-curvature interactions alter the spacetime geometry and shift the photon sphere, which directly modifies the apparent size and shape of the "black hole shadow"—the capture silhouette cast against background illumination and imaged by millimeter very-long-baseline interferometry (e.g., the Event Horizon Telescope). In this paper, the authors numerically construct the shadow of a Kerr black hole perturbatively deformed by two independent cubic curvature couplings ($\beta_5$ and $\beta_6$) without assuming separability of the geodesic equations (which generally fails in deformed spacetimes where Carter's constant is lost). Using an adaptive 8th-order Hamiltonian ray tracer in a local zero-angular-momentum observer (ZAMO) frame, they track null geodesics across 1000 screen angles and localize the capture boundary via 1D bisection. They validate their results with decoupled ODE-tolerance and boundary-root convergence tests, demonstrating how cubic curvature corrections induce distinct, spin-dependent deformations that can serve as strong-field null tests of General Relativity.

Characterising this sample of lens-galaxies requires accurate measurements of their physical properties. However, standard catalogue photometry often blends the light from the foreground lens and the lensed background source, limiting the reliability of derived galaxy parameters. We present a homogeneous catalogue of photometric redshifts and physical properties for 9538 galaxy-scale strong lenses identified in Euclid's DR1 strong-lens sample. We use deblended multiwavelength photometry obtained from the lens modelling of Euclid and ground-based images with PyAutoLens. The photometric redshifts of the lens galaxies are estimated using the template-fitting code Phosphoros. The stellar masses, SFRs, stellar ages, and metallicities are inferred through SED fitting with Prospector, adopting a flexible non-parametric SFH and a Salpeter IMF. The robustness of the inferred parameters is assessed through comparisons with spectroscopic redshifts and external galaxy surveys. The sample of lenses spans a broad redshift range of $0.13\lesssim z_{\rm phot} \lesssim 1.98$, with a median $z_{\rm phot} = 0.68^{+0.33}_{-0.29}$. The sample is dominated by massive quiescent galaxies with a $M_\ast$ range $[10^{10},\,10^{12.1}]\,M_\odot$ and a median $\log_{10}(M_\ast/M_\odot) = 11.39^{+0.29}_{-0.33}$. papers.abstract: We present 15 072 high-confidence strong lens candidates in Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), spanning 2000 deg$^2$. These comprise 6073 grade A ('sure lens') and 8999 grade B ('probable lens') systems, which we publish alongside a further 9010 grade C ('possible lens') candidates. With more high-confidence candidates than all previous catalogues combined, this sample establishes a large, homogeneous data set of galaxy-scale strong lenses with high-resolution imaging, transforming strong lensing from a field of rare discoveries to a robust statistical tool for astrophysics and cosmology. Of the roughly 900 million sources in DR1, we searched the 68 million passing our catalogue selection using a bespoke discovery pipeline that synthesises scores from five machine-learning models with visual classifications from around 7000 citizen scientists and 67 strong lensing experts. Beyond classical Einstein rings, our catalogue includes 84 candidate double-source-plane lenses and over 1000 candidate disc lenses, two exotic classes with few previously known examples, as well as several hundred candidate lensed AGN and quasars. We deliver automated lens models for the combined grade A+B systems, and photometric redshifts and stellar population properties for the deflector galaxies, providing immediate science-ready data products. We find that the majority of the deflector galaxies are massive and quiescent, with stellar masses of $\log_{10}(M_\ast /M_\odot) = 11.39^{+0.29}_{-0.33}$ (Salpeter initial mass function; 16th-84th percentile range). The deflector galaxies span a range of photometric redshifts ($z=0.68 ^{+0.33}_{-0.29}$), extending to higher redshifts than previous ground-based lens samples, and the lenses have a typical Einstein radius of $0.85 ^{+0.44}_{-0.24}$ arcsec. Extrapolating by area, we expect over 100 000 high-confidence strong lens candidates in the Euclid Wide Survey.

conclusions: Unveiled 15,072 high-confidence strong lens candidates in Euclid DR1 (6,073 grade A 'sure' lenses and 8,999 grade B 'probable' lenses), with over 93% representing brand-new discoveries and establishing the largest homogeneous strong lensing sample to date.

Characterized the deflector population as predominantly massive, quiescent galaxies with median stellar masses of $\log_{10}(M_\ast/M_\odot) = 11.39^{+0.29}_{-0.33}$, photometric redshifts of $z = 0.68^{+0.33}_{-0.29}$, and typical Einstein radii of $\theta_{\rm E} = 0.85^{+0.44}_{-0.24}\text{ arcsec}$, extending the lens baseline to higher redshifts than ground-based surveys.

Identified significant samples of rare lens morphologies, including 84 candidate double-source-plane systems (which provide cosmographic distance ratios independent of the Hubble constant), over 1,000 disc-galaxy lenses, and several hundred lensed AGN/quasars.

Achieved an estimated completeness of $81^{+9}_{-17}\%$ for grade A systems and $43^{+7}_{-8}\%$ for grade A+B systems (primarily bounded by human vetting capacity), extrapolating to an anticipated yield exceeding 100,000 high-confidence lenses across the completed Euclid Wide Survey.

papers.abstract: We present the method used to identify the $15\,000$ high-grade galaxy-galaxy strong lens candidates in Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Given that lenses are intrinsically rare systems and the DR1 data set is vast, this lens search was conducted in a number of stages: a catalogue-level cut; a machine-learning and ensemble search; a two-stage citizen-science search, and finally grading of lens candidates by strong lens researchers. In this paper, we describe each search stage and their respective results. This search was enabled by the automated classification of over 68 million objects by neural networks, more than 4.5 million classifications of $300\,000$ objects by citizen-scientist volunteers, and the inspection of over $30\,000$ objects by strong lens researchers. We find this multi-stage approach helps maximise the number of lenses identified, while minimising inspection requirements of both citizen scientists and strong lens researchers. We measure a completeness in our comprehensive search of $0.73_{-0.15}^{+0.08}$ to grade A ('definite') systems and $0.34_{-0.06}^{+0.05}$ to grade A+B ('definite' + 'probable') systems. Our search therefore identifies the majority of the definitive strong lens systems in the DR1 area with the remainder likely to be fainter or more ambiguous cases. We find that researcher grading remains subjective; in this work we implement calibration to account for biases of individual inspectors and highlight the benefit of lens modelling (ECLIPSE-C) in determining the nature of a lens candidate. This paper forms part of the ECLIPSE series, here focussing on the discovery pipeline used to identify lens candidates in Euclid DR1; an overview of the lenses discovered is presented in ECLIPSE-A.

conclusions: Identified 15\,072 grade A ('definite') and grade B ('probable') galaxy-galaxy strong lens candidates in the Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) footprint.

Achieved an estimated search completeness of $0.73^{+0.08}_{-0.15}$ for definitive grade A systems and $0.34^{+0.05}_{-0.06}$ for grade A+B systems, with completeness primarily limited by faint sources and small Einstein radii.

Demonstrated that standalone neural network classifiers achieve 74% purity at 21% completeness, showing that incorporating citizen scientists (Space Warps) before expert inspection is vital for achieving high completeness without overwhelming researchers.

Found that human expert grading suffers from individual subjective biases, which were mitigated through consensus calibration and highlight the need for automated lens modeling and spectroscopic follow-up in future Euclid releases.

papers.abstract: Galaxy-scale strong lenses provide precise measurements of galaxy mass distributions, magnified views of distant galaxies, and a competitive cosmological probe. Historically, such studies have been limited to hundreds of lenses, with automated modelling methods proving difficult to scale. We present automated lens modelling of 15 072 strong-lens candidates from Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), over an order of magnitude larger than any previously modelled sample. Using PyAutoLens-JAX, we perform three fits with multi-Gaussian expansion (MGE), pixelised, and Sérsic representations of the source, adopting an isothermal ellipsoid mass model with external shear. These fits provide foreground lens-light subtraction, adaptive Delaunay source reconstructions, and deblended photometry. More than 20 expert inspectors visually assess the resulting models, and each model is assigned the classification on which at least 75% of its inspectors agree. Of the 6073 grade A (secure) lens candidates, inspectors classify 4098 (67.5%) as successfully modelled, 580 (9.6%) as failures, 317 (5.2%) as multi-galaxy lenses, 15 (0.2%) as double-source-plane lenses, and 7 (0.1%) as unsure if lens, while 1032 (17.0%) reach no consensus and 24 (0.4%) have incomplete models. For the 8999 grade B (probable) candidates, the modelling success rate falls to 43.1%, primarily reflecting an increase in cases without consensus (37.6%), rather than a comparable increase in agreed failures (12.9%). Successfully modelled grade A and B systems have a median effective Einstein radius of 0.85 arcsec and a median total $I_E$-band source magnification of 8.1. We publicly release the successful lens models, their inferred properties, and magnified-source reconstructions through the ECLIPSE catalogue, demonstrating automated modelling at Euclid sample sizes and enabling population-level strong-lensing science.

conclusions: The pipeline successfully modelled 7,980 systems in total, achieving a 67.5% success rate on secure (grade A) candidates (4,098 of 6,073) and 43.1% on probable (grade B) candidates (3,882 of 8,999) under a strict ≥75% expert agreement threshold.

The dominant cause of identified modelling failures was inaccurate foreground lens-light subtraction (31.4%), followed by segmentation errors (18.6%), whereas the lower success in grade B systems primarily stemmed from human ambiguity over whether candidates were genuine lenses (37.6% lacked consensus).

Successfully modelled systems yield a median effective Einstein radius of $\theta_{\rm E} = 0.85''$ (16th–84th percentile range of $0.61''$–$1.21''$) and a median source magnification of $\mu = 8.1$ in the Euclid $I_{\rm E}$ band.

The authors publicly release the ECLIPSE catalogue—including lens parameters, mass maps, deblended imaging, and reconstructed sources—enabling large-scale statistical studies of galaxy mass profiles and dark matter substructure.

papers.title: Anatomy of LyC Escape in MEGATRON: Connecting Feedback Physics to Demographics, Leakage Timescales, and Explorations of ISM Density as a Tracer of Escape Fraction
papers.authors: Nicholas Choustikov, Harley Katz, Taysun Kimm, Matthew J. Hayes, Aaron Smith, Crystal L. Martin, Shyam H. Menon, Larrance Xing, Joki Rosdahl, John Chisholm, Aayush Saxena, Martin P. Rey, Adrianne Slyz, Julien Devriendt, Alex J. Cameron, Anatole Storck, Corentin Cadiou
papers.abstract: Constraining the Lyman Continuum (LyC) escape fraction ($f_{\rm esc}$) of high-redshift galaxies is essential to connect the abundant populations revealed by \textit{JWST} to cosmic reionization. We investigate this interplay using {\small MEGATRON}, a suite of zoom simulations with detailed radiation/chemistry and varied feedback prescriptions. We find that feedback physics simultaneously regulates UV source counts, LyC escape fractions, and escaping ionizing luminosities ($\dot{N}_{\rm ion,esc}$), producing different reionization histories. These differences are governed by the delay between a starburst and LyC escape: efficient early feedback and lower-density environments enable photons to escape while pre-supernovae stellar populations remain strongly ionizing. Consequently, models that produce fewer UV-bright galaxies yield earlier LyC escape and reionize sooner than models with more abundant UV sources and delayed LyC emission. Furthermore, UV-faint galaxies follow a common physical sequence in ISM structure with increasing $f_{\rm esc}$ irrespective of feedback physics: stronger leakers ($1\%\leq f_{\rm esc}\leq 50\%$) exhibit evidence of strong photoionization and SNe feedback alongside post-starburst star formation histories, while extreme leakers ($f_{\rm esc}\geq 50\%$) have also cleared their cold/dense ISM. We find that electron densities inferred from the $\rm [O\,{II}]\,\lambda\lambda3727$ doublet are a candidate diagnostic of $f_{\rm esc}$, with lower densities around $\rm H~{\small II}$ regions selecting stronger leakers. Moreover, this density can trace the early evolution of $f_{\rm esc}$, whereas UV slope-based calibrations over-predict $\dot{N}_{\rm ion,esc}$ for individual young galaxies by up to two orders of magnitude. Overall, the delayed duty cycle of LyC leakage must be accounted for when UV source counts are interpreted in the context of reionization.

conclusions: Feedback-driven time delays govern reionization: Efficient early feedback (e.g., hypernovae and high star-formation efficiency per free-fall time) rapidly clears low-density escape channels before massive stars die, completing reionization by $z \sim 8.5$ despite producing fewer UV-bright sources, whereas weaker feedback delays escape until ionizing production fades, ionizing only $\sim 33\%$ of the volume by $z \sim 8.5$.

Universal ISM sequence in UV-faint leakers: UV-faint galaxies exhibit a consistent physical progression with increasing escape fraction irrespective of feedback model, where intermediate-to-strong leakers ($1\% \le f_{\rm esc} \le 50\%$) feature post-starburst star formation histories shaped by photoionization and supernovae, while extreme leakers ($f_{\rm esc} \ge 50\%$) have evacuated their dense, cold neutral ISM.

$[\mathrm{O}\,{\rm II}]$ electron density as a robust $f_{\rm esc}$ tracer: The electron number density $n_e([\mathrm{O}\,{\rm II}])$ derived from the $[\mathrm{O}\,{\rm II}]\,\lambda\lambda 3727$ doublet traces local escape channel clearance, reliably identifying stronger LyC leakers via lower densities across all investigated feedback implementations.

UV-slope calibrations fail for young starbursts: Standard empirical calibrations of $f_{\rm esc}$ based on the UV continuum slope $\beta$ fail to account for the delayed duty cycle of LyC escape, overpredicting the escaping ionizing luminosity ($\dot{N}_{\rm ion,esc}$) of young galaxies ($\tau_* \lesssim 5\text{ Myr}$) by up to two orders of magnitude.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Anapole Dark Matter at LZ: Minimal, Elastic and Testable
papers.authors: Sourav Bera, Suvam Maharana, Poulami Mondal
papers.abstract: Majorana fermions can carry neither charge nor dipole moments, leaving the anapole moment as their leading electromagnetic interaction. A stable Majorana fermion is therefore a minimal realization of electromagnetically interacting dark matter. The momentum dependence of the anapole interaction produces a harder recoil spectrum than standard momentum-independent interactions. We show that this makes elastically scattering anapole dark matter a viable interpretation of the single high-energy nuclear-recoil event recorded by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, in a region where almost no background is expected. Curiously, the same coupling that fits the LZ data also yields the observed dark matter abundance at a mass of about 300 GeV, and is consistent with collider searches and indirect detection. The scenario is testable, predicting further events at lower energies, which the full LZ run will probe and a next-generation detector such as XLZD will decisively test.

conclusions: **Viable explanation for anomalous LZ event**: Elastic scattering via an electromagnetic anapole operator ($a_\chi \bar{\chi}\gamma^\mu\gamma^5\chi \partial^\nu F_{\mu\nu}$) enhances the high-energy recoil tail, fitting the $248\text{ keV}$ event and disfavoring the background-only hypothesis at $2.9\text{--}3.1\sigma$ local significance for $m_\chi \gtrsim 300\text{ GeV}$.

**Thermal relic coincidence**: The direct-detection best-fit coupling ($a_\chi \simeq 1.05 \times 10^{-6}\text{ GeV}^{-2}$ at $m_\chi \simeq 300\text{ GeV}$) independently yields the observed cosmological cold dark matter abundance ($\Omega_\chi h^2 \approx 0.12$) via standard early-Universe thermal freeze-out.

**Consistency with complementary bounds**: Because the $P$-odd anapole annihilation is $p$-wave suppressed ($\langle \sigma v \rangle \propto v^2$), indirect detection bounds from Fermi-LAT/H.E.S.S. are evaded, while remaining consistent with white dwarf heating constraints and ATLAS $139\text{ fb}^{-1}$ monojet search limits.

**Near-term testability**: The model predicts unobserved events in LZ's intermediate energy window ($250 \le \text{S1c} < 500\text{ phd}$), which can be probed at $2.6\text{--}3.2\sigma$ significance with the full $15.3\text{ t}\cdot\text{yr}$ LZ exposure and decisively confirmed or ruled out at $>9\sigma$ by the future $200\text{ t}\cdot\text{yr}$ XLZD detector.

For Majorana fermions (particles that act as their own antiparticles), charge and dipole moments are forbidden by symmetry, leaving the anapole moment—a velocity- and momentum-dependent electromagnetic coupling akin to a toroidal current—as their primary channel to interact with ordinary matter. By reconstructing the nuclear recoil spectrum and detector response within a non-relativistic effective field theory framework, the authors show that this momentum dependence naturally hardens the recoil spectrum, successfully accounting for the LZ event with $2.9\text{--}3.1\sigma$ local significance for masses $m_\chi \gtrsim 300\text{ GeV}$. Strikingly, the best-fit interaction strength simultaneously reproduces the observed cosmological dark matter relic density via standard thermal freeze-out while cleanly evading existing collider and astrophysical bounds. This provides a minimal, predictive dark matter benchmark that avoids fine-tuning and will be decisively tested by the complete LZ dataset and next-generation detectors like XLZD.

papers.title: Silent Heavy Fields: An Exclusion Rule for the Cosmological Collider
papers.authors: Shuntaro Aoki, Zhehan Qin, Masahide Yamaguchi, Yuhang Zhu
papers.abstract: The cosmological collider uses oscillatory signatures in primordial correlators to probe heavy fields during inflation. This probe has blind spots, as heavy fields can keep ticking in time while remaining silent in the correlators. In this letter, we derive an exclusion rule under which cosmological collider signals vanish. The rule covers two classes of diagrams where a de Sitter invariant heavy sector couples covariantly to a single external field at one vertex. We first prove it for exchanges mediated by the two-point function of the heavy sector to all loop orders, using a spectral decomposition followed by a field redefinition. The result then extends to one-loop polygons by matching their oscillatory contributions onto those of the first class. The approximate signals of previously studied processes that fall into these classes must therefore be revisited. As a nonvanishing example, we derive the leading signal of a triangle loop for the first time in a toy model motivated by chemical potentials.

conclusions: **Exclusion rule for cosmological colliders**: Oscillatory cosmological collider (CC) signals in the squeezed limit vanish to all loop orders for bulk two-point exchanges and to all orders in the soft expansion for one-loop $N$-gon diagrams, provided the heavy sector possesses de Sitter (dS) covariant dynamics and couples locally and covariantly to a single external field at the soft vertex.

**Mechanism**: Spectral decomposition maps bulk two-point exchanges to tree-level linear scalar mixings that can be eliminated via a local field redefinition; for $N$-gons, operator pinching in the soft limit maps the hard subgraph onto local operators, reducing the diagrams to auxiliary bubbles that inherit this vanishing result.

**Impact on existing literature**: Prior claims of non-vanishing signals in dS-invariant loop processes (such as $W/Z$ bubbles in the cosmological Higgs collider or neutrino loops in leptogenesis) were artifacts of expanding heavy-field propagators at late times at the soft vertex, where such expansions are invalid.

**Evading silence via chemical potentials**: Breaking dS boost symmetry via a chemical potential $\kappa$ restores the oscillatory signal; the authors present the first analytical calculation of a Whittaker triangle loop, finding the leading bispectrum amplitude scales as $\kappa^{-6}e^{6\pi\kappa}$ at large $\kappa$ and vanishes linearly as $\kappa \to 0$.

While massive fields oscillate in time, these temporal 'ticks' do not always translate into observable spatial oscillations in the final correlators. In this paper, the authors establish an 'exclusion rule' proving that cosmological collider signals strictly vanish for two wide classes of diagrams—arbitrary two-point bulk exchanges and one-loop polygons—whenever the heavy sector is de Sitter invariant and couples covariantly to a single external field. They show that earlier predictions of one-loop collider signals in these classes were mathematical artifacts of premature late-time expansions, and they demonstrate that generating a non-zero signal requires breaking de Sitter symmetry, deriving the first exact analytical result for a triangle loop with a chemical potential.

papers.abstract: The Euclid near-infrared processing function (NIR PF) converts the raw observations acquired by the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) into calibrated images and source-level products. Following the first implementation delivered with the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1), the NIR PF has been revised for the first major Euclid Data Release (DR1), with improvements to detector-level processing, calibration, image reconstruction, and quality control. The DR1 processing includes observations covering more than $1900\,\rm{deg}^2$ and has produced $71\,659$ calibrated near-infrared (NIR) images. We assess the performance of the processing chain through extensive astrometric and photometric validation. The astrometric solution reaches an average root-mean-square (RMS) of 10 mas, remaining below 20 mas for 99% of the dithers in all three NISP bands. Temporal variations in the instrumental throughput are typically corrected to a level of 2 mmag RMS, while the relative photometric accuracy reaches 0.9% for sources brighter than 19 mag in $Y_\mathrm{E}$, $J_\mathrm{E}$, and $H_\mathrm{E}$, and the residual spatial variations of the photometric calibration across the focal plane are at the level of approximately 10 mmag for the entire sample. Despite some remaining limitations, the DR1 NIR imaging products are consistent with the required astrometric and photometric performance over the large area covered by this release.

conclusions: **Survey Volume**: The DR1 pipeline processed over $1900\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ of sky, producing $71\,659$ science-ready near-infrared exposures across the $Y_\mathrm{E}$, $J_\mathrm{E}$, and $H_\mathrm{E}$ filters.

**Astrometric Precision**: The astrometric solution achieves an average root-mean-square (RMS) error of $10\,\mathrm{mas}$ (remaining below $20\,\mathrm{mas}$ for $99\%$ of exposures), ensuring precise multi-band source matching for photometric redshift determinations.

**Photometric Performance**: Relative photometric accuracy reaches $0.9\%$ for sources brighter than $19\,\mathrm{mag}$, spatial calibration variations across the focal plane are constrained to $\sim 10\,\mathrm{mmag}$, and temporal throughput variations (including ice deposition effects) are corrected to an RMS of $2\,\mathrm{mmag}$.

**Systematics & DR2 Priorities**: Remaining detector systematics—notably persistence trails from previous exposures (currently mitigated via a 5-hour history mask), readout $1/f$ stripes, and bright-star internal reflection arcs appearing in $\sim 3\%$ of images—are characterized to guide dedicated correction pipelines in DR2.

ai.summary: To measure cosmological parameters accurately from galaxy clustering and weak lensing, raw detector images from space telescopes must first be cleaned of instrumental artifacts, optical distortions, and detector memory effects. In this Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) paper, the collaboration presents the Near-Infrared Processing Function (NIR PF) pipeline, which processes raw exposures from the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) over $1900\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ into $71\,659$ calibrated images in the $Y_\mathrm{E}, J_\mathrm{E},$ and $H_\mathrm{E}$ bands. The authors implement improvements in background estimation, flat-fielding, throughput variations (such as ice accumulation on the mirrors), and masking of persistence (residual signal lingering in infrared detectors after bright exposures). This validation confirms that Euclid's first near-infrared data release meets its rigorous sub-percent photometric and milliarcsecond astrometric requirements for cosmological science.

papers.title: Machine-Learning Reconstruction of Intergalactic Medium Column-Density Maps from Observed Ly$α$ Emission Cubes
papers.authors: Xihan Deng, Christopher Martin, Aaron Smith, Sultan Hassan, Drew M. Miles, Nikolaus Z. Prusinski, Vincent Picouet, Mateusz Matuszewski, Zeren Lin, Jake S. Bennett
papers.abstract: Understanding the large-scale structure of the intergalactic medium (IGM) is essential for studying galaxy evolution, particularly at $z \sim 2$--$6$, when cold filaments in the cosmic web are considered a primary mechanism for fueling galaxy growth. At these redshifts, Ly$\alpha$ emission shifts into the optical regime and serves as the primary tracer of diffuse IGM for ground-based integral field units (IFUs). However, detections remain limited by low signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) and the complexities of resonant scattering. We present a proof-of-concept machine-learning framework to reconstruct IGM gas column-density maps from noisy Ly$\alpha$ IFU emission cubes. Using Keck Cosmic Web Imager (KCWI) observations of $z \sim 2.3$ protoclusters as a case study, we train a custom convolutional neural network (CNN), the Column Density Estimator (CDE), on a simulated dataset combining IllustrisTNG100 with simplified radiative-transfer calculations and an approximate treatment of KCWI noise. The CDE successfully reconstructs broad filamentary structures in the simulated test set under these adopted assumptions. Applied to observed KCWI data, the CDE predicts gas column-density maps containing filamentary structures extending over $\gtrsim 40''$ ($\sim 1$ comoving Mpc), consistent with an IGM interpretation. The observed reconstructions remain conditional on the adopted models. These results illustrate the potential of the CDE framework for connecting diffuse Ly$\alpha$ observations with simulations of the IGM.

conclusions: **Deep learning for IGM reconstruction:** The authors develop the Column Density Estimator (CDE), a convolutional neural network (CNN) that reconstructs 2D intergalactic medium (IGM) gas column-density maps directly from noisy 3D Lyman-$\alpha$ (Ly$\alpha$) integral field unit (IFU) data cubes, bypassing the complex analytical inversion of resonant radiative transfer.

**Simulated validation:** Trained on IllustrisTNG100 cosmological hydrodynamical simulation slices coupled with simplified Ly$\alpha$ radiative transfer and mock Keck Cosmic Web Imager (KCWI) noise, the network accurately recovers broad filamentary structures across the test set.

**Detection of $\sim 1\text{ cMpc}$ filaments:** When applied to real KCWI observations of $z \sim 2.3$ protoclusters, the CDE predicts coherent filamentary gas structures extending over $\gtrsim 40''$ (corresponding to $\sim 1$ comoving Mpc), consistent with physical expectations for cosmic web gas fueling galaxy evolution at cosmic noon.

**Model dependence:** Because the reconstructions are tied to the specific subgrid physics of IllustrisTNG and approximations in the radiative-transfer training set, the resulting column-density values remain model-dependent rather than absolute ab initio measurements.
