To tackle this, the authors introduce the Column Density Estimator (CDE), a convolutional neural network designed to reconstruct 2D gas column-density maps directly from noisy 3D Ly$\alpha$ IFU data cubes. The model is trained on IllustrisTNG100 cosmological hydrodynamical simulations post-processed with simplified Ly$\alpha$ radiative transfer and realistic noise tailored to the Keck Cosmic Web Imager (KCWI). When applied to real KCWI observations of $z \sim 2.3$ protoclusters, the CDE recovers coherent filamentary structures extending over $\gtrsim 40''$ ($\sim 1\text{ comoving Mpc}$). This demonstrates a promising proof of concept for using machine learning to bypass intractable radiative transfer inversions and directly image the cosmic web feeding high-redshift galaxies.

papers.abstract: Euclid is a European Space Agency mission mapping the extragalactic sky, aiming to provide the most-accurate 3D view of the Universe at optical and near-infrared wavelengths, by measuring the photometric redshifts of billions of galaxies. Within the Euclid Consortium, this task is executed by the PHZ Organisation Unit. PHZ takes as input the multi-wavelength photometry of Euclid and ground-based data, and returns as output the source classification, photometric redshifts for the Euclid core science (i.e., cosmology), and photometric redshifts plus physical parameters and absolute magnitudes for non-cosmological science. As part of the first Euclid Data Release (DR1), we describe the details of the DR1 pipeline for non-cosmological science, along with the released data products, and their validation. The non-cosmological science data products are obtained with NNPZ, a nearest-neighbour algorithm developed within PHZ that infers the properties of each target galaxy from its closest matches, in colour-magnitude space, within a reference sample of galaxies with known redshifts and physical parameters. We built this reference sample from Euclid observations of COSMOS, one of the Euclid Auxiliary Fields, labelling each galaxy with redshifts and physical parameters derived from the COSMOS2020 multi-wavelength photometry, consistently with the Euclid core-science results. Combined with the adjustments and priors required to generalise the results across the entire extragalactic sky, this approach yields high-quality and internally consistent data products. We tested the performance using both internal metrics and comparisons to ancillary data sets (e.g., COSMOS2020, 3D-HST, and DESI) and scaling relations (e.g., the star-forming main sequence); the results are in line with expectations and pre-DR1 simulations for both the Euclid Wide Survey and Euclid Deep Fields.

conclusions: **Empirical reference sample via NNPZ:** The Euclid DR1 non-cosmological pipeline uses the nearest-neighbour algorithm NNPZ trained directly on real Euclid observations of the COSMOS field matched to COSMOS2020, avoiding synthetic template mismatch and maintaining consistency with the core cosmology photo-$z$ run.

**High photo-$z$ accuracy:** For the Euclid Wide Survey (limiting magnitude $I_{\rm E} \sim 24.8$), the pipeline achieves a scatter of $\sigma_{\rm NMAD} = 0.021$ in the North and $0.027$ in the South, with outlier fractions of $3.7\%$ and $7.6\%$, significantly improving upon pre-flight synthetic template baselines.

**Physical parameter recovery:** Inferred stellar masses and star formation rates (SFR) reproduce the standard star-forming main sequence; comparisons against DESI $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ and $\mathrm{H}\beta$ spectroscopic measurements show an SFR dispersion of $\sigma_{\rm NMAD} \approx 0.5\,\mathrm{dex}$ with an outlier rate of $\sim 16\%$, reflecting the known limits of broad-band SED fitting.

**Massive catalog scale:** DR1 delivers validated photo-$z$ probability distributions and physical parameters for nearly 880 million detected sources across more than $1900\,\mathrm{deg}^2$, creating the largest homogeneous galaxy property catalog to date.

ai.summary: In wide-field imaging surveys like Euclid, measuring the distances (photometric redshifts, or photo-$z$) and physical properties (such as stellar mass and star formation rate) for hundreds of millions of galaxies is essential for mapping cosmic structures and galaxy evolution without expensive spectroscopic follow-up. This paper presents the Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) processing function for non-cosmological science developed by the Photometric Redshifts (PHZ) Organization Unit. Instead of matching broad-band colors solely to synthetic stellar population synthesis templates, the pipeline uses the nearest-neighbour algorithm NNPZ anchored to real Euclid observations of the COSMOS auxiliary field labeled with high-precision COSMOS2020 photometry. This approach produces an internally consistent, empirically validated catalog of galaxy physical properties and photo-$z$ probability distribution functions for nearly 880 million sources across $>1900\,\mathrm{deg}^2$.

papers.abstract: The Euclid mission is designed to address fundamental questions on the nature of dark energy and dark matter by mapping the extragalactic sky with a wide-area survey complemented by targeted deep observations. The required scientific performance places stringent demands on the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), which transforms raw telemetry into calibrated, validated, and scientifically exploitable products. The SGS is a distributed system comprising the Euclid Science Operations Centre, the Science Data Centres, Instrument Operation Teams, and supporting Organisation Units, within a common architectural and procedural framework. This paper presents the SGS as implemented for Data Release 1 (DR1), describing its organisation, architecture, processing functions, and operational model. We outline the main components of the SGS common infrastructure. A key element is the Euclid Archive System (EAS), the central metadata repository based on a common data model. It comprises a Distributed Storage System, providing scalable storage of data files across the Science Data Centres; a Data Processing System used by the pipelines to register and access files and their lineage; and a Science Archive, distributing validated data products. Processing is coordinated by a common orchestration framework based on the Infrastructure Abstraction Layer, providing workflow management and resource abstraction of distributed compute clusters. Software development, integration, and deployment are supported by the Common Development Environment. We describe daily operations, calibration, and quality control, followed by the DR1 production campaign, including processing flows, validation strategy, and computational and data volumes. This infrastructure enabled Euclid DR1, involving 35 million jobs across nine Science Data Centres and 6.7 million core-hours, demonstrating robustness and scalability of the SGS.

conclusions: **Demonstrated large-scale distributed processing**: The Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS) successfully coordinated the Data Release 1 (DR1) campaign across nine national Science Data Centres (SDCs), executing over 35 million jobs and logging 6.7 million core-hours.

**Petabyte-scale data management verified**: As of January 2026, the Distributed Storage System (DSS) manages over 80 million files encompassing 4.5 PB of data across SDCs, backed by 7.5 TB of central metadata tracking complete data lineage and provenance.

**Validated operational pipelines for future releases**: Automated daily processing, instrument calibration, and collaborative quality-control validation were proven robust and scalable, establishing the operational baseline for larger upcoming survey releases.

ai.summary: Transforming raw satellite telemetry into high-precision cosmological catalogs requires a massive, automated computing infrastructure capable of managing distributed storage, calibrating detector artifacts, and preserving full data provenance. In this paper, the Euclid Collaboration presents the architecture, operational framework, and performance of the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS) deployed for Data Release 1 (DR1). The authors detail the software and hardware ecosystem, notably the Euclid Archive System (EAS) metadata repository, the orchestration layers coordinating pipelines across nine national Science Data Centres, and the protocols for daily calibration and quality control. While technical rather than theoretical, this overview describes the data processing backbone that delivers the science-ready galaxy and weak lensing catalogs used by the cosmology working groups.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the methodology and results of the astrometric calibration applied to the Euclid Near-Infrared (NIR) images in the Euclid Data Release 1, focusing on the techniques used to model and correct instrumental distortions, as well as the assessment of calibration quality. This work details the calibration pipeline, including quality control tests, and the evaluation of astrometric residuals against the Gaia DR3 catalogue and internal consistency metrics based on data encompassing more than one year of Euclid operation: the achieved accuracy is 30 mas for 97% of the total area, thus exceeding the requirements for Data Release 1. For the remaining 3%, accuracy declines due to a persistence correction issue: a method to correct the issue is presented. Furthermore, we discuss the stability of the solution over time, its dependence on source properties and instrument configuration, and outline the improvements planned for future Euclid data releases to enhance the astrometric calibration accuracy and efficiency.

conclusions: Exceeding DR1 requirements: Across 4,000 observations spanning 1,950 deg² during Euclid's first year, the NISP NIR astrometric calibration achieves an average precision of ~10 mas (<0.1 detector pixels) with negligible systematic offset (<2 mas) relative to Gaia DR3, well within the 30 mas mission requirement.

Instrumental stability: Optical distortion patterns across the focal plane are stable over time within ~10 mas, showing minimal dependence on telescope rotation or time, and chromaticity effects remain negligible (<1 mas/mag).

Detector persistence mitigation: Image persistence—residual charge trapped in detector pixels after exposure to bright stars—led to excessive source masking and degraded accuracy (>30 mas) over <5% of the area (predominantly detectors DET13 and DET14); a refined intensity and radius flagging threshold successfully restores precision.

Multi-band and optical alignment: Cross-matching between different NISP near-infrared filters and the optical VIS instrument demonstrates high internal positional consistency across Euclid's focal plane.

ai.summary: For wide-field cosmological surveys like Euclid, accurate cosmological measurements (such as galaxy clustering and photometric redshifts) fundamentally rely on precise astrometry—mapping pixel coordinates on the detectors to true celestial coordinates on the sky. In this Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) paper, the collaboration presents the astrometric calibration pipeline for the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) imaging data over more than one year of operations (~1,950 deg²). Using the Gaia DR3 astrometric catalogue as a reference and the Scamp tool, the authors model optical distortions across dithers using polynomial representations and characterize residual positional errors across the focal plane. The calibration achieves an average precision of ~10 mas, surpassing the DR1 requirement of 30 mas across 97% of the survey area, and establishes a refined masking strategy to correct localized degradation caused by detector persistence artifacts (afterglows from bright sources).

papers.abstract: This paper reviews how Euclid's top-level calibration requirements were translated into a calibration plan, how this plan is implemented and maintained during the survey, and how it performs in the current DR1 release. We show that DR1 already meets or exceeds most end-of-mission spectrophotometric calibration requirements. The construction of spectroscopically complete and pure samples relies on ongoing data acquisition for the Euclid Deep Survey, while point-spread-function modelling and shear calibration are still converging to their stringent accuracy requirements. With all DR1 data reprocessed with the DR1 pipeline configuration, more subtle effects have been detected and characterised, and correction strategies have been developed for DR2. These include improved absolute flux calibration, astrometry, charge-persistence correction, shutter effects, wavelength calibration, and spectrophotometric corrections for water-ice contamination. Finally, synthetic photometric transformations between Euclid and each of Roman, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope, are presented.

conclusions: **Spectrophotometric requirements met early**: DR1 observations already meet or surpass the majority of Euclid's stringent end-of-mission spectrophotometric calibration benchmarks across both the VIS (optical) and NISP (near-infrared) instruments, ensuring dependable absolute and relative flux measurements.

**PSF modeling and shear calibration progression**: Point-spread-function (PSF) modeling and weak lensing shear calibration are steadily converging toward the extreme percent-level precision required to avoid biasing cosmic shear signals, forming the primary rationale for deferring full shape catalogues to later data releases.

**Empirical correction strategies for DR2**: Reprocessing of DR1 telemetry successfully identified and characterised secondary instrumental systematics—including optical water-ice condensation, near-infrared detector charge persistence, shutter timing variations, and astrometric distortions—providing proven mitigation recipes for the upcoming DR2 pipeline.

**Cross-mission photometric transformations**: Synthetic colour and flux transformations were derived between Euclid ($I_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, Y_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, J_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}, H_{\scriptscriptstyle\rm E}$) and complementary space observatories (Roman, JWST, and CSST), establishing a unified photometric framework for joint multi-survey cosmological analyses.

ai.summary: To constrain dark energy and modified gravity using cosmic shear and galaxy clustering, space telescopes must achieve unprecedented photometric and astrometric accuracy so that minute instrumental distortions are not mistaken for real cosmological signals. This paper presents the calibration framework and observational verification for Euclid's Data Release 1 (DR1), detailing how high-level survey requirements were translated into in-flight self-calibration strategies, deep-field monitoring sequences, and routine calibration observations. The authors demonstrate that DR1 already meets or exceeds most end-of-mission spectrophotometric calibration requirements, while detailing the ongoing refinement of point-spread function (PSF) modeling and shear calibration necessary for shape measurement catalogues. In addition, the paper characterises second-order instrument effects—such as water-ice accumulation on cold mirrors, detector charge persistence, and shutter timing—and derives synthetic photometric transformations connecting Euclid with Roman, JWST, and CSST to enable joint cosmological analyses.

papers.abstract: The Euclid mission was designed around the need for thermo-optical and mechanical stability, stray-light suppression, low outgassing, and precise guiding. After three years in space, a wealth of data is available to assess the performance in these areas. We review the L2 halo-orbit design and consumables budget. Solar stray-light gradually increases by 14\% per year and is consistent with meteoroid puncturing, but remains low overall. Data loss from high solar activity has declined notably since the maximum of the 25th Solar cycle passed. The thermodynamical response of the optical elements to a thermal step impulse follows sigmoidal growth curves, entering the asymptotic equilibration regime after 21--46 hours. Water-ice contamination has affected data from both instruments and requires continued monitoring; we review detection and decontamination methods, and Euclid's contamination history. High-precision measurements of the zodiacal background reveal, at eight sigma significance, the subtle modulation caused by the changing perspective on the dust distribution due to the L2 halo-orbit libration. These data also show that conservative pre-launch estimates overestimated the out-of-field stray-light by factors of 4 (H band) to 27 (I band). Telemetry data demonstrate excellent guiding, and enable highly significant detections of solar radiation pressure and of thermal-emission recoil from Euclid's unilluminated dark sides. Lastly, we present a list of 34 meteoroid impacts, discuss their mechanical and optical signatures, and derive a minimum detectable impactor mass of 5e-7 g.

conclusions: **Thermo-optical stability and stray light**: Residual stray light from insulation punctures grows by $\sim 14\%$ per year due to micrometeoroid damage, but out-of-field stray light across all optical and near-infrared bands is a factor of 4 to 27 better than conservative pre-launch requirements.

**Ice accumulation and mitigation**: Water-ice condensation on cold optics (such as fold mirror FoM3, which led to 300 $\mathrm{deg}^2$ of lost VIS data early on) has been brought under control using targeted in-flight thermal decontamination procedures.

**Guiding and consumables**: Cold-gas micro-propulsion and guiding telemetry show excellent tracking stability—sensitive enough to detect solar radiation pressure and asymmetric thermal recoil—with propellant reserves projected to last until 2040.

**Space environment at L2**: The spacecraft has weathered solar maximum storms and recorded 34 confirmed micrometeoroid impacts (rate of $\sim 1.5\ \mathrm{month}^{-1}$, sensitivity down to $5 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{g}$) with no lasting degradation to survey capabilities.

ai.summary: To execute high-precision weak lensing and galaxy clustering measurements, space observatories at the Sun-Earth second Lagrange point ($L_2$) must maintain sub-milliarcsecond pointing precision, extreme thermal stability, and pristine optical surfaces. This Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) technical paper reviews the spacecraft's operational performance and environmental response over its first three years in orbit, analyzing telemetry, thermal drifts, ice accumulation, and micrometeoroid impacts. The authors show that despite early operational hurdles—including stray-light leaks in thermal insulation, solar-flare X-ray penetration, and water-ice frost on optical elements—active mitigation strategies and thermal de-icing have preserved core survey capabilities, with background stray-light levels performing significantly better than pre-launch requirements.

papers.title: Satellite pairs in the Local Group: from spatial clustering to dynamical associations in observations and $Λ$CDM simulations
papers.authors: Mariana P. Júlio, Marcel S. Pawlowski, Noam I. Libeskind
papers.abstract: We investigate the incidence and physical nature of satellite galaxy pairs in the Local Group using updated observational data for the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31), together with analogues from the HESTIA constrained cosmological simulations. Our comparison uses three distinct simulated Local Group analogues drawn from the HESTIA suite, allowing us to assess the observed pair statistics against multiple cosmological realisations of the Local Group environment. We identify close nearest-neighbour associations by comparing the observed satellite distributions with isotropic populations that reproduce the radial distributions of each host, and investigate their physical nature using line-of-sight velocities, proper motions, and gravitational binding estimates. We find that the MW exhibits a significant excess of close satellite associations relative to isotropic expectations, with a pairing efficiency of $\sim53\%$, nearly twice that found in the simulated analogues ($\sim17$-$27\%$). This excess persists after applying a stellar mass cut ($M_\star > 10^4\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) to match the resolution limits of the simulations. In contrast, the M31 satellite system is broadly consistent with isotropy, with a pairing efficiency of $\sim28\%$. However, only a minority of pair candidates exhibit coherent kinematics or are likely to be gravitationally bound, indicating that most represent transient alignments or remnants of common group infall rather than long-lived binary satellites. These results suggest that the MW hosts an unusually rich population of phase-space-correlated satellites, likely reflecting its recent accretion history, whereas M31 is more consistent with typical $\Lambda$CDM expectations.

conclusions: **Milky Way spatial pair excess**: The Milky Way exhibits a high satellite nearest-neighbour pairing efficiency of $\sim 53\%$ (retaining $\sim 52\%$ after applying a completeness cut of $M_\star > 10^4\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$), roughly double the $\sim 17\text{--}27\%$ found in the HESTIA cosmological analogues, demonstrating significant spatial clustering over isotropic expectations.

**Contrast with Andromeda (M31)**: In contrast, M31's satellite system has a pairing efficiency of $\sim 28\%$, consistent with an isotropic distribution within distance uncertainties, highlighting that satellite clustering properties are host-specific and sensitive to stochastic accretion histories.

**Scarcity of gravitationally bound pairs**: Only $\sim 10\%$ of simulated HESTIA pairs and $\sim 38\text{--}43\%$ of observed MW candidate pairs satisfy mutual gravitational binding criteria ($b \equiv 2GM / (\Delta r \Delta v^2) \ge 1$), meaning relative kinetic energy dominates in the vast majority of associations.

**Transient remnants over long-lived binaries**: Requiring spatial proximity, velocity coherence, and gravitational binding simultaneously leaves only $\sim 19\text{--}29\%$ of MW pairs and $\sim 8\text{--}11\%$ of simulated pairs intact, demonstrating that most associations are unbound remnants of recent group infall (e.g., alongside the LMC) or chance alignments rather than long-lived binary dwarfs.

ai.summary: In hierarchical $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, satellite dwarf galaxies orbiting hosts like the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31) are expected to frequently fall in together in small groups before tidal forces gradually disperse them. To determine whether observed close pairs are gravitationally bound binaries or transient phase-space alignments, the authors compared 3D positions, line-of-sight velocities, and proper motions from the Local Volume Database against isotropic distributions and Local Group analogues from the HESTIA constrained cosmological hydrodynamical simulations. They find that the MW displays a marked excess of spatial pairs (pairing efficiency $\sim 53\%$) relative to both isotropic random draws and simulated analogues ($\sim 17\text{--}27\%$), whereas M31 remains broadly consistent with an isotropic population ($\sim 28\%$). Crucially, combining spatial proximity with full phase-space kinematics and gravitational binding estimates reveals that only a small fraction of candidate pairs are mutually bound, demonstrating that the MW's pair excess primarily reflects recent group accretion events (such as the Magellanic system) rather than stable, long-lived binary dwarfs.

papers.title: The astrometric precision of incoherent pulsar timing arrays
papers.authors: Anna C. Tsai, Dylan L. Jow, Ue-Li Pen
papers.abstract: We address the astrometric precision with which a pulsar timing array (PTA) can localize a single astrophysical gravitational-wave source, in the regime where pulsar distances are poorly constrained compared to the gravitational wavelength. Using simple matched-filter, map-making simulations, we calculate the astrometric precision of the intrinsic PTA residual response as a function of the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where the SNR is that of the source in the matched-filter map, and find that the median angular error decreases as $\sqrt{\ln 2/3}\,/[\mathrm{SNR}\sqrt{\ln\mathrm{SNR}}]$ over the relevant SNR range, with a pre-factor we derive from first principles. At an SNR of 6, this log term coming from the singular core of the convolution kernel produces an angular error approximately $1.4$ times smaller than for a Gaussian beam. We compare this sky-averaged maximum precision with the precision achieved across the sky by the pulsars of the International Pulsar Timing Array (IPTA) DR2. For a map with SNR of 6, the intrinsic array precision is $3.3^\circ$. For the IPTA configuration at the same SNR, the median precision over the sky is worse due to sparse sampling of the underlying pulsar residual response, approximately $8.9^\circ$; however, for sources in $14\%$ of the sky, the high local pulsar density yields a precision better than $3.3^\circ$.

conclusions: **Sharper SNR scaling from singular response**: The median astrometric error of an incoherent PTA scales as $\gamma_{\rm med} \approx \sqrt{\ln 2 / 3} \, / [\mathrm{SNR}\sqrt{\ln\mathrm{SNR}}] \approx 27.5^\circ / [\mathrm{SNR}\sqrt{\ln\mathrm{SNR}}]$; the logarithmic enhancement stems from the singular core of the quadrupolar response kernel, delivering an angular error $\approx 1.4$ times smaller at $\mathrm{SNR}=6$ than a conventional Gaussian beam ($1/\mathrm{SNR}$).

**Intrinsic array precision**: For an idealized, dense, uniform array (4800 pulsars), the intrinsic sky-averaged astrometric precision is $3.3^\circ$ at map $\mathrm{SNR}=6$ (equivalent to a $5.2\sigma$ peak detection, comparable to current PTA sensitivities).
**Realistic IPTA DR2 performance**: With the current, sparsely distributed pulsars in IPTA DR2, the sky-median precision degrades to $8.9^\circ$ at $\mathrm{SNR}=6$ due to non-uniform sky coverage.

**Sky-density trade-off**: In the $14\%$ of the sky where pulsar density is highest, IPTA DR2 outperforms the uniform limit ($< 3.3^\circ$), but this comes at the expense of substantially poorer localization across the remaining $86\%$ of the sky.

**Need for distance coherence**: Incoherent searches (Earth-term only) are fundamentally limited to degree-scale localization; reaching the sub-degree or arcminute precision required for host-galaxy identification will necessitate measuring pulsar distances to subparsec accuracy to model pulsar terms coherently.

ai.summary: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) detect nanohertz gravitational waves (GWs) from supermassive black hole binaries by measuring correlated pulse arrival times across Galactic millisecond pulsars, but because pulsar distances are typically known with uncertainties much larger than a nanohertz wavelength, current single-source searches must operate "incoherently" by utilizing only the Earth term. Treating PTAs as an imaging telescope, the authors derive the intrinsic astrometric precision—how accurately an incoherent PTA can localize an individual GW point source on the sky—using matched-filter map-making simulations across varying signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). They demonstrate analytically and numerically that the singular core of the quadrupolar response function yields a localization error that scales as $\propto 1/[\mathrm{SNR}\sqrt{\ln\mathrm{SNR}}]$, outperforming a standard Gaussian beam by a factor of roughly $1.4$ at an SNR of 6. While an idealized, uniform pulsar array achieves an intrinsic sky-averaged precision of $3.3^\circ$ at $\mathrm{SNR}=6$, the realistic, non-uniform IPTA DR2 array achieves a median precision of $8.9^\circ$ (though beating the uniform limit in the $14\%$ of the sky with the highest pulsar density). Ultimately, this work establishes the fundamental localization limits of incoherent PTAs and highlights that achieving the arcminute precision needed for host-galaxy identification will strictly require measuring precise pulsar distances to unlock coherent phase modeling.
